After the Cold War, NATO was reconceived as a “cooperative-security” organization whose mandate was to include two main objectives: to foster dialogue and cooperation with former adversaries in the Warsaw Pact and to “manage” conflicts in areas on the European periphery, such as the Balkans. In keeping with the first objective, NATO established the North Atlantic Cooperation Council (1991; later replaced by the Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council) to provide a forum for the exchange of views on political and security issues, as well as the enhance European security and stability through joint military training exercises with NATO and non-NATO states, including the former Soviet republics and allies. Special cooperative links were also set up with two PfP countries: Russia and Ukraine.
NATO in the former Yugoslavia and expansion into eastern Europe
The second objective entailed NATO’s first use of military force, when it entered the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1995 by staging air strikes against Bosnian Serb positions around the capital city of Sarajevo. The subsequent Dayton Accords, which were initialed by representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Republic of Croatia, and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, committed each state to respecting the others’ sovereignty and to settling disputes peacefully; it also laid the groundwork for stationing NATO peacekeeping troops in the region. A 60,000-strong Implementation Force (IFOR) was initially deployed, though a smaller contingent remained in Bosnia under a different name, the Stabilization Force (SFOR). In March 1999 NATO launched massive air strikes against Serbia in an attempt to force the Yugoslav government of Slobodan Milošević to accede to diplomatic provisions designed to protect the predominantly Muslim Albanian population in the province of Kosovo. Under the terms of a negotiated settlement to the fighting, NATO deployed a peacekeeping force called the Kosovo Force (KFOR).
The crisis over Kosovo and the ensuing war gave renewed impetus to efforts by the European Union (EU) to construct a new crisis-intervention force, which would make the EU less dependent on NATO and U.S. military resources for conflict management. These efforts prompted significant debates about whether enhancing the EU’s defensive capabilities would strengthen or weaken NATO. Simultaneously there was much discussion of the future of NATO in the post-Cold War era. Some observers argued that the alliance should be dissolved, noting that it was created to confront an enemy that no longer existed; others called for a broad expansion of NATO membership to include Russia. Most suggested alternative roles, including peacekeeping. By the start of the second decade of the 21st century, it appeared likely that the EU would not develop capabilities competitive with those of NATO or even seek to do so; as a result, earlier worries associated with the spectre of rivalry between the two Brussels-based organizations dissipated.
During the presidency of Bill Clinton (1993–2001), the United States led an initiative to enlarge NATO membership gradually to include some of the former Soviet allies. In the concurrent debate over enlargement, supporters of the initiative argued that NATO membership was the best way to begin the long process of integrating these states into regional political and economic institutions such as the EU. Some also feared future Russian aggression and suggested that NATO membership would guarantee freedom and security for the newly democratic regimes. Opponents pointed to the enormous cost of modernizing the military forces of new members; they also argued that enlargement, which Russia would regard as a provocation, would hinder democracy in that country and enhance the influence of hard-liners. Despite these disagreements, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and Poland joined NATO in 1999; Bulgaria, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Romania, Slovakia, and Slovenia were admitted in 2004 (these former Soviet and Warsaw Pact states later formed an extraordinary group known as the Bucharest Nine as a response to Russian aggression in the region). Albania and Croatia acceded to the alliance in 2009.
NATO relations with Russia in the post-September 11 world
Meanwhile, by the beginning of the 21st century, Russia and NATO had formed a strategic relationship. No longer considered NATO’s chief enemy, Russia cemented a new cooperative bond with NATO in 2001 to address such common concerns as international terrorism, nuclear nonproliferation, and arms control. This bond subsequently frayed, however, due to regional aggression by Russian Pres. Vladimir Putin. After Russia invaded Georgia in 2008, NATO strengthened ties with the latter country and established the NATO-Georgia Commission “to help Georgia achieve its goal of membership in NATO.” In 2014 pro-Russian Ukrainian Pres. Viktor Yanukovych fled months of popular protests, and Russia responded by invading the Ukrainian autonomous republic of Crimea. Russia illegally annexed Crimea and fomented uprisings in Ukraine’s Donbas region in an effort to reassert control over its neighbour. Ukraine checked the Russian-backed campaign in the Donbas, and NATO reaffirmed its support for Ukraine’s democratically elected government and its internationally recognized borders.
Events following the September 11 attacks in 2001 led to the forging of a new dynamic within the alliance, one that increasingly favoured the military engagement of members outside Europe, initially with a mission against Taliban forces in Afghanistan beginning in the summer of 2003 and subsequently with air operations against the regime of Muammar al-Qaddafi in Libya in early 2011. As a result of the increased tempo of military operations undertaken by the alliance, the long-standing issue of “burden sharing” was revived, with some officials warning that failure to share the costs of NATO operations more equitably would lead to unraveling of the alliance. At the time, however, most observers regarded that scenario as unlikely.
Later, the burden-sharing issue was raised once more by U.S. Pres. Donald Trump, who repeatedly criticized other NATO members for failing to devote a sufficient portion of their budgets to defense spending. Trump questioned the relevance of NATO and discussed withdrawing the United States from the alliance; even the suggestion of such an action was seen as a boon to Putin. However, Trump’s national security team moved to reassure allies that the U.S. remained committed to NATO, and, by the end of Trump’s term in 2021, the U.S. troop presence in Europe was almost entirely unchanged.
NATO and the Russian invasion of Ukraine
By the end of 2021, Russia had begun a massive military buildup along the Ukrainian frontier under the guise of joint maneuvers with the Belarusian army. In February 2022 there were as many as 190,000 Russian troops along the Russo-Ukrainian border, in Belarus, in Russian-occupied Crimea, and in the Russian-backed separatist enclave of Transdniestria in Moldova. On February 24 Putin announced the beginning of a “special military operation” and launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Although the Russians made some early gains, their advances soon stalled against a spirited Ukrainian defense.
Ukrainian Pres. Volodymyr Zelensky appealed to Western countries for military aid, and individual NATO members began a massive transfer of hardware to bolster the Ukrainian arsenal. The administration of U.S. Pres. Joe Biden took a leading role in marshaling the response to the greatest threat to European security since World War II. The speed and unity of NATO’s reaction to Russian aggression in Ukraine dramatically dispelled any doubts about the continued relevance of the alliance.
Sweden and Finland, two countries with a long history of neutrality, announced their intention to join NATO in the wake of the Russian invasion, and the U.S. deployed additional military assets to Poland and the Baltic states. In June 2022, at the first annual NATO summit since the invasion, NATO Secretary-General Jens Stoltenberg announced “the biggest overhaul of our collectivedeterrence and defense since the Cold War.” In addition to formally inviting Sweden and Finland to join the alliance, Stoltenberg declared that NATO’s rapid reaction force, a collection of air, sea, and land units maintained at a state of high readiness, would increase from 40,000 troops to more than 300,000. In April 2023 Finland became the 31st member of NATO, but Sweden’s accession was held up by objections from Turkey and Hungary until March 2024, when Sweden became the alliance’s 32nd member.

Qatari mediators held talks in Tehran for more than 12 hours on Friday in an effort to reach a deal to restart direct negotiations between the U.S. and Iran and avoid an outbreak of war after the midterms, according to diplomatic sources.
The discussions will continue in Doha, Qatar, on Saturday.
Why it matters: The U.S. is now just days away from a possible military operation that would inflict enormous damage on Iran and likely lead to retaliatory strikes against Israel and a host of Gulf countries.
Driving the news: A diplomatic source said Qatari mediators were in regular contact with the White House during Friday's daylong session.
"There was positive progress. Talks are still ongoing in an effort to unlock a deal between the U.S. and Iran," the source said.
The Qataris are prodding the U.S. and Iran to agree on a set of reciprocal steps that would be implemented over a few days and get the parties back to direct talks on the Iranian nuclear program and other issues.
A U.S. official said two competing demands have stymied the talks so far: the Trump administration's insistence that Iran make nuclear concessions as part of resuming talks, and Iran's stipulation that the U.S. first lift its naval blockade, release frozen funds and allow it to sell oil.
The Qataris are trying to convince Iran to allow U.N. inspectors to visit its bombed nuclear sites as a confidence-building measure that the U.S. would respond to with some sanctions relief.
The intrigue: Inside Trump's inner circle, there are different opinions on what he should do.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are highly skeptical that any nuclear agreement can be reached with the current Iranian regime. They think Trump's legacy should be to weaken the regime even more, including with further strikes, a U.S. official said.
The person said that while Vice President Vance and Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner want to resume negotiations, Trump is skeptical Iran will ever agree to a deal he finds acceptable.
"There are talks. They want to talk. They keep talking. ... We have time, frankly. It's a war, but it is not a typical war," Trump told reporters on Friday.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who is leading an economic pressure campaign dubbed "Operation Economic Outcast," is one of Trump's closest aides urging him to let the initiative play out rather than rush back into combat.
Zoom out: Countries in the region like Egypt, Turkey, Iraq, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have been urging Iran to agree to resume negotiations before the midterms, a regional source said.
One U.S. official said Trump might be more inclined to order a major military operation if Republicans lose badly in the midterms.
"If he feels embarrassed or disenfranchised he will do something bold. That's what everyone are telling the Iranians. Their best shot to get a deal is right now," the official said.
A White House official said the election results won't be a factor in Trump's decision-making about Iran.
The leaders of Saudi Arabia and Turkey urged Trump in recent days to allow more time for diplomacy.
At the same time, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is lobbying Trump to launch a joint operation against Iran immediately after the election.
The big picture: Renewed war could lead to massive destruction not only in Iran but in Gulf countries, exacerbating the global energy crisis.
Iran has vowed to respond to any U.S. strikes on its energy infrastructure by attacking oil and gas facilities in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Kuwait and Bahrain.
Any U.S. attack on Iran would be conducted jointly with Israel. Iran would likely retaliate with missile strikes, while Hezbollah could also wage attacks on Israel.

Hundreds of residents left the stricken town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine on Friday during a US-backed local ceasefire marking the most significant pause in fighting since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
Those who opted to head back to Ukrainian-controlled territory reached the city of Anapa, in Russia’s Krasnodar region, on Friday afternoon, according to a message published on Telegram by David Arakhamia, a member of Zelenskyy’s negotiating team. They will then be flown to Belarus before being transported back to Ukraine along with a Ukrainian delegation led by human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets.
Officials and volunteers were at pains to reassure residents that they would ultimately return to Ukraine despite the lengthy detour, which contrasts sharply with the 15-minute drive it took before the war to cross the Dnipro river and reach the city of Kherson.
“Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will be given the opportunity to do so safely. At the same time, those who decide to remain will be able to stay and will receive all the necessary humanitarian assistance,” Lubinets wrote on Telegram.
Fewer than 2,000 people are thought to remain in Oleshky, down from 24,000 before Russia captured the city in 2022. It came under fire from both sides after Ukraine retook Kherson on the other side of the Dnipro river, with Russian troops launching drones from Oleshky and Ukrainian forces firing back in an attempt to hit Russian supply lines. In 2023, the destruction of the Kakhovka dam by Russian forces flooded Oleshky, killing hundreds.
Conditions had deteriorated sharply over the past year, with drone strikes and mined roads cutting residents off from food and medical supplies, Ukrainian officials, volunteers and former residents told the FT. An international campaign and repeated appeals by Pope Leo XIV drew attention to their plight earlier this year.
The local ceasefire was reached in part through the Pope’s involvement as well as mediation efforts by US first lady Melania Trump as part of Washington’s renewed push to end the war in Ukraine.
Negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the US are due to resume peace talks in Abu Dhabi in early November after discussions were suspended in February following the outbreak of war in Iran.
With Donald Trump’s Republican Party facing midterm elections on Tuesday, the US president has stepped up pressure on Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he blamed for rising diesel prices.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has acknowledged that Ukraine over the past two weeks has largely refrained from striking Russian refineries, though attacks resumed on Friday morning. Russian deputy prime minister Alexander Novak claimed that three refineries and one chemical plant had been attacked. Ukrainian drone manufacturer Fire Point said on Friday that Russia’s Novokuybyshevsk refinery had been targeted overnight in Samara region. Social media footage showed the facility in flames.
Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said Kyiv’s actions were going against Trump’s demands.
Ahead of the Oleshky evacuation, Russia and Ukraine observed a local truce for three days in which Russian forces demined the main road heading to Oleshky. Both sides said they had not registered any ceasefire violations, an unprecedented occurrence since 2022.
The ceasefire also held in the city of Kherson, just 6km across the Dnipro river from Oleshky. Russian forces captured Kherson in March 2022 but were driven out later that year. Its remaining 64,000 residents — barely a quarter of the prewar population — have since endured relentless Russian drone attacks launched from the opposite bank, often deliberately targeting civilians.
Since the ceasefire began on Tuesday, residents in Kherson have ventured back on to the streets and driven their cars without the constant threat of drone strikes that has hung over the city for the past three years.
The sudden silence has left many bewildered. “It really feels as if that terror, when just going out on the street is scary, never happened,” one Kherson resident told the FT via text. Scores of people travelled to the “red zone”, the riverside area most exposed to Russian drone and artillery attacks, to check on their properties.
The truce remained strictly limited to Kherson and Oleshky, however.
On Thursday, a Russian jet-powered drone hit a railway platform in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro, killing 14 people. Five people, including two teenage girls, also died on Thursday from strikes in Kremenchuk in central Ukraine and in the northern city of Chernihiv.
A wave of ballistic missiles also hit Kyiv on Thursday evening, with Ukraine’s air force reporting that it had not succeeded in intercepting any of them.
Writing on X, Zelenskyy denounced the attacks as “deliberate strikes against civilians, brazen in their cruelty, and the Russians are carrying them out right as the humanitarian operation in Oleshky is unfolding”.

articles.title: SafePay Ransomware Breached Over 600 Critical Infrastructure Organizations, CISA Warns - CPO Magazine

The SafePay ransomware group has targeted more than 600 critical infrastructure organizations worldwide since 2024, according to a joint advisory by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and partner agencies.
The FBI, CISA, United States Secret Service (USSS), Germany’s Landeskriminalamt Rheinland-Pfalz, the United Kingdom’s National Crime Agency, and the United Kingdom’s North West Regional Organised Crime Unit jointly authored the report.
The joint security advisory ranked SafePay ransomware among the most active in 2026, with victims spread worldwide, from the Americas to Europe and Australia.
It listed the group’s tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) and indicators of compromise (IOCs) and advised network defenders to implement the recommended mitigations.
SafePay ransomware targets over 600 critical infrastructure organizations
CISA and partner agencies warned that SafePay ransomware has compromised over 600 critical infrastructure organizations across North America, South America, Europe, and Australia.
“Since SafePay first came onto the scene in 2024, it’s added 595 victims to its data leak site,” said Rebecca Moody, Head of Data Research at Comparitech. “The 595 added to its site are likely companies that haven’t met its ransom demands, meaning there are probably many more that have paid the gang to either have their systems decrypted or their stolen data deleted. The fact that CISA has seen over 600 attacks across critical infrastructure sectors alone only adds to this likelihood.”
“Of the 595 victims we’ve logged through our tracker, 94 of these attacks have been confirmed by the entity involved. Data breach notifications issued in these confirmed attacks have seen nearly 20 million individual records affected,” noted Moody. “Key targets for the group include healthcare (47 attack claims in total), manufacturers (97 attack claims in total), retailers (47 attack claims in total), and government organizations (31 attack claims in total).”
SafePay ransomware employs tactics to gain initial access, including brute-forcing passwords, using compromised credentials, compromising VPNs, and exploiting security vulnerabilities.
The exploited security flaws include information disclosure, authentication bypass, missing authentication for critical functions, deserialization of untrusted data, and improper access control vulnerabilities: CVE-2020-3259, CVE-2023-20269, CVE-2023-27532, CVE-2024-40711, and CVE-2024-40766, respectively. While the security advisory lists SafePay TTPs, other ransomware groups such as Akira employ similar tactics.
“SafePay hit at least 600 organizations without a single zero-day,” said Jacob Krell, Senior Director: Secure AI Solutions & Cybersecurity, Suzu Labs. “The joint advisory from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) lists five vulnerabilities used for initial access, the newest published in September 2024, the oldest patched more than six years ago. Six hundred critical infrastructure organizations had years of free scanner coverage and Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog entries for every one of these flaws, and still never got the window to apply them.”
After gaining access, SafePay employs living off the land (LOTL) techniques by leveraging legitimate Windows administrative tools to escalate privileges, traverse laterally, gain persistence, and exfiltrate data. SafePay ransomware uses FileZilla, 7-Zip, RClone, and WinRAR to compress data and WinSCP and RClone to exfiltrate data.
“Once inside the network, SafePay actors establish control by creating new accounts or taking over existing ones,” the agencies wrote. “They then use legitimate system tools to move through the network, identify valuable files, and disable security protections to avoid detection.”
The group also disables security software and changes privileged users’ passwords to lock them out of the system, preventing any containment measures.
The ransomware group also uses AnyDesk and TeamViewer to maintain persistence, halt the Volume Shadow Copy Service to stop backups, and reset Network Attached Storage to prevent recovery efforts.
“SafePay actors may disrupt recovery operations by deleting shadow copies and resetting network-attached storage devices containing backups,” the agencies warned.
The last step involves encrypting the victim’s files and dropping a ransom note demanding payment in cryptocurrency. According to the cybersecurity advisory, SafePay is a double-extortion ransomware group that threatens to leak stolen data online to force victims to pay. It contacts the victim organization through a representative to negotiate, and lists organizations that refuse to pay on a dark web leak site.
However, the FBI warns that paying the ransom does not guarantee recovery of the encrypted files and urges impacted critical infrastructure organizations to report extortion attempts.
“This particular attack is interesting for two pretty mundane reasons,” said John Strand, Owner, Black Hills Information Security. “First, they’re going after municipalities and critical infrastructure because, as we keep finding out, these organizations will pay. Look at how many people are affected when services go down. Add the political pressure to get those services restored, and attackers see a good chance of getting paid.”
CISA’s guidelines on defending critical infrastructure against SafePay ransomware
The authoring agencies advised network defenders to limit the threat actor’s activity by restricting administrative privileges to necessary users, implementing multi-factor authentication, protecting credentials, and implementing security controls.
They also advised network defenders to update and harden VPNs, firewalls, and other edge devices to prevent the threat actor from gaining access and maintaining persistence.
Once compromised, critical infrastructure organizations should act quickly by isolating compromised hosts and beginning threat hunting.

articles.title: UK brings forward defense spending target, pledging billions to Ukraine - CNBC
articles.summary: UK brings forward defense spending target, pledging billions to Ukraine  CNBC
articles.full_text:
The U.K. has set out a target date for defense spending to rise to 3% of GDP, as the finance minister announced billions in aid for Ukraine in a “clear message to Moscow”.
John Healey on Wednesday set a target date of 2030 for the 3% figure, while reaffirming its NATO commitment to reach 3.5% by 2035.
Healey, who resigned as defense minister under the previous government over insufficient spending, presented his first annual budget as finance minister and highlighted a “new era of threat”.
“Today we send a clear message to Moscow: Britain will stand with Ukraine for as long as it takes,” he said as he announced an additional £10 billion ($13.3 billion) in economic and military support, based on loans, export finance guarantees, as well as £500 million in urgent military funding for this winter.
The government will set out the details of how it will meet its defense spending targets at the spending review next year, Healey told lawmakers.
“As we look ahead to the spending review, we start from a position of strength, with spending at that higher base, there will be choices we have to make about priorities,” he said.
“Today, I’m getting work underway to get there in a fiscally sustainable way,” Healey said against the backdrop of strained public finances and increasing borrowing costs.
Healey also said the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank will deploy up to £5 billion over the next four years into defence, dual-use technologies and other sectors supporting national security to strengthen the UK defense industrial base, support domestic supply chains and attract private investment.
Chris Beauchamp, chief UK market analyst at investing and trading platform IG, said Healey’s announcement lacked detail but “it looks like defence will get the money Healey said was needed when he was defence secretary.”
“The precise path will come through next year, but it seems like the spending bonanza for Rolls-Royce and others is still on the way. It just might take a little while to arrive,” he added.
Healey also announced that Rolls-Royce will develop its next-generation turbine engine technology in partnership with the U.K. government, in an investment worth £2.5 billion.

Senator Chris Murphy says he has been briefed on the US's plan to restart the war on Iran, calling it "insane" and saying it would lead to a "devastating escalation".
"You've heard a preview that it would be a short-duration plan. I'll just say this: their plan is insane," Murphy said, speaking at an event organised by the Middle East Institute in Washington, DC, on Wednesday.
"It will lead to devastating escalation and the likely destruction of our commitment to the rule of law."
Murphy, a member of the Senate Foreign Relations and Appropriations committees, made the comments after American media reported on Wednesday that the US warned several Gulf Arab countries to be prepared for a short, intense military offensive against Iran after the US midterm elections on 3 November.
The warning sent by diplomatic and military channels is the latest indication that the US and Israel are preparing to launch another round of attacks against Iran, in an effort to weaken Tehran and force it to negotiations, according to a report in The Wall Street Journal.
"There's been open reporting as to what we may be planning and the civilian infrastructure we may be targeting," Murphy said.
"They've been asked by the president to develop a plan - whether they believe it will work or not, I do not know. But the plan that they have developed will lead, in my view, to a prolongment and an escalation of this war that will be devastating for our security interests.
"We are seeing the president ready another devastating military campaign after the election, just as illegal as the first iteration was at the time, where Americans are fed up with this war."
'The plan that they have developed will lead, in my view, to a prolongment and an escalation of this war that will be devastating for our security interests'
- Senator Chris Murphy
Murphy spoke at the Middle East Institute about his trip to Qatar and Saudi Arabia earlier this month, assessing the war's impact on the region.
He is the first Democratic senator to visit the region since the US-Israeli war on Iran began on 28 February. Murphy met with leaders including Qatar's emir, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
The WSJ reported that US forces have been restocking their munitions in the region, and bomber aircraft and jet fighters are preparing for attacks, according to officials.
It also reported that the US military is moving a Patriot missile defence system from Texas to Israel to support defences, according to flight-tracking data and two officials. The Patriot system includes radar equipment, missile launchers and interceptor missiles.
Next month, an aircraft carrier strike group and a Marine expeditionary unit will also join around 20 other warships operating in the Middle East, the report said.
Last week, the US press also reported that US troops and diplomats have been evacuating posts in the Middle East.
NBC News reported that the State Department ordered a further reduction in staff at diplomatic posts in the region.
'A cover-up'
Murphy said during his trip that he was part of a number of classified briefings and spoke to military leadership about the damage and "the reality" there.
"Our base in Bahrain is obliterated; it is not usable, and our base in Qatar is usable but at a much lower level capacity, and it is pretty clear that we still don't have the ability to protect any of our diplomats or our troops... right now," he said.
Murphy added that he saw first-hand the US's "cover-up" in hiding the cost of war.
"The trip was incredibly valuable, not just to get a sense of how rattled the entire region is, but to really see first-hand a cover-up that is underway, a dizzying and coordinated attempt to try to hide from the American people and from Congress the costs and the consequences of this war," he said.
"It's like nothing I've ever seen in my now 20 years in the United States Congress."
The Pentagon told Congress last week that the US-Israeli war on Iran, now in its eighth month, had cost the US $47.1bn through 16 October, a rise from the previous $37.5bn cited by US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. Bombs, missiles and other types of ammunition made up over 60 percent of the total costs.
US President Donald Trump hasn't made a final decision yet, but is inclined towards launching a major attack that could target Iranian infrastructure and nuclear sites, according to several reports.
"We may do another little Epic Fury," Trump said at a rally in Florida last week, using the US military's term for its war on Iran.

Strikes and rallies are planned over rising living cost and the shift of public funds to arms. Unions are demanding wage increases in line with inflation; while dockworkers in 17 countries are mobilising against the war.
Strikes are planned across Italy on Friday, with widespread disruption expected as trade union Unione Sindacale di Base called on both public and private sector workers to strike, mobilise and protest, including at a major demonstration in Rome.
Renewed student protests are also expected to return to the street in major cities across Italy.
Meanwhile, the Cobas unions, together with Adl, Clap and Sial, have also called for a general strike across the public and private sectors, excluding transport.
The strike will also be a new test for public order, as students are set to return to the streets in all the main cities across Italy.
Friday's protests are directed against the rising cost of living, which unions say makes it increasingly difficult for people to cover essential expenses, as well as military spending.
Rail services are expected to be disrupted from 21:00 on Thursday until 20:59 on Friday, while the strike in air transport is expected to last for the entirety of Friday.
In local public transport, the impact will vary from city to city. The strike is also expected to affect taxi services throughout Friday, while motorway staff will begin their strike in the evening on Thursday.
Also on Friday, dock workers will mobilise globally against arms trafficking, rearmament policies and the militarisation of ports.
The action has been organised by several unions, including USB in Italy, the CGT in France and other trade union organisations in Greece, Turkey, Morocco and the Basque Country.
According to the organisers, workers from more than 100 ports in 17 countries and four continents have joined the mobilisation.
In Italy the protests will affect, among others, the ports of Genoa, Livorno, Trieste, Civitavecchia, Ancona, Ravenna and Gioia Tauro.
What are unions demanding?
Among USB's key demands is for wages to rise in line with the cost of living, including through the reintroduction of the "scala mobile", a mechanism previously used to automatically adjust wages in line with inflation.
The union is also calling for measures to bring down the costs of essential goods, household bills and rents, and for a reduction in VAT on basic necessities.
According to USB, the government is allocating too many resources to military spending, while funding for health care, education and other public services remains inadequate.

articles.title: Democratic senator blames Egypt press crackdown on US military aid decision - BBC
articles.summary: Democratic senator blames Egypt press crackdown on US military aid decision  BBCEgypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr  The GuardianEgyptian Court Orders News Site Closed as Critics Warn of a Crackdown  The New York TimesCourt orders closure of one of Egypt’s last independent media outlets  NBC NewsEgypt’s crackdown on press draws criticism on Capitol Hill  The Washington Post
articles.full_text:
A top Democratic senator has blamed a crackdown on independent journalism in Egypt on a decision by the Trump administration to waive human rights conditions on US military funding to the country.
Chris Murphy, who sits on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, accused the US government of "abandoning" the Egyptian people after it lifted restrictions relating to more than $300m of defence assistance.
Over the last month a series of arrests has taken place of journalists at two of the few remaining independent news outlets in Egypt, where newspapers and TV stations are closely controlled by the authorities.
The US State Department told the BBC it waived conditions on a portion of military aid to Egypt in September due to the country's "importance to US national security interests".
Murphy, speaking at the Middle East Institute (MEI) in Washington this week, said he was in no doubt the two were linked.
"The minute that money was released, the crackdown began in an absolutely devastating way," he said.
On Tuesday a court in Cairo ordered the closure of the news website Madr Masa and fined its editor-in-chief Lina Attalah in what Amnesty International called "a crushing blow to press freedom".
Earlier this month, authorities arrested six journalists at the independent fact-checking platform Matsda2sh and charged them with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
The Egyptian Embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment.
Cairo has remained a close regional ally of the US despite what human rights groups say are widespread abuses under President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi's government, including torture and enforced disappearances.
Sisi denies there are political prisoners in Egypt. He has previously said stability and security are paramount, adding authorities have promoted rights by trying to provide basic needs such as jobs and housing.
Washington sends Egypt £1.3bn ($1.73bn) per year, making it one of the world's biggest recipients of US military assistance.
US law allows up to £320m of the funding to be withheld, conditioned on Egypt meeting democracy and human rights requirements. But these restrictions can be waived by the administration on national security grounds.
In September, Secretary of State Marco Rubio waived human rights conditions on $320m of military aid in light of Egypt's role since the launch of the US war with Iran, according to a letter addressed to various Congressional committees. Egypt assisted negotiations between the US and Iran.
Exercising the waiver authority was "essential" for the US-Egypt relationship, "particularly in light of Egypt's helpful role following Operation Epic Fury," according to the September 4 memo seen by Reuters which bore Rubio's signature.
Asked by the BBC about the move in light of this month's arrests of journalists, the State Department said the waiver was "due to Egypt's importance to US national security interests, the concrete security cooperation Egypt provides to the United States, and the need to maintain that cooperation to address regional security challenges".
It added it maintained dialogue with Cairo on a "full range of issues" but would "not comment on private diplomatic conversations".
Rubio's move followed a similar decision by the Biden administration in 2024, when then Secretary of State Anthony Blinken waived human rights conditions to grant the full military aid allocation to Egypt as the US sought Cairo's role in mediating between Israel and Hamas in the war in Gaza.
Under Biden prior to 2024, the US withheld portions of the annual military allocation over Egypt's human rights record.
Murphy, who chairs a congressional committee on the Middle East and counterterrorism, said he had been a critic of both the Biden and Trump administrations over the issue.
"To the extent that there was any glimmer left of political speech in Egypt, it is gone for one proximate reason: The United States government abandoned the people of Egypt and decided to remove all conditions on our funding," Murphy told the MEI.
"Any hope of a true, meaningful political opposition rebirthing in Egypt has been shattered by this decision," he added.
US military aid to Cairo began after the 1978 Camp David Accords and the peace treaty that followed between Egypt and Israel. Successive administrations have viewed the world's most populous Arab country as a critical US ally in the region.
The group Reporters Without Borders describes Egypt as one of the world's biggest jailers of journalists.
The conviction of Lina Attalah and the closure of Madr Masr marked an unprecedented escalation in repression of press freedoms in Egypt, according to Timothy E Kaldas, Deputy Director of The Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, a Washington DC-based think tank.
He said both the US and European Union had been prioritising their strategic relations with Egypt over human rights and the rule of law in the country.
"It's been fostering a sense of impunity on the part of the Egyptian authorities that we're seeing play out," he told the BBC.
"Egypt is getting signals from both sides of the Atlantic that human rights and the rule of law are no longer a priority, and they're testing the limits of that."
He added: "The fact that they're not getting more robust pushback reinforces the wrong message."

articles.title: Only the Gulf Can End the Iran War
articles.summary: The Arab monarchies must help Washington and Tehran save face.
articles.full_text:
For everyone involved, the war in Iran has been a strategic failure. The United States and Israel have shown that they can achieve a few military objectives, such as sinking Iran’s navy. But after eight months of fighting and pressure, they have also proved that they cannot forcibly realize their main ambitions, including regime change, destroying Iran’s nuclear program, or even reopening the Strait of Hormuz—a waterway that was not closed when the war began. The Islamic Republic, for its part, has demonstrated that it can survive intense bombings. Yet it cannot break the American military’s economically suffocating blockade and has thus far failed to achieve its goal of putting an end to indefinite threats of war against Iran.
In theory, the war’s descent into a painful stalemate should open the door to diplomatic outcomes. But both sides have proved incapable of making the concessions necessary to strike a deal. Instead, they appear to prefer a mutually destructive status quo that maintains the delusion of achievable victory and which they can justify with the continued pain they inflict on their adversaries. As a result, rather than moving toward a settlement, both sides are threatening renewed attacks.
But there is a face-saving way for Iran and the United States to extricate themselves from this conflict: a cease-fire brokered and managed by the Gulf Arab states. The deal would begin with Gulf countries providing economic relief to Iran in exchange for Iran lifting its restrictions on the Strait of Hormuz. This would, in turn, allow the United States to lift its own blockade. The Gulf states would also need to commit to taking steps to deter Washington from resuming strikes on Iran in the future. But neither the United States nor Iran would need to make direct concessions to the other, and each would avoid the most painful compromises. The United States, for example, would not have to lift its “maximum pressure” campaign, and Iran would not have to agree to limit its nuclear program. Gulf states could then use their leverage to sustain the cease-fire until conditions permit a more comprehensive agreement.
Serving as the guarantor of a cease-fire comes with real costs and risks for the Gulf, but its countries have good reason to accept them. They are part of the battlefield on which the Iran war is being fought, and should the conflict continue indefinitely, it could pose a threat to the very economic and political models on which they are built. The Gulf depends on oil and gas exports to sustain itself, and there is no way it can completely bypass the Strait of Hormuz in shipping its energy resources abroad. Its efforts to diversify away from hydrocarbons, meanwhile, are also vulnerable to renewed attacks from Iran.
Securing a cease-fire will not be easy. It requires that the Gulf countries overcome their own lack of cohesion, that Iran prioritize economic recovery and forgo explicit guarantees about U.S. behavior, and that the United States gives Gulf countries the space necessary to reach a deal. Even if successful, the resulting agreement will not address the underlying issues driving the war. But with scant alternatives on the horizon, it is the best—and perhaps the only—way to ease the pain for everyone.
SAVING FACE
In theory, a U.S.-Iranian agreement should be straightforward. There is a historical template for deals between Iran and the United States—Tehran agrees to constrain or give up a specific behavior, and Washington agrees to give it money and recognition—that could apply neatly to the current conflict. In the Algiers Accords of 1981, for instance, Iran agreed to release American diplomats it held hostage in exchange for frozen funds and a commitment by the United States not to intervene in Iran’s internal affairs. In the 2015 nuclear deal, Tehran accepted strict limits on its nuclear program in return for sanctions relief and an implicit acceptance of its right to enrich uranium. Today, Iran could stop impeding maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz (and perhaps eventually make concessions on its nuclear program), and Washington could grant it some combination of sanctions relief, cash, and acknowledgment of Tehran having a formal role in the waterway.
In practice, however, reaching this understanding will be extremely difficult. One reason is technical: Iran won’t make the nuclear concessions that U.S. President Donald Trump wants, and the United States will not provide the upfront, irreversible financial incentives that Tehran demands. But the bigger problem is reputational. To justify his quixotic war and decision to withdraw from the 2015 nuclear deal, Trump wants sweeping concessions from Tehran. Iran, for its part, is loath to settle for fewer benefits than it received from the United States in their ill-fated June memorandum of understanding, in which Washington pledged significant relief. As a result, both sides feel compelled to sustain the confrontation, even though doing so is mutually detrimental.
The Gulf states cannot resolve the dispute over Iran’s nuclear program. But they can bring about relative peace by helping address other essential issues. The United States may not be willing to pay Iran for merely opening the Strait of Hormuz, but its Gulf partners have the wealth and the motivation to offer the regime immediate economic concessions. Those partners could, for instance, give Iran some form of humanitarian and reconstruction funding. Iran, in turn, would stop attacks on ships transiting the strait and on Gulf states themselves. In response to Iran ceasing its attacks on commerce, the United States would lift its own blockade, and the Gulf states and Iran would establish a temporary deconfliction mechanism for shipping that acknowledges Iran’s role in the waterway without establishing unacceptable precedents for international commerce. This mechanism could require that ships use Iran’s preferred traffic pattern but would not formalize Iranian control over the passage.
This particular arrangement would not resolve Iran’s other core objective—prohibiting the United States and Israel from launching a renewed military campaign. This concern is harder to address. The United States may lack a credible military endgame, and the war might be unpopular domestically, but that has not stopped an erratic Trump from drawing up plans for renewed military action. But the Gulf states can provide Iran with assurances that they would use their leverage with Washington to help deter future attacks. For example, in May, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia temporarily paused U.S. access, basing, and overflight—the approvals that allow the United States military to use Gulf countries’ territory and airspace—because of concerns about the United States’ plans for escorting merchant ships through the Strait of Hormuz. The tactic worked: the United States paused the operation.
 The Gulf states will need to improve internal cohesion.
The United States might bristle at handing Iran negotiations over to the Gulf countries. But ultimately, U.S. officials should be able to spin this deal as a win. Trump, for instance, could exit the war while telling Americans that he saved the world from high energy prices without making the kind of economic and nuclear concessions to Iran that the Obama administration did under the 2015 agreement. He could likewise boast about the steps he took to weaken Iran, and, in the absence of a nuclear deal, point out that his self-proclaimed “maximum pressure” sanctions remain in place. In fact, in some ways, a Gulf-brokered deal is exactly the kind of “America first” foreign policy Trump promised. It would let the region take on the burden of managing a bad actor, including responsibility for providing most of the necessary concessions. Trump would have stumbled into the outcome. But he would still leave office with an empowered set of allies more capable of managing their own security.
Iran, for its part, would not only get significant economic benefits. It might also advance its goal of reducing the United States’ influence in the region. After all, if Israel or the United States undermines an arrangement down the road, it will only accelerate the decline of Washington’s credibility and influence with its Gulf partners. The United States has already placed its relationship with these countries under stress by going to war with Iran, something they did not ask for and for which all have suffered serious consequences. A Gulf state deal would thus allow Tehran to leverage any future U.S. military campaigns against Iran to further drive a wedge between the United States and its regional partners.
Iran has repeatedly made clear that its top war-related priority is to end the war on terms that reduce the likelihood of a future conflict. To some extent, Iran has already achieved this benchmark with the pain it has inflicted on the global economy. Assuming this war eventually ends, the next time an Israeli prime minister asks an American president to approve an attack on Iran, that president will have to weigh global economic instability against Israeli security interests. The threat posed by Iran, in the absence of a nuclear breakout or massive terrorist attack, may not outweigh the risk to the global economy. Israel might act independently of the United States, but doing so would risk further damaging the U.S.-Israeli relationship and invite Iranian retaliation without American protection.
But this deterrent is effective only once the current iteration of the war ends. If the war continues, Iran will forfeit the future de facto security guarantee that the Strait of Hormuz and geography provide. The longer this conflict goes on, the more it favors those in Israel or the United States advocating for regime change or endless war. articles.title: Don’t Go Backward on China Policy
articles.summary: The folly of a hawkish restoration.
articles.full_text:
Nearly halfway through his second term in office, U.S. President Donald Trump has undercut both the United States’ capacity to protect its interests related to China and its role as a provider of regional security in Asia. His undisciplined approach to dealing with Beijing, in which he has focused on building warm personal ties with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and discounted or ignored long-standing sources of tension between the two countries, has reduced Washington’s leverage to shape the relationship. At the same time, Trump’s sustained attacks on allies and partners have driven them to hedge against the United States and strengthen their ties with China. Beijing, in turn, has successfully cast itself as a steady counterweight to an erratic Washington: in 25 of 36 countries that the Pew Research Center surveyed in the spring of 2026—among them Australia, Canada, France, Germany, and Mexico—more respondents had a favorable view of China than of the United States.
Given the failures of Trump’s second-term strategy, many Democrats and even moderate Republicans may try to strike more hawkish postures on China after the midterm elections and during the 2028 presidential campaign. This temptation is understandable: there is a strong desire to provide a contrast to a flailing approach and correct what Trump has gotten wrong. But succumbing to it would be dangerous. If Congress and future presidential candidates reflexively adopt a more aggressive stance toward China, they could both undercut a future administration’s capacity to preserve vital diplomatic space with Beijing and further disquiet allies and partners that do not want to be trapped in a new twilight struggle. Overcorrecting Trump’s China policy would also be unlikely to help candidates get elected or boost their public profile in the run-up to 2028. Recent polling shows that only a small share of Americans in seven battleground states view China as an enemy or consider it to be one of the top threats to U.S. security.
The goal for the next Congress and, eventually, Trump’s successor, should be to prioritize steady competence over performative toughness in dealing with China. Political point scoring and wistful nostalgia for strategies that discount Beijing’s mounting power, and growing domestic support in the United States for great-power calm, would compound Trump’s mistakes rather than mitigate them. A smarter, more coherent China policy—one rooted in disciplined competition with Beijing, patient efforts to build goodwill with anxious allies and partners, and vigorous efforts to refresh the domestic sources of U.S. strength—can make life safer, healthier, and more affordable for Americans.
NEW FRIEND ON THE BLOCK
Trump’s views on China are iconoclastic in Washington, and even at odds with other members of his own administration and party. Whereas most policymakers agree that China is the United States’ foremost strategic competitor, Trump has embraced a narrow conception of competition focused primarily on the size of China’s trade surplus and its export of chemicals used to make fentanyl. He also sees Xi less as a determined geopolitical foe than as a transactional business rival with whom he can negotiate to stabilize bilateral ties.
This judgment—that dealing with China can and should be nonideological and transactional—was also present in Trump’s first term in office. It even survived the COVID-19 pandemic, during which Trump, believing that Xi had exported the virus, empowered senior advisers to implement a hard-line approach to China that included challenging the legitimacy of Chinese Communist Party rule and openly calling for political change. But Trump’s core views did not dictate U.S. policy as greatly then as they do now because he had less command over his own administration during his first term and was less dominant over the Republican Party as a whole.
Trump has also been chastened into a more realistic appreciation of Beijing’s power. China is the only country in the world that stared down Trump’s April 2025 tariff barrage and forced him to retreat. In 2026, Beijing used Washington’s fear of a fresh economic rupture to deter Trump from targeting major Chinese banks as part of his global efforts to squeeze Iran’s economy. Even as the president claims to be ushering in a new era of U.S. dominance, he has had to acknowledge China as a “near peer”—a designation that his administration codified in its 2025 National Security Strategy. Similarly, he has touted the prospect of a “G-2” of the United States and China, making allies and partners worry that he is privileging Beijing’s sensitivities over their concerns.
 Trump’s mishandling of China policy has opened space for a new strategy.
In some discrete areas, the Trump administration continues to view China through a competitive lens. For example, it is reducing U.S. dependence on Chinese rare-earth exports through initiatives such as Project Vault, an effort to stockpile critical minerals, and pressuring countries to forswear participation in Chinese-led artificial intelligence initiatives. And even as Trump lambastes allies and partners, alleging that they exploit U.S. beneficence, Washington is deepening its security cooperation with treaty allies in Asia, including Australia and the Philippines, and stepping up its training of troops in Taiwan.
Yet on balance, the president has been more conciliatory than competitive toward China. And with his other foreign policy goals—dominating the Western Hemisphere, pushing for regime change in Iran, and ending the war in Ukraine—vying for priority, Trump has devoted far less attention to the world’s most consequential bilateral relationship than many observers had expected when he retook office. His various retreats on China have left the United States worse off: he has undermined Washington’s leverage over Beijing while causing U.S. allies and partners to question whether they should align with a country that prefers a veneer of stability with China to coordinated efforts to address Chinese assertiveness abroad and repression at home.
OVERCORRECTING THE RECORD
Because Trump’s China policy places him at odds with much of the foreign policy bureaucracy and the vast majority of lawmakers, including those within his own party, there will likely be pent-up pressure to resume intense strategic competition with China. Candidates seeking the 2028 presidential nomination, in particular, will be tempted to pledge to take a tougher approach to Beijing, potentially including calls to curtail high-level diplomatic exchanges between U.S. and Chinese officials or adopt more expansive measures to limit China’s technological progress. But attempting to restore or make minor updates to the status quo that existed before Trump’s second term—or to go even further in an effort to project ostensible strength—would be misguided.
Most obvious, the nearly decadelong U.S. effort to slow Chinese innovation through sanctions, tariffs, and export controls is foundering. In AI, for example, Chinese companies are finding workarounds to such efforts and advancing their capabilities alongside those of their U.S. peers. Any sustainable attempt to limit technology access also requires multilateral cooperation; as Washington’s ties with many of its closest allies and partners fray, questions are mounting about whether any coalition can thwart Beijing’s technological strides and would be willing to bear the costs of trying to do so.
At the same time, China is widening its lead in sectors such as electric vehicles, advanced robots, and life sciences. Attempting to construct a technological moat around the United States is unlikely to help it regain its competitiveness. Instead, Washington will need to strike a better balance between mitigating the security risks of Chinese investment and collaboration and securing commercial benefits from Chinese knowledge and industry. The United States could gain from using the same technology transfer practices that China employed against U.S. companies starting in the late 1970s, when Washington led in many cutting-edge technologies. In battery manufacturing, for instance, U.S. firms would benefit from acquiring know-how from their Chinese competitors, and both countries would gain if their laboratories pooled capabilities to accelerate the discovery of cures to diseases such as cancer.
The United States also may not be able to pick up where it left off before Trump retook office because even its well-wishers no longer can treat his foreign policy as an aberration. He won a second term after losing in 2020, and he did so more decisively than in 2016. Although U.S. allies and partners would welcome a more multilateralist administration after Trump, they will find it difficult to overlook the possibility that aggressive unilateralism will periodically shape Washington’s foreign policy. Merely eschewing Trump’s crude bullying will not be enough to rebuild trust; his successor must avoid treating allies and partners as instruments of strategic competition.
 The inescapable reality is that both countries will remain interdependent.
Paradoxically, though, Trump’s mishandling of China policy has opened the political space for a new, more durable strategy to emerge. Previously, proponents of sustained high-level diplomacy between the United States and China were often dismissed as shortsighted, Chinese investment in the United States was seen as a Trojan horse, and critiques of zero-sum conceptions of bilateral relations were considered naive. But Trump’s actions have shifted the Overton window of what is possible, creating room for a wider variety of ways to work productively with China.

articles.title: India opposes second-class UN Security Council seats - News Karnataka
articles.summary: India opposes second-class UN Security Council seats  News Karnataka
articles.full_text:
New York: India has called for comprehensive reforms of the United Nations Security Council, warning that creating new permanent seats without veto powers would leave their occupants with “second-class” status and fail to address the existing concentration of decision-making power.
India’s Permanent Representative to the UN, Ambassador Harish Parvathaneni, made the remarks during an Inter-Governmental Negotiations (IGN) plenary debate on the veto in the UN General Assembly on Monday. He said the veto must be exercised with restraint, particularly on issues concerning international peace and security, and should not become an instrument of narrow political expediency.
Parvathaneni argued that reform cannot focus on the veto alone. Changes must also address the Council’s membership categories, regional representation, size and working methods. He called for negotiations based on a clear text, with defined timelines and milestones, to move the long-running reform process forward.
India reiterated its position that if veto powers continue to exist, all permanent members of a reformed Security Council should enjoy the same rights and responsibilities.
India questions the use of the veto
The Security Council is the UN body responsible for maintaining international peace and security. It has 15 members, comprising five permanent members and 10 non-permanent members elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms.
The permanent members, commonly known as the P5, are China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States. Each has veto power over substantive resolutions, allowing any one of them to block a proposal even when the remaining Council members support it.
Addressing the General Assembly debate, Parvathaneni said the veto was not merely a privilege but a responsibility that should be exercised with great restraint.
“India has always maintained that the veto, which is right now a prerogative only of the five permanent members of the Security Council, is a responsibility that must be exercised with great restraint, especially on matters bearing upon the maintenance of international peace and security. It should not be an instrument of narrow political expediency,” he said.
The envoy cited the historical record of veto use to underline India’s concerns. According to his remarks, the veto had been exercised 331 times on around 200 resolutions during the UN’s existence.
He also noted that two of the five permanent members had not exercised a veto for more than three and a half decades, while most vetoes or threats to use them had come from the other three.
The figures, he argued, highlighted the need to examine how the veto affects the Council’s ability to respond to international crises and how its use should be addressed as part of wider institutional reform.
India says 2022 veto initiative has limitations
Parvathaneni also referred to a UN General Assembly initiative adopted in 2022 to increase scrutiny of the veto.
Under General Assembly Resolution 76/262, a debate is mandated in the General Assembly whenever a permanent member exercises its veto in the Security Council. The mechanism was intended to encourage accountability and provide a forum for member states to discuss the use of the power.
However, the Indian envoy said the experience since the initiative’s adoption had not produced the change many had anticipated.
“The veto initiative of 2022 was seen as a harbinger of change by mandating a General Assembly debate every time a veto is cast. However, the actual record of the large number of vetoes cast since Resolution 76-262 was adopted tells a contrary story,” he said.
While acknowledging the intent behind the initiative and efforts to address vetoes in situations involving mass atrocities, Parvathaneni argued that incremental steps could not resolve the deeper structural problems affecting the Council.
He said restricting the veto without addressing the Council’s composition and functioning would leave its fundamental decision-making dynamics largely unchanged.
“The lived experience shows that piecemeal approaches, however well-intentioned, are bound to fail. Limiting the veto cannot be separated from the questions of categories of membership, regional representation, size, and working methods. We need to move forward on all five clusters together,” he said.
India’s position is that reform should be negotiated as a comprehensive package rather than through isolated changes that leave other areas of disagreement unresolved.
New permanent members without veto powers would face inequality
A central element of India’s position is that any expansion of permanent membership must provide new permanent members with the same rights as the existing P5.
Parvathaneni said a reformed Council should not establish a new category of permanent members with fewer powers.
“India’s position on the veto is principled and well known. It is aligned with the common African position. We reiterate that as long as a veto exists, it must be held by all permanent members of a reformed Council. Fairness and justice demand that all permanent members enjoy the same rights and responsibilities,” he said.
He warned that creating a separate category of permanent members without veto rights would add another layer of inequality to an institution already facing criticism over its composition.
“A new category of permanent members with or without the veto would only further complicate a discussion that’s already very difficult and would further entrench the very inequity we are seeking to correct,” he said.
Parvathaneni added that a reform which created long-term members without veto powers would not fundamentally change the way decisions are made by the existing permanent members.
“A reform that expands the UN Security Council by creating another category of long-term members without the veto effectively makes them second-class members and would not change the decision-making dynamic of the P5,” he said.
India has consistently argued that the Council should expand both its permanent and non-permanent categories. It maintains that adding only elected members would increase the Council’s size without adequately addressing the concentration of authority among the five permanent members.
India flags informal and de facto vetoes
The Indian envoy also argued that the problem of veto power extends beyond formal vetoes cast against draft resolutions.
He pointed to procedures in which decisions can be blocked through informal consensus requirements, including presidential statements, press statements and decisions taken by sanctions committees.
“The veto is not only what is cast in the open. There is the effective or the de facto veto that every Council member, elected and non-elected, holds over presidential statements, press statements, decisions of sanctions committees where the unwritten rule of consensus allows a single member to hold or block a proposal, most often without explanation,” he said.
Such practices, according to India’s argument, can prevent proposals from moving forward even when no formal veto is recorded.
Parvathaneni also criticised the use of consensus in the negotiations on Security Council reform, saying procedural disagreements had contributed to the lack of progress.
He referred to General Assembly Decision 62/557, which established the framework for the IGN process. According to the Indian envoy, the decision identifies the widest possible political acceptance as the guiding principle rather than requiring consensus in every instance.
“In the same vein, the argument of consensus has been harnessed as a disguised or a de facto veto in the IGN process as well. Resolution 62-557, the foundational decision for the IGN, is clear. The guiding principle is the widest possible political acceptance, not consensus. Seventeen cycles later, we have no outcome to show for it,” he said.
The IGN is the intergovernmental process through which UN member states discuss proposals for reforming the Security Council. India has called for the negotiations to progress towards formal, text-based discussions with clear milestones.
India recalls the Council’s 1965 expansion
Parvathaneni also cited the Security Council’s only major expansion, which took place in 1965.
That reform increased the number of non-permanent members from six to 10, while the five permanent members retained their positions and veto powers.
“The only expansion of the Council in 1965 enlarged the non-permanent category alone. The ratio of permanent to elected members moved from five to six to five to ten and further strengthened the relative power of the P5,” he said.
India argues that the change did not fundamentally alter the balance of authority within the Council because the permanent members retained their exclusive veto rights.
The historical example was used to support India’s case for a broader reform that addresses membership categories, representation and decision-making procedures together.
The Council was established in 1945, following the Second World War. India maintains that its structure must now reflect contemporary geopolitical realities rather than continue to be shaped primarily by the circumstances of its creation.
India seeks a permanent seat and greater representation
India has long sought permanent membership of the Security Council, arguing that the current structure does not adequately represent the modern international order.
Its position includes calls for greater representation for regions that remain underrepresented and for a Council capable of responding effectively to contemporary international challenges.
India has also sought a non-permanent seat for the 2028–29 term. Elections are scheduled for June 2027, when India and Tajikistan are set to contest the sole seat allocated to the Asia-Pacific Group, according to PTI.
India last served on the Council during 2021–22, its eighth term. Its earlier terms were 1950–51, 1967–68, 1972

Delivered India's statement at the UNGA Plenary on the use of the Veto
Highlighted:
➡️ Veto is a responsibility, not a tool of narrow expediency. We note that two of the P5 have not exercised veto for over three and a half decades. Most vetoes or threats of vetoes have emanated from three of the P5.
➡️ Piecemeal reforms will not work. All five clusters of UNSC reform must be addressed together.
➡️ Veto initiative of 2022 was seen as a harbinger of change. However, actual record of large number of vetoes cast since UNGA 76/262 tells a contrary story.
➡️ Unwritten consensus rules enable de facto vetoes in Council decisions and sanctions committees.
➡️ Consensus cannot become a disguised veto in the Inter Governmental Negotiations (IGN).
➡️ India aligns with the Common African Position: As long as the veto exists, all permanent members must enjoy equal rights.
➡️ New long-term seats without veto powers would create second-class members and perpetuate inequity. All permanent members, including new ones, must enjoy equal rights.
➡️ Begin text-based negotiations with clear timelines. The UNSC must reflect today's realities, not those of 1945.
— Parvathaneni Harish (@AmbHarishP) October 26, 2026
“India reiterates its call for a comprehensive approach towards Security Council reforms. The starting point is early commencement of text-based negotiations, with clearly defined timelines and milestones. Addressing the veto in isolation does not change the decision-making dynamic of the P5," the Indian envoy added.
The five permanent members, known as the P5, are China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States. They currently hold veto power over substantive Security Council resolutions.
India argued that meaningful reform must address five interconnected areas: membership categories, regional representation, the Council's size, working methods and veto powers. Harish also questioned the compatibility of periodic elections with the concept of permanent membership.
India also stressed that the veto must be exercised with restraint, particularly when decisions concern international peace and security. Harish warned against using the power to advance narrow political interests.
“India has always maintained that the veto, which is right now a prerogative only of the five permanent members of the UN Security Council, is a responsibility that must be exercised with great restraint, especially on matters bearing upon the maintenance of international peace and security. It should not be an instrument of narrow political expediency," Harish said.
Highlighting the historical use of the veto, the ambassador said it had been exercised 331 times on around 200 resolutions over the United Nations' history.
He noted that two of the five permanent members had not used the veto for more than three and a half decades, while most vetoes or threats to use the power had come from only three P5 members.
Harish also referred to the 2022 Veto Initiative, under which the UN General Assembly holds a debate whenever a permanent member casts a veto. The mechanism was introduced to strengthen accountability and scrutiny of veto use.
However, he said the substantial number of vetoes exercised since the adoption of UN General Assembly Resolution 76/262 presented a contrasting picture of the initiative's impact.
Harish raised concerns about informal consensus-based procedures within the Security Council, arguing that these can allow a single member to block proposals without formally casting a veto.
“The veto is not only what is cast in the open. There is also the ‘effective or de facto veto’ that every Council member, elected and non-elected, holds over presidential statements, press statements and the decisions of sanctions committees, where the unwritten rule of consensus allows a single member to hold or block a proposal, most often without explanation," Harish said.
His remarks highlighted India's concern that decision-making practices can give individual members the ability to obstruct proposals even when no formal veto is recorded.
India's position is that reform must address both the Council's membership structure and its decision-making procedures. Harish maintained that equal rights and responsibilities should guide any expansion of permanent membership for as long as veto power remains part of the Security Council's functioning.

articles.title: Rival US and Russia resolutions on disputed Western Sahara are defeated in UN Security Council - Yahoo
articles.summary: Rival US and Russia resolutions on disputed Western Sahara are defeated in UN Security Council  Yahoo
articles.full_text:
UNITED NATIONS (AP) — Russia vetoed a U.S.-drafted resolution Friday that would have supported Morocco's demand for sovereignty over the disputed Western Sahara and ended the U.N.'s 35-year peacekeeping mission, which was charged with helping to prepare a referendum on the future of the mineral-rich territory.
The U.N. Security Council then defeated a Russian-drafted resolution to extend the mandate of the peacekeeping mission for a year. The 3-1 vote with 11 abstentions meant the United States didn't have to use its veto because the resolution failed to get the minimum nine "yes" votes in the 15-member body.
The U.N. mission's mandate will now expire on Saturday, bringing an end to its operations.
Morocco annexed Western Sahara, a former Spanish colony also believed to have considerable offshore oil deposits, in 1975, sparking a conflict with the Polisario Front, which represents the indigenous Sahrawi people.
The United Nations brokered a ceasefire in 1991 and established a peacekeeping mission to monitor the truce and help prepare a referendum on the territory's future. It has never taken place because of disagreements on who is eligible to vote.
Last year, the U.N. Security Council approved a resolution backing Morocco's claim to the Western Sahara, a significant shift that aligns with the Trump administration's support for the North African country.
That resolution referred to Morocco's proposal for wide-ranging autonomy for the territory as the basis for negotiations and made no mention of a referendum on self-determination. Morocco's plan to maintain sovereignty over the territory also is backed by Britain, France and others, while Russia and China have long favored holding a referendum that includes independence as an option.
The U.S.-drafted resolution put to a vote Friday went much further. It would have ended the peacekeeping mission on April 30, 2027, and created a new political mission no longer preparing for a referendum. It would have affirmed "that genuine autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty is the only feasible solution to negotiate a mutually acceptable solution."
Russia's rival resolution would have simply extended the current mandate of the peacekeeping mission until Oct. 31, 2027.
U.S. Ambassador Mike Waltz said Russia's veto prevents "historic steps toward finally ending a 50-year conflict." But he said the United States will continue working with U.N. special envoy Staffan de Mistura and both parties "to negotiate a lasting peace."
Morocco's royal palace, which oversees the kingdom's foreign policy, said, however, that the Western Sahara conflict should no longer remain on the Security Council's agenda.
"The UN political process, which has unfortunately been marked by the procrastination of the other parties, their stubbornness in creating a blockage and perpetuating the status quo, is thus suspended," the palace said in a statement.
Russia's U.N. Ambassador Vassily Nebenzia blamed those who opposed Moscow's resolution for the demise of the mission. He said Russia vetoed the U.S. draft because it sidelined the longstanding proposal for "a just, free and fair solution on the basis of self-determination" for the Sahrawi people.
Sidi Omar, the Polisario Front's U.N. representative, thanked Russia for vetoing the U.S. resolution, saying it "would have undermined the free exercise by the Sahrawi people of their inalienable right to self-determination and independence."
"Moreover, by seeking to legitimize Morocco's illegal and forcible occupation of Western Sahara, the resolution would not only torpedo the foundations of the U.N. peace process but would also have set a very dangerous precedent that threatens broader regional and international peace and security," he said.
As for the Polisario Front going forward, Omar told reporters, "We remain fully committed to the peace process — but a peace process put back on the right track, a peace process that will lead to enabling our people to exercise their inalienable right to self-determination and independence."
___
Akram Oubachir contributed to this report from Rabat, Morocco

articles.title: Gulf states must rethink trillion-dollar defence in light of US-Iran war, says report - The Guardian
articles.summary: Gulf states must rethink trillion-dollar defence in light of US-Iran war, says report  The GuardianThe Struggle for a New West Asian Order: The Forty-Fourth Newsletter (2026)  Tricontinental: Institute for Social ResearchIn Search of a New Order: Arab Options and Gulf Security  Middle East Council on Global AffairsGulf Arabs’ alliances with middle powers hint at new Mideast  The Christian Science MonitorGulf’s unravelling security order: Who will secure Re...
