Gulf states are going to have to reconfigure their trillion-dollar defences given the damage inflicted on their economies and the questionable continued value of US bases in the face of Iranian attack, according to a study by the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
The report says that in the weeks before the 8 April ceasefire, 12 regional states, overwhelmingly in the Gulf, faced 4,670 Iranian one-way attack drones and more than 1,400 ballistic missiles. Nearly half were aimed at the United Arab Emirates. Although the vast majority were repelled, one estimate of the damage to energy infrastructure cited by the report is put as high as $58bn (£43bn).
Iran would portray either a reduction or complete withdrawal of US forces from the region as “a strategic success and vindication of its steadfastness, but also use it to embarrass the Gulf states about their decades-long courtship of US protection”.
The report says the war also highlights another “uncomfortable truth for the Gulf states: not only has their trillion-dollar acquisition of US weapons not translated into US protection at the crucial time, but their respective militaries are also not adequately prepared for the new kind of attritional air war to which they are being exposed”.
Despite huge investment in mainly US armaments, the report identified significant shortcomings: “overwhelming reliance on US-supplied air- and missile-defence systems and munitions; a failure to achieve regional defence integration; a shortage of minesweeping capability; limited retaliatory options; and the prohibitive costs stemming from an overdependence on expensive, high-end systems to take down relatively inexpensive drones and missiles”.
The report is neutral on whether the divided Gulf states should seek a new non-aggression pact with Iran, but notes that the US-Iran war has shown longstanding defence and security partnerships with the US “have failed to ensure adequate protection against Iranian aggression”.
It adds: “If anything, US military bases and defence partnerships with the US have provided Iran with another pretext for attacks against the Gulf states.”
Public opinion on the US in the Gulf has also been shifting, it says, “from security provider to strategic liability”.
Any reduction or withdrawal of US forces from the Gulf region would be portrayed by Iran “as a strategic success and vindication of its steadfastness” and would also be used “to embarrass the Gulf states about their decades-long courtship of US protection,” the report notes.
The study comes after Chris Murphy, the Democrat senator and member of the senate foreign relations committee, said a debate was under way in the US military about the value of seeking to rebuild the damaged US bases in the Gulf.
Murphy said the Gulf state leadership “want us to rebuild” and “to keep a presence in the region”, but asked: “What good is it to have a base in the region to protect American interests if within 24 hours of a hot war starting, it is wiped off the map?
“We would be criminally incompetent as stewards of taxpayer dollars if we were to rebuild bases that are blown up within hours of the next war starting.
“So clearly, we are going to have to have a smaller footprint in the region, and the limiting principle on the footprint that we rebuild will be ‘what can we protect?’ because we clearly cannot protect the scope of our footprint today and if we can’t protect it, it is useless.”
Murphy suggested that, at the very least, the US may need to relocate its bases in the eastern Mediterranean further away from Iranian missiles.

articles.summary: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine  BBCUkraine’s Zelenskyy praises US over $2.1bn Patriot missile deal but warns it could take years  The GuardianUS greenlights $2.1bn sale of Patriot interceptors to Ukraine  Financial TimesUS approves potential $2.1 billion sale of scarce Patriot missiles to Ukraine  CNNNATO top commander sees no delays in delivery of Patriot missiles to Ukraine  Ukrinform
articles.full_text:
The United States has approved the sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine, a critically-needed munition for defence against escalating Russian aerial attacks.
However Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has warned it could take "several years" for the deliveries to arrive.
The US State Department said the advanced PAC-3 interceptor missiles would cost $2.1bn (£1.6bn) and would be "funded entirely" by Kyiv's allies in Europe and Canada.
On Friday night Zelensky repeated his calls for the US to speed up the release of its Patriots - the only effective weapon in downing Russia's deadly ballistic missiles.
The latest move comes after a row between Zelensky and Donald Trump earlier this month when the US eased sanctions on Russia as part of a deal to secure Russian diesel.
The US president stated it was time for Ukraine to get a new leader to strike a deal to end the war with Russia. Moscow launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, having earlier seized Crimea and parts of Donbas in the east.
Tensions eased after Zelensky held talks with US envoys in Oslo on 20 October.
In Friday's statement, the State Department said "this proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe".
It said "Ukraine will pay for this purchase with donations from Canada, Germany, and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds, financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan".
The statement said the "principal contractor" would be American company Lockheed Martin, adding that "no US funds are involved in this sale".
Meanwhile, at the G20 foreign ministers' meeting European diplomats protested over the presence of Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov by refusing to stand for an official photograph.
The meeting is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
"Let me say this directly to the Russian Foreign Minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Lavrov at the summit, accusing his government of killing innocent civilians in Ukraine.
Zelensky said earlier this week that Ukraine had been waiting almost a month for the US to sign off on critical missile supplies which his country was running critically low on.
In a post on X late on Friday, he welcomed the US announcement but said Ukraine needed the Patriot missiles "right now".
He said Russia was intensifying its attacks on key energy infrastructure ahead of winter with "more than 30 Russian strikes" on "critical parts" of Ukraine's power grid over the past two weeks.
Kyiv desperately needs the interceptors but there is a global shortage of the munitions due to their use by the US in its war against Iran.
It is not clear what the production schedule will be for the Patriots - but it is understood the order is for new builds rather than existing missiles, meaning there is unlikely to be any kind of rapid delivery to Ukraine.
Patriots also have lengthy production times, with only 600 missiles produced per year according to the US Department of Defence.
In July, Trump said Washington had "not agreed" to license Ukraine to produce Patriots - three weeks after offering the country such a right.
Additional reporting by Victoria Bourne

Pentagon officials have in recent weeks asked several NATO countries to tone down their rhetoric regarding the threat posed by Russia, arguing that some statements by European leaders and officials have undermined continental security, four people familiar with the matter said.
Among the nations that have received messages urging them to keep public statements in check are Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity. It was not clear if the messages, which were delivered in bilateral meetings, were conveyed to other European governments.
The U.S. requests come as the Trump administration restarts an effort to press for a negotiated end to the full-scale war in Ukraine, now well into its fifth year. The latest push has blended incentives for Russia – including sanctions relief – with pressure on Ukraine to halt its attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.
Asked for comment, a Pentagon official said: “Private conversations among allies are just that, so we will not comment on these allegations.”
Among the comments that have drawn U.S. officials’ attention are suggestions by European leaders that Russia is cornered and resorting to increasingly desperate measures as its invasion of Ukraine slows to a crawl, one of the people said.
Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby, a key figure in an ongoing review of U.S. troop levels in Europe, was one of the U.S. officials delivering the message, the people said. Reuters could not determine what other officials were involved.
None of the people, who include three European officials and a U.S. official, suggested the advice was communicated in a confrontational manner.
Avoid ‘poking’ Russia
The U.S. messages reflect a debate within NATO regarding how to publicly address the threat of an increasingly assertive Russia.
Some Western officials have argued that emphasizing the threat posed by Moscow could play into the hands of the Kremlin, which they say seeks to sow fear and undermine support for Ukraine.
Others argue European governments must be transparent to show their electorates that sacrifice and resources are needed to keep Moscow at bay. That is especially true as Russia appears to accelerate a covert campaign of sabotage throughout the continent.
Russia has denied that it is pursuing such a campaign.
One of the people familiar told Reuters that Colby told a Baltic official recently that there should be no “poking” directed at the Russians.
The person said Colby pointed to Europeans publicly suggesting that Russia was “cornered like a rat” as an example of unhelpful rhetoric.
It was not clear what specific statement Colby was referring to. However, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal referred to Putin as a “rat in a corner” in late September, suggesting the Russian leader was resorting to sabotage efforts in Europe as Russia had become increasingly bogged down in Ukraine.
“We are helping you. The Americans are there,” said a separate European official, describing the Pentagon’s recent private messaging. “Just don’t be loud. Don’t make noise.”
In a separate recent meeting, the Pentagon urged an Estonian delegation to be “measured” in its communications, according to a person briefed on the encounter, though the person did not say Pentagon officials complained about any specific statement.
The defense ministries of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia did not respond to requests for comment, while NATO declined to comment.
Moscow tests Europe’s resolve
One of the European officials said that the Pentagon’s advice, while cordial, was baffling, given that intelligence services in the Baltic states have in recent months consistently played down the probability of Russia testing NATO’s mutual defense provisions.
Other NATO intelligence services, by contrast, have publicly warned that Russia could dramatically ramp up its sabotage campaign in the near future.
The Pentagon messages to NATO officials come at a fraught time for European security.
Moscow has recently intensified its campaign of deniable attacks on NATO countries, Western intelligence officials have said.
On Wednesday, German prosecutors said two Belarusians were arrested for allegedly planning to set fire to a building or critical infrastructure facility in the Nuremberg area. In September, the German government blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, allegations Moscow has denied.
At the same time, U.S. officials have been discussing potential business deals with Russia as part of the Trump administration’s push for peace in Ukraine. Those efforts have drawn mixed reactions from European officials, many of whom are pushing for the Kremlin’s continued economic isolation.
Pentagon planners, meanwhile, are reviewing Washington’s force posture in Europe, a process that could see a sharp drawdown in America’s troop presence on the continent.
US officials have said European NATO members need to assume more responsibility for their own defense, particularly as the US focuses on threats in the Middle East, Latin America and East Asia.

articles.title: The Korean Peninsula’s Way Forward – OpEd - Eurasia Review
articles.summary: The Korean Peninsula’s Way Forward – OpEd  Eurasia Review
articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways:
- The Korean Peninsula remains a suspended conflict more than 70 years after the 1953 armistice, with North Korea’s nuclear arsenal the chief obstacle and past demands for complete denuclearization before talks having failed to alter Pyongyang’s calculations.
- The article advocates a stepwise process of reciprocal security guarantees, a verifiable freeze on testing and fissile-material production, gradual disarmament linked to sanctions relief and assistance, and eventual replacement of the armistice by a peace agreement, without requiring immediate reunification.
- Progress depends on re-engaging all six-party-talk participants—North Korea, the United States, China, South Korea, Japan and Russia—so that major-power rivalry and arms transfers do not undermine risk-reduction and inter-Korean dialogue.
The Korean Peninsula is one of the most persistent security challenges in the modern international system. More than 70 years after the Korean War’s armistice, North and South Korea are divided by a heavily militarized border, two vastly different political systems, and deep mistrust of each other. North Korea’s nuclear weapons program has become one of the greatest threats to peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula and in the region, while South Korea’s security is closely tied to its alliance with the United States. At the same time, the strategic rivalry between major powers in the region, including the United States, China, and Russia, has intensified and permeates the attempts at conflict management on the Korean Peninsula.
A peace settlement of the Korean War will have to be based on a stepwise transformation of conflict-ridden coexistence into peaceful coexistence via reciprocal security guarantees, stepwise nuclear disarmament, and new inter-Korean relations as well as broader regional dialogue. Reaching complete denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula need not be a precondition for negotiations towards said peace guarantee, but it has to remain the long-term goal while relevant security goals are implemented stepwise. Other nations of the region can be encouraged to join the dialogue with a view to their security interests in order to achieve a long-lasting, stable peace in the region based on mutual trust and on sustainable, peaceful relations between all nations involved.
The Korean Peninsula has been divided since Japan’s defeat in 1945 when the United States and the Soviet Union respectively occupied the two halves of the peninsula. In 1948, separate governments were established in each half of the Peninsula. Since then, the two Koreas have engaged in a 70-year military confrontation that culminated in the Korean War in 1950-53. The Armistice Agreement, which brought an end to the war, did not lead to a Comprehensive Peace Agreement that could establish a lasting peace on the Korean Peninsula and instead remains a mere suspended conflict between the two Koreas.
Most importantly, the nuclear arsenal of North Korea is the biggest single obstacle to peace on the Korean Peninsula today. The failure of past negotiations, the piling of sanctions on top of sanctions, and diplomatic isolation of Pyongyang have all failed to change the calculations of the North Korean leadership, who believe the nuclear force is the greatest strategic asset that they possess. The desire to disarm North Korea completely of nuclear weapons before negotiations is unrealistic and represents a dead-end approach to policy on the Korean Peninsula. Instead, the focus should be placed on how to prevent an increase in the nuclear arsenal of North Korea and how to reduce the chances of conflict. This can be achieved through a phased approach to nuclear disarmament, with the first stage being a verifiable cessation of nuclear and missile testing and a halt to production of nuclear weapons and materials, followed by subsequent stages of disarmament as confidence is increased.
Negotiations regarding denuclearization need to be conducted on the basis of reciprocity and with the mutual understanding of what is meant by credibility. The compliance of one party with agreed verifiable measures must be reciprocated by the other party with corresponding incentives including humanitarian assistance and appropriate security assurances. This is especially pertinent with regard to the relaxation of sanctions and corresponding increase in assistance. However, any violations must immediately incur corresponding sanctions.
However, all of these dynamics are inextricably linked with the larger strategic competition between the US, China, and Russia in the region, especially given the latter’s rapidly increasing relations with Pyongyang. To this end, the US needs to balance its alliance commitments with direct engagement with Seoul, while Beijing would need to encourage DPRK restraint in return for support for any agreements reached by Pyongyang with third parties. And while it may be uncomfortable for many to recognize, Russia’s growing relations with the DPRK cannot help but complicate international pressure on Pyongyang for denuclearization, and therefore must be engaged to prevent transfers of arms or technology that could destabilize the region and circumvent any future arms control agreements.
This security architecture bears significant relevance to Japan’s interests. This is why Japan must assist South Korea and the United States while engaging in attempts at negotiations to bring about peace on the Korean Peninsula. It is essential that all major actors from the six-party talks — North Korea, the United States, China, South Korea, Japan, and Russia — return to the negotiating table. Within this framework, North Korea will have to agree to denuclearization in return for security guarantees and economic incentives. A peace agreement that would put an end to the armistice agreement signed in 1953 will have to be concluded to bring about peaceful settlement of the Korean War.
First, peace should not be defined as immediate reunification given the two different political systems and economic structures that have developed in the two countries over several decades and that are still evolving. In the short term, therefore, the main goal should be to decrease hostility, to save human lives and to allow future generations to decide their own fate without external pressure. This requires a fundamental shift in perception on the part of both sides: i.e., that one side’s security does not have to come at the expense of the other’s insecurity.
Success will be measured by the extent to which people from both sides of the divide can live in greater security, with dignity and freedom from war. While immediate unification is highly unlikely to be the aim of any lasting settlement of the Korean conflict, there will, in the end, be sufficient progress towards rapid reconciliation to enable future generations of Koreans to determine their own future, free from the military fears of foreign invasion that currently constrain them so much. Pending that day, imaginative use of crisis communications and risk reduction strategies; sustained inter-Korean dialogue and intercourse, as well as a matching diplomatic effort by the major outside powers involved in the region, will constitute practical, verifiable and lasting evidence of the positive.
The opinions expressed in this article are the author’s own.

articles.title: What to know about the Melania Trump-brokered ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky - AP News
articles.summary: What to know about the Melania Trump-brokered ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky  AP News
articles.full_text:
A small city in southern Ukraine, cut off for months by fighting, has got a brief pause in the nearly 5-year-old war so that aid can get in and residents can get out.
U.S. first lady Melania Trump brokered the localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine around Oleshky, a Russian-occupied city that she said is “on the brink of disaster.”
A local pause in fighting started at 3 a.m. Tuesday to allow medicine, food and water to be taken to Oleshky before evacuation corridors are opened later in the week. The situation in Oleshky is desperate, with food and medical supplies running perilously low for the up to 2,000 people still there, as drones and land mines restrict movement.
Ukrainian, Russian and U.S. negotiators reached the deal Friday. Officials on all sides have confirmed it, but many details haven’t been released.
Melania Trump voices hope for the Oleshky mission success
After the deal was announced, the first lady voiced hope for the success of the humanitarian mission and hailed the importance of Pope Leo XIV’s support for the effort.
“It is great to have (the) pope’s support,” she said. “I hope everything goes as it’s planned.”
Leo spoke earlier this month with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin, urging them to allow humanitarian aid into Oleshky and the safe evacuation of civilians.
Asked if she had spoken with Zelenskyy or Putin, the first lady and U.S. President Donald Trump said both.
“I think she’s doing better than the professionals right now,” the president said.
Asked if she would visit Ukraine, Melania Trump responded: “We will see.”
Oleshky has been without power, heat or water
Oleshky is located in Ukraine’s partially occupied Kherson region. It sits on the Dnipro River, which separates Ukrainian forces from the city’s Russian occupiers. Moscow’s forces captured it on the first day of the full-scale invasion, which started on Feb. 24, 2022. Its buildings were shelled and burned.
In June 2023, floodwaters swamped the city after the Kakhovka Dam collapsed in an explosion that an Associated Press investigation found was likely caused by the Russian military. Hundreds of residents were killed.
Once home to about 24,000 people, the city has had scarce food and medical supplies for months. There is no electricity, heat or running water. Roads out of town are mined and lined with burned-out cars, and drones buzz overhead. With another harsh winter approaching, those still there face death from hunger or disease.
Moscow and Kyiv have blamed each other for the humanitarian crisis.
Ukraine has repeatedly appealed for a local ceasefire to organize evacuations. As the occupying power, Russia is obligated under international law to make sure civilians under its control have what they need to survive.
Ceasefire, aid and then evacuations
The deal sets out three stages: a ceasefire, followed by delivery of humanitarian aid and finally the evacuation of civilians who want to leave Oleshky, according to Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman and its chief negotiator in the talks.
Before any aid moves, mines will be cleared on the routes into the city, Lubinets said. He told the AP that the ceasefire will last several days and apply across the Kherson region and neighboring areas essential to the operation.
Russia’s chief of the general staff, Gen. Valery Gerasimov, said that Russian forces would carry out “engineering reconnaissance” and ensure that the “humanitarian convoy” can move safely into the city.
Russia’s human rights ombudswoman, Yana Lantratova, who took part in the negotiations, said firstly that they plan to establish what residents need and then deliver food, medicine, hygiene products and other essentials. She said anyone who wants to leave the combat zone will be guaranteed safe passage.
Few details have been announced
Civilian negotiators from Russia and Ukraine have only announced a few details about how the ceasefire or the aid mission will proceed, citing the sensitivity of the negotiations. Officials involved have declined to say whether Melania Trump would travel to Ukraine.
Lubinets said provisions will be made for evacuees to travel to Ukraine or Russia or remain in the town after access roads have been de-mined. He added that civilian representatives from Ukraine, the United States, and Russia will travel to Oleshky.
“The operation will be carried out gradually and is extremely challenging to implement,” he said, adding that the three countries involved had signed a ceasefire and evacuation plan.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the evacuation would likely take several days.
The first lady took up the issue at the U.N.
Melania Trump began talks on Oleshky after she heard about the situation at one of her events during the U.N. General Assembly session in September, the White House said. She and a representative then worked directly with leaders from Russia and Ukraine to set the terms. She had already been working with officials from both countries on a separate matter.
“When Melania Trump learned about the situation in Oleshky, the negotiation process began under her coordination,” Lubinets said. He said that the sides spent several weeks discussing ideas and developing “new approaches, mechanisms and tools” to help civilians there survive.
Helping children in conflict zones has become one of her signature issues during her husband’s second term. She hosted a U.N. Security Council meeting on the issue earlier this year. Last year, she wrote to Putin about efforts to reunite families with children she described as “ displaced by the war.” Her senior adviser, Marc Beckman, said she has helped reunite nearly three dozen children.
Zelenskyy has lobbied various world leaders for help reuniting children that he says were taken by Russia after the invasion began in 2022. The International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Putin for war crimes in 2023, accusing him of personal responsibility for the abductions of children from Ukraine.
Tensions between Washington and Kyiv are rising
The localized ceasefire comes as tensions increased to new highs between the Trump administration and Ukraine’s government. Kyiv has faced restrictions on the satellite internet system it relies on to knock down Russian attacks, with the U.S. president and other top American officials sending mixed messages about who was responsible for decreasing the speed of the Elon Musk-made Starshield system.
Donald Trump also recently waived new Russia sanctions, reached an agreement with Russia to import diesel fuel and pushed Zelenskyy to make a deal to end the war. In renewed efforts to revive the peace process, Trump envoy Steve Witkoff traveled to Norway last week for talks with Zelenskyy before meeting with Putin in St. Petersburg, Russia.
Zelenskyy has emphasized the importance of the United States to renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war, including a possible joint meeting with Trump and Putin.

articles.title: Inside Melania Trump's secret diplomatic role in the Russia-Ukraine ceasefire deal - Fox News
articles.summary: Inside Melania Trump's secret diplomatic role in the Russia-Ukraine ceasefire deal  Fox News
articles.full_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Moscow and Kyiv remain locked in a yearslong grinding war, but in one Ukrainian city, the fight has quieted — and soon the Russian-occupied aging population in Oleshky will be offered humanitarian relief and a way out.
Behind the localized ceasefire is an unlikely mediator: first lady Melania Trump. And her diplomatic effort in the war-torn region is not over, Fox News Digital has learned.
Trump spent weeks moderating between Russian and Ukrainian officials to hammer out a deal over the devastated city in Ukraine's Kherson region, ultimately winning the trust of both governments to serve as their "exclusive intermediary," according to a senior adviser for the first lady.
The agreement brought officials from both countries together in Belarus last week to sign off on a detailed humanitarian operation aimed at getting food, clean water, medicine and doctors into Oleshky, Ukraine, and providing safe passage out for residents who want to leave.
Fox News Digital obtained the signature pages of the agreement, signed Oct. 23 by Russia's human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova, and her Ukrainian counterpart, Dmytro Lubinets. The documents also lay out plans for continued humanitarian operations in the region coordinated with the first lady.
For the Slovenia-born first lady, the war in her native Europe was not entirely unfamiliar territory: she had already mediated exchanges of Ukrainian and Russian children. Negotiating an agreement to stop the fighting, however, marked a significant expansion of that role.
Just across the Dnipro from the Ukrainian-held city of Kherson, Oleshky was once home to roughly 24,000 people. Russia seized the city at the outset of its 2022 invasion, and years of occupation and fighting have reduced its population to around 2,000, many of them elderly.
The city now sits squarely on the front line.
Russian forces use Oleshky as a base for attacks across the river into Kherson, while Ukrainian forces target Russian positions in and around the city. Roads have been mined, food and medicine have become scarce and basic services have largely collapsed.
"It's hell there," Yuri Sobolevsky, deputy chairman of the Kherson regional council, told The New York Times. "People need to be evacuated from there, 1,000%. They're living 24/7 under risk of death."
For Ukraine, the humanitarian mission presents a difficult tradeoff. The civilians trapped in Oleshky are Ukrainians in desperate need of food, medicine and a safe route out. But the city remains under Russian occupation and sits on an active front line, meaning halting attacks long enough to reach them also means temporarily easing military pressure on Russian forces operating in the area.
Getting Russia and Ukraine to stop firing at each other has proven extraordinarily difficult — not just for the first lady, but for her husband and his administration, which has spent much of President Donald Trump's second term trying to bring the war to an end.
In Oleshky, however, both sides found a narrow point of agreement.
Oleshky first came onto Trump's radar during United Nations General Assembly week in September, when the city's worsening humanitarian crisis was raised at a Fostering the Future Together event that she hosted.
By then, the first lady had already worked with both governments to reunify 34 Ukrainian and Russian children with their families across six separate efforts, according to her exclusive senior adviser Marc Beckman, building relationships she was able to leverage when she turned her attention to Oleshky.
"The first lady's relationship with both Russia and Ukraine has been, over time, substantial," Beckman told Fox News Digital. "There's a lot of trust, and there's been a lot of success."
Her team first approached Ukraine and asked whether Kyiv would authorize Trump to serve as its "exclusive intermediary" with Russia. Ukraine agreed in a formal letter, Beckman said. Trump's team then approached Moscow, and Putin responded with a letter granting her the same role on Russia's behalf.
From there, Trump began negotiating with the highest levels of government in Russia and Ukraine, with both Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy involved in the talks, Beckman said.
The U.S. side of the negotiating effort was unusually small. Asked how involved the traditional White House national security apparatus was, Beckman said Trump handled the effort. "It's just the first lady," Beckman said.
"The devil is in the details," Beckman said of the negotiations. "There were moments in time where things became complicated."
What began as an effort to get food, water and medicine to a city on the brink of collapse quickly became an extraordinarily detailed negotiation over how to temporarily stop two armies from fighting.
The agreement remains narrowly focused on humanitarian operations in and around Oleshky and does not halt fighting elsewhere in Ukraine, where Russian and Ukrainian forces continue to battle along a sprawling front.
Trump and Beckman worked through maps, roadways and aerial imagery with the two sides, Beckman said. They negotiated what military equipment could enter the area, how civilians would be evacuated and even arranged refrigerated trucks to recover bodies expected to be found along the way.
"We know all of the military equipment that will be brought in," Beckman said. "We even went as far as organizing for refrigerated trucks for the bodies that are going to be there."
"It's going to be a very bad scene," he added. "That's the level of detail that the first lady was involved in."
The negotiations eventually produced a plan mapped out not just by weeks and days, Beckman said, but by the hour.
Russian and Ukrainian officials reconvened in Belarus at 4 a.m. New York time Friday for what was supposed to be a 5 a.m. signing. But negotiations continued for nearly three more hours, with Trump participating by video, before both sides finally agreed to the terms and signed at 7:40 a.m.
The ceasefire was initially slated to begin Oct. 29, but the two sides moved the startup by two days, with the guns falling silent at 4 a.m. Moscow time Tuesday. Its geographic scope was also expanded beyond Oleshky to provide safe passage through the surrounding Kherson region for humanitarian convoys.
"It was almost like momentum clicked," Beckman said.
Russian Gen. Valery Gerasimov, chief of the General Staff, confirmed Russian forces would cease fire along the Kherson axis and facilitate the safe movement of humanitarian convoys into Oleshky.
The humanitarian mission itself will be led by civilians from both countries, keeping Russian and Ukrainian troops apart as aid enters the city and residents are evacuated.
"If the Ukrainian, the Russian militaries were going throughout Oleshky, they would just kill each other," Beckman said.
Four American journalists from Newsmax will also accompany the mission to interview residents and document where they choose to go, providing a record of their decisions as civilians are evacuated from Russian-held territory.
The humanitarian mission is expected to last about one week, with a goal of wrapping up in early November. If more time is needed, Beckman said both sides could negotiate an extension with the first lady again participating in the talks.
The agreement also envisions a role for Trump beyond the immediate Oleshky operation.
Under the terms signed by the two sides, Russia and Ukraine are expected to establish regular humanitarian aid deliveries and repatriation efforts in communities across the Kherson region following the Oleshky mission, with Trump's assistance and coordination.
Those efforts would take place as needed, but at least once a month, according to the agreement.

articles.title: The Caspian at War’s Edge: Proxy Conflict, Eroding Axes, and Rising Middle Powers - trendsgroup.org
articles.summary: The Caspian at War’s Edge: Proxy Conflict, Eroding Axes, and Rising Middle Powers  trendsgroup.org
articles.full_text:
With much of the world’s attention fixed on the war in the Arabian Gulf and the crisis surrounding the Strait of Hormuz, another strategically vital basin, the Caspian Sea, is quietly emerging as a new arena of geopolitical contestation. Long regarded as a safe haven, the Caspian has held immense importance for its littoral states in terms of energy, trade, and logistics.
Since the Soviet Union’s collapse, these states agreed to bar the presence of non‑littoral armed forces, a stance that safeguarded regional autonomy and stability. This framework enabled countries such as Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan, and Kazakhstan to advance ambitious maritime and transport infrastructure projects along the basin, reinforcing the Middle Corridor transit route and positioning the Caspian as a linchpin of Eurasian connectivity.
Recent developments in Caspian Sea security carry long‑term consequences well beyond the region. Against the backdrop of two major conflicts, the Russia‑Ukraine war and the U.S.‑Iran confrontation, the basin has faced unprecedented breaches. In 2025, Ukrainian drones struck Russia’s Filanovsky oil platform, marking the first attack of its kind in the Caspian. Just months later, in March 2026, Israeli missiles targeted Iranian naval assets at Bandar Anzali, drawing sharp criticism from other littoral states. These incidents culminated in renewed Ukrainian drone strikes on Iranian positions, provoking harsh rhetoric from Tehran.
From Kyiv’s perspective, strikes on Iranian military assets are justified given Tehran’s close alignment with Moscow. From Tehran’s vantage point, however, these Western‑endorsed actions are seen as deliberate attempts to erode its capabilities and diminish its presence in the Caspian. The shifting power dynamics suggest that influence is gradually slipping away from Tehran and Moscow, opening space for other littoral states to assert themselves as more consequential maritime security actors.
Securitization of the Caspian Sea
With the shifting geography of the Russo‑Ukrainian war and the ongoing U.S.–Iran confrontation, the Caspian basin risks emerging as a new theater of intensive military operations. Such a development would undermine the region’s critical energy infrastructure and disrupt East–West trade corridors. For the principal regional actors, notably Iran and Russia, the Caspian Sea has traditionally occupied a secondary position compared to the Gulf or the Black Sea. This relative neglect stems from the fact that the basin has posed fewer immediate security challenges, largely due to the decades‑long consensus among littoral states prohibiting the presence of non‑regional powers in the Caspian.
Nevertheless, the situation radically changed when in March 2026, Israeli fighter jets carried out an audacious and long-range air operation to target Iranian naval vessels and buildings on the Caspian Sea. The strikes hit Iran’s multiple missile boats, including onshore naval infrastructure around the main port of Bandar Anzali, thus complicating security issues in the basin for other regional states, namely Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, and Turkmenistan.[1]
For the last decade, the aforementioned countries have heavily invested in the construction of maritime and energy infrastructure in the Caspian Sea, fostering the development of the Middle Corridor transit route. Stretching from China through Central Asia, the Caucasus, and onward to Türkiye, this corridor sustains historic East–West trade links while offering a viable alternative pathway. As these countries increasingly prioritized energy and trade partnerships via the Caspian basin and strengthened their naval forces while diplomatically maneuvering between East and West, the same basin has simultaneously served as a strategic platform for the Iran–Russia axis amid ongoing conflicts.
For Russia and Iran, the Caspian route not only facilitates energy cooperation and trade flows but also the movement of technologies and materials relevant to sustaining both war economies under sanctions pressure, such as drone components and dual-use technologies.[2] Therefore, in terms of the Russia-Iran axis, the Caspian route functions as a critical node in a broader resilience architecture underpinning long-term strategic convergence between the two. Nevertheless, both parties apprehend that in the last five years, the long-term power balance is shifting away from Tehran and Moscow, as other littoral states unveil enormous efforts to rebuild strong flotillas in the Caspian to tackle potential threats and protect their strategic assets.
Ukraine’s recent long‑range drone strikes against a Russian military‑industrial enterprise, an oil refinery, a fuel and lubricants depot, and transport vessels underscored the limitations of Moscow’s naval power and its diminishing regional influence. A similar vulnerability was revealed in Iran’s inability to safeguard its naval assets during the latest wave of Ukrainian drone attacks, highlighting the broader challenges faced by both states in protecting maritime infrastructure under evolving conflict dynamics.[3] As such, Caspian’s historical status as a “safe haven” for the Moscow-Tehran axis has come under question.
The potential air strikes toward the Caspian in the near future will likely force Russia and Iran to consolidate efforts on multi-level air defense systems and drone monitoring, including the deployment of additional troops and warships.[4] This scenario illustrates how two distinct conflicts converge within a single geographic space, gradually evolving into an emerging Eurasian conflict system in which allied actors are increasingly interdependent. In this context, the Caspian basin provides a unique platform for the coordination of economic and military exchange for the Moscow-Tehran axis.
Moreover, unlike Russia, Iran has demonstrated hesitancy in pursuing open confrontation with Kyiv, a posture that can be attributed to practical limitations. At the same time, Tehran signals preparations for an expanded campaign of air strikes targeting its assets in the Caspian Sea, including the northern provinces of Gilan and Mazandaran. A further source of vulnerability stems from Iran’s longstanding neglect of maritime infrastructure in the Caspian basin, where strategic focus has consistently been directed toward the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz.[5]
In retaliation, Iran and Russia may further increase the deliveries of military components via the Caspian route as part of efforts to deter future Ukrainian drone attacks targeting maritime infrastructure. Although Russia places considerable value on this partnership, Iran currently possesses only limited capacity to deliver substantial quantities of weaponry. In addition, the evolving geopolitical dynamics across greater Eurasia, coupled with persistent security gaps, have compelled non‑regional actors such as Ukraine and Israel to partially view the Caspian basin as an additional theater of war. Indeed, the prospect of conflict spillover into the Caspian region and its littoral states has emboldened regional actors to pursue large‑scale modernization of naval forces and air defense systems, investing in advanced technologies while simultaneously seeking new alliances, such as the emerging Azerbaijan‑Kazakhstan partnership.
Emerging alliances in the Caspian Sea
In recent years, the security of the Caspian basin has emerged as a central concern for nearly all littoral states, driven above all by the imperative to safeguard trade routes. The rapid expansion of the Middle Corridor and the development of critical maritime infrastructure along this axis, highly vulnerable to potential air strikes, underscore the urgency of ensuring its protection. Consequently, there is a growing recognition that the resilience and capacity of the land routes underpinning this transit corridor must be strengthened to guarantee its long‑term security.[6] In light of the continuing disruption of global supply chains due to the ongoing conflicts in Europe and the Middle East, the disruption of the Middle Corridor would have grave consequences both for Western countries and the landlocked Central Asian states.
Recently, Azerbaijan, Türkiye, and Kazakhstan introduced a new partnership framework aimed at enhancing coordination in joint military exercises, naval drills, and air defense systems. For example, in 2023, joint tactical naval exercises held in the Azerbaijani sector of the Caspian Sea between the Azerbaijani and Kazakh Naval Forces near Baku, marking the first such joint exercise between the two and followed by another exercise dubbed Caspian Breeze-2025, were the first-ever large-scale naval drills.[7] The drills specifically covered repelling asymmetric threats, assisting vessels in distress, and live fire drills at sea and against air targets.[8] Moreover, in 2024, Azerbaijani special forces participated in the “Eternal Brotherhood” exercises alongside Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Türkiye, conducted under a scenario focused on the protection of strategic infrastructure and military bases.[9]
While these exercises laid the foundation of a new interregional security format, they also highlighted the importance of regional alliances between “middle powers” like Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan to maintain stability in the Caspian basin. Undoubtedly, such measures enable Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Kazakhstan to strengthen coordination and management in partnership with Türkiye, widely regarded as the principal regional military power.
Beyond bilateral formats, the parties have also established a productive framework within the Organization of Turkic States (OTS), which not only deepens military cooperation but also paves the way for expanded economic and trade ties among member states, thereby elevating the strategic role of the Middle Corridor route.[10] The re-emergence of the OTS as an influential interregional organization since 2022 overlapped with the extension of the Middle Co

articles.title: The Next Congress Needs to Reclaim Its Oversight of the Department of Defense - War on the Rocks
articles.summary: The Next Congress Needs to Reclaim Its Oversight of the Department of Defense  War on the Rocks
articles.full_text:
Join War on the Rocks and gain access to content trusted by policymakers, military leaders, and strategic thinkers worldwide.
Since returning to office in January 2025, the Trump administration has aggressively exercised executive authority across the federal government. Meanwhile, Congress has not adequately applied its oversight role to rein in the executive branch, particularly over the Department of Defense. We have watched these dynamics with specific interest, in discussions with congressional staff over bills and appropriations, and in conversations with our clients.
Congress adjourned at the end of September until after the midterm elections following an unproductive summer legislative session, particularly on foreign policy. While Congress passed a long-debated Russia sanctions bill in September, President Donald Trump has already issued a waiver to it in Moscow’s favor. The Senate failed to pass a procedural resolution challenging Trump’s war powers in Iran. Moreover, Congress has done little to advance the defense authorization bill: While the House barely passed its version of the Fiscal Year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act in July, Senate Democrats blocked their chamber’s version of the bill in protest over the war with Iran in the same month, and have not advanced the bill since. Not coincidentally, Republicans find themselves facing significant election losses, defending their record and a historically unpopular president and administration amidst an ongoing war and executive overreach.
Nowhere has executive expansion been more pronounced than at the Department of Defense, where the administration has asserted broad control over defense contractors, authorized legally dubious strikes on alleged drug smugglers, and conducted decapitation operations against foreign regimes. Recently, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth outlined even more significant expansions of department power and recently declared he will shrink the general/flag officer corps by 20 percent despite bipartisan concerns. Republican leaders have largely acceded to this consolidation of executive power, and their reasons for going along are straightforward. Members of Congress largely live in fear of their voter bases and face the most risk from the president opposing them in primary elections or suppressing the Republican vote in general elections, as demonstrated in the many high-profile primary losses by Republican incumbents this year following Trump endorsements of their opponents.
Yet while the record of the current Congress may seem like continued surrender to the administration’s strategic and fiscal goals for the military, the details of the current dynamic reveal a more complicated situation. Quietly, in the FY26 National Defense Authorization Act and in the evolving FY27 bill, Congress has established tools to reclaim its constitutional role in shaping U.S. defense strategy — relying on procedure, statutory mandates, and funding decisions rather than public confrontation to do so.
While Congress has so far failed to defend the very limits to executive power it authored, the coming months will set the scene for an oversight role amid a more complicated dynamic. With the midterm elections increasingly likely to give Democrats at least partial control of Congress, congressional oversight will be challenging. The administration has announced in response to recent statutes born of the FY26 National Defense Authorization Act that it does not believe Congress has the authority to limit its power or has outright refused to follow congressional direction. Congress cannot legally enforce its statutory requirements over a disobedient executive: It must use its constitutional powers to impose compliance through appropriations, oversight, and even impeachment.
Regardless of how difficult, a future Congress can and should use its powers to limit executive overreach and reassert its role in overseeing national defense.
Over the past year and a half, the Trump administration expanded executive power and concentrated decision-making at a scale with few modern precedents, most prominently within the Department of Defense. Operationally, it executed a series of large-scale military actions — including strikes in Venezuela, expansive maritime interdictions in the Caribbean, and a sustained offensive campaign against Iran — all conducted with little congressional oversight or authorization. At the same time, the administration pursued structural changes to Department of Defense leadership, removing senior civilian and uniformed leaders at an unprecedented pace while advancing plans to remove additional military leaders and merge U.S. Northern Command and Southern Command into a new Western Hemisphere Command. Major acquisition programs and contracts were also canceled or restructured, while defense contractors have been subjected to heightened Department of Defense control, which may be inconsistent with existing statutory and regulatory frameworks.
These shifts — and the tensions between the executive and legislative branches — were first and most clearly reflected in the documents that now define U.S. defense strategy: the 2025 National Security Strategy, the 2026 National Defense Strategy, and the recent National Defense Authorization Acts.
The 2025 National Security Strategy marked a decisive narrowing of U.S. global influence. Adding narrative structure to President Trump’s own strategic instincts, it rejected post-Cold War assumptions of global primacy in favor of regional balances of power and selective engagement in world affairs. In a break from what has historically been U.S. defense strategy to focus on threats posed by China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea, the National Security Strategy prioritized the Western Hemisphere, homeland defense, migration control, and economic security. China was framed as a competitor to be managed rather than a systemic adversary threatening democratic nations, and allies were similarly viewed as transactional partners: pay more for defense or face less U.S. commitment. Ironically, the administration’s war against Iran highlights its lack of consistency within any strategic framework.
The 2026 National Defense Strategy, directed by longtime China hawk Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby, attempted to reconcile this worldview with operational realities. It continued to treat China as the pacing military challenge and emphasized deterrence by denial, forward posture, and coordination with allies. At the same time, it incorporated the administration’s Western Hemisphere-first priorities, producing a document that straddled competing imperatives, aligning rhetorically with the White House while preserving core elements of traditional U.S. defense posture.
In contrast, Congress articulated a far more historically consistent position of U.S. global leadership through funding and statutory direction. The FY26 National Defense Authorization Act and related appropriations sustained a U.S. role in international stability with a globally-postured, competition-centric military along with strong support for and commitment to Europe, Ukraine, and the Indo-Pacific.
The National Defense Authorization Act has historically served as Congress’ vehicle for providing direction in defense strategy: authorizing programs, setting toplines, and providing broad guidance on U.S. relations with allies and adversaries while leaving operational discretion to the executive branch. While the National Defense Authorization Act often reflects continuity and consensus rather than confrontation, Congress and the president have regularly diverged in the past on how each views national security risks, including disagreements over troop commitments, capabilities, and oversight. The Goldwater-Nichols Act of 1986 restructured the joint command system over Pentagon objections, the Nunn-Cohen Amendment to that bill established U.S. Special Operations Command despite resistance from the services, and post-9/11 Congresses used the bills to constrain executive discretion on detention, interrogation, and intelligence reporting.
The FY26 National Defense Authorization Act and the emerging FY27 bill expand on this construct. Rather than ratifying the administration’s narrower concept of American power and exercising broad authorizations, with the recent bills, Congress has diverged from the president’s view — as was previously noted in another War on the Rocks article specifically highlighting Congress’ attempts to check the administration on acquisition. Strategic directives in the National Defense Authorization Acts show Congress asserting its own judgment and intention to preserve U.S. global influence, reinforce commitments to allies and partners, and hold the Department of Defense accountable through prescriptive reporting and notification requirements on force deployment and leadership changes. In doing so, it challenges the assumption that defense strategy, force posture, and alliance management are solely executive prerogatives.
Preserving U.S. Global Influence & Continuing Commitments to Allies
The FY26 National Defense Authorization Act’s Senate preface proclaims the congressional view that the United States is operating in “the most dangerous threat environment since World War II,” driven by an “axis of aggressors” — China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea — whose shared resources and objectives threaten U.S. international influence and security. The FY27 National Defense Authorization Act drafts reflect a similar perspective. The Senate executive summary states that its singular goal in increasing defense funding is to deter the “axis of aggressors”, noting that these nations share “ambition and weapons” with an eye to weaken the United States and rupture alliances among democracies.

articles.full_text:
- India pushes for comprehensive reforms in UN Security Council.
- Veto power must be for all permanent members.
- Calls for text-based negotiations with clear timelines.
India has pushed for comprehensive reforms in the United Nations Security Council (UNSC), adding that the veto power held by the five permanent members must be used with restraint rather than narrow political goals. India’s Permanent Representative to the UN, Parvathaneni Harish, vouched for text-based negotiations on Security Council reforms, with clear timelines and milestones.
What Were The Key Points In India’s Stance
Text-Based Negotiations:India called for the immediate launch of negotiations with clear timelines and milestones covering all five reform clusters together (membership categories, regional representation, council size, working methods, and the veto).
Veto Power Statistics: Ambassador Harish noted that the veto has been cast 331 times across roughly 200 resolutions in the UN's history, with most vetoes or threats coming from only three of the five permanent members (P5). Harish also mentioned the Veto Initiative of 2022, which mandates a United Nations General Assembly debate whenever a veto is cast, with the stated objective of strengthening accountability. However, he said the number of vetoes exercised since the adoption of UN General Assembly Resolution 76/262 presented a contradictory picture.
Recommended For You
The "De Facto Veto":India highlighted hidden blocking mechanisms, pointing out that unwritten consensus rules allow any elected or non-elected member to act as a "de facto veto" over presidential statements, press releases, and sanctions committees. “The veto is not only what is cast in the open. There is also the ‘effective or de facto veto’ that every Council member, elected and non-elected, holds over presidential statements, press statements and the decisions of sanctions committees, where the unwritten rule of consensus allows a single member to hold or block a proposal, most often without explanation," Harish said.
Vouches for equal rights of all permanent members
Reiterating India’s position on the veto, Harish said it remained aligned with the Common African Position on Security Council reform. “We reiterate that as long as a veto exists, it must be held by all permanent members of a reformed Council. Russian leader Vladimir Putin stated on October 29 that Russia is prepared for a war with Europe, though it does not desire one.
Putin argued that inflicting a strategic defeat on Russia by 2030 is unlikely to be possible, according to The Moscow Times.
Speaking at a press conference following the Russia-Africa summit, Putin questioned discussions about preparing for military conflict by 2030, stating, “Many are only talking about preparing for war by 2030. Is this right? No. First of all, we are ready, but we do not want any war with Europe.”
He added that Moscow supports steps to restore relations with Europe, both as a whole and with individual nations, while issuing a warning about severe escalation: “And if it goes too far, there will be no winners at all. Let no one forget about this,” The Moscow Times reported.
Regarding maritime security, the Russian leader stated that Moscow wishes to avoid escalation in the Baltic Sea comparable to conditions in the Persian Gulf or the Strait of Hormuz. “We do not want such a situation, but we will respond to any challenge,” Putin said, emphasizing the need to uphold international law.
He noted that the Baltic situation was discussed during conversations held on the initiative of Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre.
Earlier in October, Russian special services were instructed to intensify hybrid operations across EU and NATO states, relying on agents recruited by the GRU and FSB.
Starlink receiving stations in Europe were identified among the likely targets. In Latvia, two citizens were detained on suspicion of gathering intelligence for the GRU on NATO activity, radar systems, and military infrastructure, with one allegedly photographing the Ādaži military base from a private aircraft.

articles.title: In Pompeii, a woman's wardrobe resurfaces with beauty items and jewels - Euronews.com
articles.summary: In Pompeii, a woman's wardrobe resurfaces with beauty items and jewels  Euronews.comPompeii cupboard opens window onto life before Vesuvius erupted  ReutersPerfume bottle and child’s necklace among treasures found in Pompeii wardrobe  The Guardian'Thought to be lost forever': After 2,000 years, a library buried by Pompeii’s eruption is finally revealing its secrets  BBC Science Focus MagazineNews - Household Cupboard Excavated in Pompeii  Archaeo...
articles.full_text:
Jewels, coins, tools and cosmetics: a cupboard in Cornelius Maximus's house brings to life the daily lives of Pompeii's women before Vesuvius erupted in AD 79.
The wardrobe of a woman from ancient Pompeii has come to light again. Thanks to the work of archaeologists it has been possible to recover the interior of a cabinet that held everyday items in house IX 11, 7, or the house of Cornelius Maximus, in the central area of the city buried by Vesuvius.
Looking at these objects, it is almost as if we can conjure up the life of a woman of Pompeii before the site was destroyed in AD 79. Among the finds are make-up tools(tweezers, a spatula for mixing pigments), a glass balsamarium, a perfume burner to fill the home with pleasant fragrances, a bronze lamp, alongside lead weights, probably used for a commercial activity and kept in a small wooden box of which only faint traces remain.
What was in the Pompeian woman's wardrobe
Vases and pots in bronze, glass and ceramic were also found: everyday household objects, but perhaps also heavy with memories, as in the case of an elegant little jug decorated with pine-scale motifs. There is also a necklace composed of at least 24 miniature objectsin faïence, bone, glass paste and rock crystal, all pierced for suspension and representing deities (Bes and Mercury can be identified), feet and hands, pine cones and bunches of grapes.
According to experts, such necklaces were sometimes regarded as "magical" objects used in spells and potions; in reality they are what are known as crepundia, literally 'rattles': necklaces with amulets that were given to children to protect them, but also so that they could be heard when they moved.
It was not unusual for adults to keep them too, often in small boxes or, as in this case, in cloth bags inside wardrobes, apparently as keepsakes of a childhood of which little else remained. The Roman world was characterised by a high degree of geographic mobility at all levels, from slaves to wealthy merchants, so that many people found themselves living far from relatives and parents and from the places of their childhood.
The small treasure hidden in the wardrobe
Another secret kept in the wardrobe unearthed in the excavation is a small hoard of coins: there are 38 of them, all bronze, preserved in a "cistella", a small container made of plant material using basketry techniques, the remains of which were analysed after being recovered during the dig. The presence of the coins in particular suggests that the owner or owners did not have time to recover the objects of value, whether economic or emotional.
If they were in the city at the time of the catastrophe, they will have tried to flee. If they managed to escape, they would not have returned to dig under the floors for their possessions, unlike others whose efforts have left traces revealed by recent excavations.
But perhaps they did not succeed and may be among those who, as the historian Tacitus recalls, died without heirs and whose property would have been used for the refounding of Pompeii, which ultimately never took place. These are questions destined to remain open.
The human dimension of Pompeii's past pieced back together
"Pompeii is not just a place of great works of art; it is also somewhere where the most ordinary objects restore the human dimension of the past. The value of this discovery lies in the possibility of reading together the different traces of a life: personal habits, work, memories," says the director of the Archaeological Park, Gabriel Zuchtriegel.
"We cannot reconstruct with certainty the identity of the person who lived in the house, but these fragments bring us closer to their everyday life," the director adds.
What we know about the House of Cornelius Maximus
The excavation has helped clarify some aspects of the house in which the wardrobe was found. The facade of the dwelling, tentatively attributed to a figure named Cornelius Maximus on the basis of inscriptions now no longer visible, had already been excavated in 1912. Only now, however, has part of the rooms behind it been investigated, as part of the major restoration and accessibility project for the adjacent Insula dei Casti Amanti.
Although our knowledge of the house remains partial, some highly interesting data have emerged: on the one hand, the refined Fourth Style wall paintings in the room with the wardrobe, attributable to the workshop on Via di Castricio, indicate a certain standard of living, in line with the central position of the house, which overlooks one of the main arteries of the ancient city.
On the other hand, at the time of the eruption various works were nevertheless in progress that must have affected liveability considerably. Added to this is the discovery of at least two mouse skeletons, found inside an amphora on a mezzanine. According to analyses carried out in the park's laboratory, they probably belonged to the species Apodemus sylvaticus, also known as the "wood mouse".
Mice of this kind normally live in natural environments and gardens, from where they often invade attics and storage areas in human dwellings in search of food. The two specimens found at Pompeii were not fully mature, as indicated by the degree of development of their skeletons (117 tiny fragments). The discovery adds to evidence of the presence of rodents in other Vesuvian contexts, such as the service quarters of the suburban villa at Civita Giuliana or the sewers of Herculaneum, and offers the image of an urban society that also had to contend with unwelcome guests.

articles.title: Hackers Exploited Cisco SD-WAN Flaw to Plant Malware Built to Steal Encryption Keys - The Hacker News
articles.summary: Hackers Exploited Cisco SD-WAN Flaw to Plant Malware Built to Steal Encryption Keys  The Hacker News
articles.full_text:
Hackers exploited a critical Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN flaw, fixed in February, to plant custom malware inside the systems that control an organization's SD-WAN network.
The malware, called KeyDrift, is designed to copy the keys that encrypt traffic between sites and store them for later use, Cisco Talos said on October 28. Talos calls the attacks historical but does not specify when they occurred or whether any keys were sent.
The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-20127 and has a CVSS score of 10.0. It allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to bypass authentication and gain administrative privileges on these control systems. On a Controller, the attacker can log in as a high-privileged internal account that is not root.
When Cisco disclosed the flaw in February, Talos tracked its exploitation as UAT-8616, a cluster of activity it said went back to at least 2023.
In Cisco's traditional key exchange, each SD-WAN router periodically generates an AES key for its traffic and sends it to the Catalyst SD-WAN Controller (formerly vSmart). The Controller passes the keys on to other routers. A process on the Controller called vdaemon runs the encrypted control connections that carry these keys.
On a compromised Controller, a KeyDrift component called LittleFilch hooks into vdaemon and reads control messages after they are decrypted. For a preset list of edge routers, it pulls out their IP addresses and a 32-byte field. Talos assesses that field as the AES-256 key material that the Controller passes between routers.
LittleFilch encrypts what it collects with RSA and writes it to a file. It can then send that data over UDP to an address listed in a settings file, which it deletes after reading. Talos could not recover that settings file.
The group behind KeyDrift, which Talos tracks as UAT-11473, has targeted space and satellite services, defense and aerospace technology, and policy research.
The group's infrastructure "overlaps considerably" with Silent Train, Talos assesses with high confidence. Silent Train is the name Lumen's Black Lotus Labs uses for a network of hacked small-office, home-office, IoT and business devices.
Lumen says Volt Typhoon used the network to hide its activity. CISA, the NSA and the FBI said in 2024 that Volt Typhoon is a Chinese state-sponsored cyber group.
Talos links UAT-11473 to Volt Typhoon only through the infrastructure overlap. It does not say the two are the same group, or how UAT-11473 relates to UAT-8616, the cluster it reported in February.
Separately, Lumen said on October 28 that Volt Typhoon was exploiting CVE-2026-20127 by late 2025 and continued to exploit it after Cisco disclosed the flaw in February. Lumen does not tie that activity to KeyDrift.
KeyDrift primarily starts via modified runit scripts that Cisco SD-WAN devices use to launch their services, according to Talos. In one version, the script for the SSH service starts a loader script, conf_sshd, before the real SSH server. The conf_sshd script writes vdaemon's process IDs to a file, and a tool called rsshd injects KeyDrift's main module, PolyFlame, into each of those processes.
PolyFlame runs in memory inside vdaemon. It can act as a TinyShell-like backdoor that runs commands and reads and writes files, or as a relay that forwards commands between its command server and other machines. It is built to accept commands within SD-WAN control traffic, and the analyzed samples contained no hardcoded server address.
On a compromised Validator, formerly vBond, a fake aaamgr service under /etc/sv/aaamgr/ runs a packed loader, aaamgrd, that decrypts and runs PolyFlame. Cisco's real aaamgr component is a Python package and does not normally run as a compiled service.
There are also signs of timestomping: commands the group ran copied the timestamps and permissions of existing files onto its own files.
CVE-2026-20127 affects the Catalyst SD-WAN Controller (formerly vSmart), Manager (formerly vManage), and Validator (formerly vBond), regardless of their configuration. On-premises systems are affected, as are Cisco's hosted SD-WAN cloud deployments, including the Cisco Managed and FedRAMP environments. Cisco added the Validator to its advisory on June 16.
Cisco says it is aware of limited exploitation of the flaw. There is no workaround, and the first fixed releases are:
| Release train | First fixed release | 
|---|---|
| Earlier than 20.9 | Migrate to a fixed release | 
| 20.9 | 20.9.8.2 | 
| 20.11 | 20.12.6.1 | 
| 20.12 | 20.12.5.3 or 20.12.6.1 | 
| 20.13 | 20.15.4.2 | 
| 20.14 | 20.15.4.2 | 
| 20.15 | 20.15.4.2 | 
| 20.16 | 20.18.2.1 | 
| 20.18 | 20.18.2.1 | 
Releases earlier than 20.9 and the 20.11, 20.13, 20.14 and 20.16 trains have reached end of software maintenance.
Until they can upgrade, on-premises customers can limit access to ports 22 and 830 to the IP addresses of known controllers and other known systems. Cisco says this step worked in a test environment, but that customers should check how well it works in their own networks. Such guardrails are already in place for Cisco's hosted SD-WAN cloud deployments.
Blocking the ports does not remove malware already on a device.
Talos advises organizations to install Cisco's fixes, follow Cisco's Catalyst SD-WAN hardening guide and watch for signs of post-compromise activity. Anyone who finds such signs should start incident response and can ask Cisco's Technical Assistance Center (TAC) for help.
That advice does not say whether upgrading removes KeyDrift from a device that was already compromised, or whether any keys should be replaced. Cisco's February remediation guide for this flaw warns that there could be "existing exploits which are still in place" from before an upgrade.
KeyDrift uses these files and locations, some given only by name:
- File: the run script under etc/sv/sshd/, modified to start conf_sshd
- Directory: /etc/sv/aaamgr/, a fake service on a compromised Validator
- File: aaamgrd, the packed loader
- File: conf_sshd, the loader script
- File: rsshd, the injector
- File: libdssl.so, PolyFlame
- File: libcommon.so, LittleFilch
- File: /tmp/system-vdaemon, the list of vdaemon process IDs
- File: /var/tmp/vdaemon.bin, LittleFilch's encrypted records
- File: /var/tmp/vdaemon.conf, LittleFilch's send settings, deleted after reading
Talos's report does not include a list of file hashes, IP addresses or domains for KeyDrift.
Talos released Snort rules on October 28 that look for inbound KeyDrift command-and-control connections: 67387 through 67416 for Snort 2, and 7:44 through 7:73 for Snort 3. Rules 65938 and 65958, already available, cover CVE-2026-20127 itself.
The October 28 rule update lists the Snort 2 rules as disabled by default, so users of the paid Snort Subscriber rule set must turn them on. The Snort 3 rules appear with no default state.
To check for exploitation of the flaw itself, Cisco says to look in /var/log/auth.log for Accepted publickey for vmanage-admin entries from unknown IP addresses. Before opening a TAC case, customers should run request admin-tech on each control component. The remediation guide also recommends rescanning those admin-tech files with the Check Bug Applicability feature on the Bug Search Tool page for bug CSCws52722.
For US federal civilian agencies, CISA's February 25 emergency directive sets out what to do if a root account compromise is found. They must report it to CISA, deploy fresh Manager, Controller and Validator instances from patched images, and move their edge routers to the new systems.

articles.title: US warns allies to prepare for possible Iran strikes, retaliation after elections, AP sources say - AP News
articles.summary: US warns allies to prepare for possible Iran strikes, retaliation after elections, AP sources say  AP News
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. officials have told several Middle East countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military action against Iran after next week’s midterm elections in the United States — as well as the possibility that Iran will attempt to retaliate against them, according to two diplomats briefed on the matter.
Both of the diplomats spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment about the sensitive warnings conveyed by U.S. diplomats and defense officials.
President Donald Trump has not made a final decision on whether to carry out new strikes against Iran, the diplomats stressed. The president, however, has repeatedly said that he is weighing ordering new military action once the critical Nov. 3 elections in the United States are over.
Those threats and the fresh U.S. urgings for allies to prepare for potential retaliation are putting the region on alert that a return to major operations could now be on the horizon.
The U.S. is warning Middle East allies that attacks against Iran may resume soon. AP correspondent Jennifer King reports.
The White House and U.S. officials declined to comment.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday in a post on X that Tehran “continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed” and is working with mediators to review ideas that Tehran included in a proposal floated last month — summarily rejected by Trump — that the Iranians still want to see used as the basis to return to a ceasefire.
Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates foreign ministry issued a statement urging the sides to “exercise wisdom and pursue political solutions to help contain tensions” and prevent a return to full-scale operations in the war that began in late February.
The U.S. has told regional allies that the new round of military action could last for several days, but regional officials are bracing for Iran and its proxy groups to retaliate — leading to a fight that could last even longer, the diplomats said.
The allies have also been urged by U.S. officials to take precautionary measures in anticipation that Iran’s response will include retaliatory strikes on energy facilities and other crucial infrastructure.
It’s unclear how soon the US military would be ready
While the U.S. has not carried out a strike against Iran since early September, the situation in the Middle East has become more complicated.
The conflict has spread, with Iran-backed Houthi rebels carrying out attacks on Saudi Arabia’s oil infrastructure and airports. A Saudi-led coalition has responded with its own deadly attacks on Houthi-held territory in Yemen.
The Wall Street Journal reported earlier on Gulf nations being briefed to be prepared for potential escalation by the U.S.
It’s unclear how soon after Election Day that the U.S. military would be ready to potentially resume strikes.
The Pentagon late last month deployed the USS Theodore Roosevelt, along with a series of amphibious landing ships with Marines aboard -- roughly 9,000 troops in all -- from San Diego to the Persian Gulf to bolster the U.S. military in the region.
At the time, one U.S. official said this deployment could lead to an unusually high naval presence of more than 20,000 sailors and Marines, as well as hundreds of aircraft, in the region, which has only occurred a handful of times in the last two decades. The Navy had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April for the first time since 2003.
Late Wednesday, reports emerged that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had fired the Pentagon’s top military planner. Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia was removed as head of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Chiefs of Staff, according to a defense official who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive personnel matters. That official said there is no immediate replacement for Sylvia and no reason has been given for the firing.
Trump, who has focused in recent weeks on campaigning for Republicans ahead of the Nov. 3 elections, has been evasive about what he plans to do next with Iran.
The war has proved to be a heavy weight on Republican candidates as they make their case to voters who are fatigued by rising gasoline prices, a byproduct of the war that’s driven up costs across nearly every sector in the global economy.
The cost of fighting the Iran war to American taxpayers has grown to $47.1 billion, according to the latest estimate the Pentagon has provided to Congress.
While campaigning for Republicans, Trump has consistently assured voters that the war’s end is near, while also threatening that a new round of bombing could be coming once the election passes.
During a campaign stop in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday, Trump said a conclusive end to the eight-month-old conflict could be coming “in a couple of weeks, if you don’t mind.”
“Somebody asked me before, when will the war in Iran end?” Trump said earlier in the same address. “I said, ‘Whenever I want it to end.’ It’ll be very quick, but we have to have it end properly, with total and complete -- a total statement, they will never have a nuclear weapon.”
Trump may be looking at a postelection timeline for possible action, but the region is on edge that Tehran could do something provocative before then -- especially if they feel U.S. actions is imminent, said Jonathan Schanzer, executive director at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a hawkish Washington think tank.
“Why would they wait until after the elections here ... if they could initiate it and potentially gain the upper hand?” he said.
___
Magdy reported from New York. AP writers Konstantin Toropin and Seung Min Kim contributed reporting.
