articles.full_text:
Toplines
Russia and Ukraine continued observing a limited ceasefire in occupied Kherson Oblast on October 28, but it remains unclear whether Ukrainian civilians will have a legitimate and duress-free choice to return to Ukrainian government-controlled Ukraine.
Ukraine’s Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets and Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova confirmed on October 28 that there were no ceasefire violations in Russian-occupied Oleshky in the first 30 hours since the agreement entered into force on the morning of October 27.
[1] US First Lady Melania Trump reported on October 27 that the limited ceasefire will cover other unspecified areas of Kherson Oblast to provide safe passage for humanitarian convoys, and sources told the BBC on October 27 that the ceasefire extends to all of Kherson Oblast.
[2] Fox News published on October 28 reported photos of the ceasefire agreement confirming that the Ukrainian delegation and Oleshky residents who wish to evacuate to Ukraine will travel to Anapa, Krasnodar Krai in Russia and then to Gomel, Belarus on October 31.
[3] The part of the agreement that Fox News reported did not provide details on how the evacuated Oleshky citizens and the Ukrainian delegation will subsequently travel from Belarus to Ukrainian government-controlled Ukraine, however.
The photos of the ceasefire agreement indicate that the Russian Dnepr Grouping of Forces (GoF) is facilitating the ceasefire.
Russian Defense Minister Andrei Belousov inspected the Russian Dnepr GoF and met with its commander, Colonel General Mikhail Teplinsky, on October 27, and the Russian Ministry of Defense (MoD) claimed that they primarily discussed Russian unmanned system operations in the area.
[4] Russian forces may use the limited ceasefire to reconstitute their forces in Kherson Oblast.
It remains unclear how Russian authorities will treat Ukrainians evacuated from Oleshky and whether Russian authorities will provide the residents a legitimate and duress-free choice to return to Ukrainian government-controlled Ukraine.
[5]
The Kremlin continues efforts to persuade the Trump administration to make economic concessions and pursue business cooperation with Russia, even as Russia continues to refuse to make any concessions of its own to end its war in Ukraine.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov claimed on October 27 that the October 9 US-Russia diesel deal is a “purely business agreement” and that there were “no conditions or stipulations whatsoever” requiring any Russian political action or security concerns in exchange for the US purchase of Russian diesel.
[6] Lavrov also noted that the informational war around Ukraine will continue and even has a “tendency to escalate.
” Kremlin Spokesperson Dmitry Peskov similarly claimed on October 13 that there is “no direct connection” between the US-Russia diesel deal and peace negotiations to end the war in Ukraine.
[7] Lavrov’s and Peskov’s statements notably contradict Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF) CEO Kirill Dmitriev’s October 12 claim that the diesel deal facilitates efforts for peace in Ukraine and Dmitriev’s October 17 claim that the suspension of some US sanctions on Russia would facilitate a “lasting peace” in Ukraine.
[8] High-ranking Kremlin officials are attempting to separate economic agreements with the United States from peace negotiations in order to obtain US economic concessions that will support Russia’s continued war effort while Russia has made no concessions that would enable any meaningful peace negotiations.
[9] Kremlin officials have repeatedly affirmed Russia’s commitment to its long-standing maximalist military goals in Ukraine and refusal to make any concessions toward a peace settlement.
[10]
Kremlin officials continue attempts to exclude Europe from peace negotiations to end the war in Ukraine while reiterating Russia’s 2021 demand for NATO to rollback its presence in Europe.
Lavrov claimed that Russian President Vladimir Putin’s October 27 call with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store demonstrated the European desire to “squeeze” themselves into peace negotiations.
[11] Russian Presidential Aide Yuriy Ushakov claimed on October 28 that Russia, Ukraine, and the United States do not plan to have European representatives at the planned trilateral peace negotiations in November.
[12] Peskov, however, claimed on October 25 that Russian would support a European peace negotiator, especially one who wants to facilitate a peace settlement.
[13] Peskov’s statement suggests that Russia will only support European negotiators who will surrender to Russia’s maximalist demands for full Ukrainian capitulation.
Lavrov’s and Ushakov’s statements came against the backdrop of the Kremlin’s recent renewal of the demands it first articulated in December 2021 that included retrograding the membership of NATO states that joined the alliance since 1997 — effectively granting Russia a veto over NATO internal policies and curtailing the sovereignty of many European states to choose to join alliances.
[14] The Kremlin has routinely tried to exclude European leaders from peace negotiations to end the war in Ukraine, including portraying the United States and Russia as the only relevant negotiating actors.
[15]
Three unidentified — possibly Russian — unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) struck a cargo ship off the coast of Bulgaria on October 28. Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov stated on October 28 that three USVs struck the Contship Jet container ship approximately “21 miles” (likely referring to nautical miles) southeast of Shalba, Bulgaria.[16] Automatic identification systems (AIS) data from Marine Traffic, a shipping tracking website, indicates that the Liberian-flagged Contship Jet ship was traveling from Haifa, Israel to Constanta, Romania, and Greek shipping company Contships Management stated that the vessel’s crew included four Ukrainians.[17] A Kremlin-affiliated Russian milblogger claimed that the Contship Jet could have been carrying unspecified cargo to Constanta, a supply hub for Ukraine.[18] The October 28 strike comes against the backdrop of recent Russian strikes against vessels in the Black Sea, including drone strikes against civilian vessels near and within Romanian territorial waters on October 13, 14, and 23 and within the Bulgarian Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) on October 5 and overnight on October 12 to 13.[19]
Russia continues to actively support Iranian-backed operations against US allies in the Middle East.
[NOTE: A version of the following text also appeared in ISW-CTP’s October 28 Iran Update.
] A Switzerland-based geospatial intelligence firm told the Associated Press on October 28 that it has consistently observed Russian military satellites positioned above major Saudi energy and military sites in the days prior to and following Houthi drone and missile strikes against Saudi Arabia.
[20] Russian satellite activity followed a similar pattern around strikes against Saudi infrastructure originating from Iraq, where the Houthis maintain a presence.
A Saudi official and a high-ranking Houthi official separately told the Associated Press that Russia is providing satellite-based targeting intelligence to the Houthis, reportedly through Iranian military advisers who are operating in Yemen.
[21] Russian pre- and post-strike imagery very likely enables the Houthis and Iranian military advisers to conduct battle damage assessments of their strikes.
[22] The geospatial intelligence firm observed 40 instances of Russian satellite positioning over Saudi military and energy sites between July 1 and October 19, including the September 10 drone strike on the Saudi East-West Pipeline.
[23] Russian support is enabling the Iranian-supported Houthi campaign to constrain Saudi Arabia’s ability to export oil during a global energy crisis that Iran has caused by striking ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
[24]
Russian support for Houthi efforts to disrupt Saudi energy exports is consistent with long-standing Russian support for Iran and its regional partners, particularly the Houthis. Russia previously provided the Houthis with satellite-based targeting intelligence to help the group strike US vessels and international shipping in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden in 2023 and 2024, for example.[25] The Houthis supported Russia, in turn, by promising to not target Russian vessels in the Red Sea and by recruiting Yemenis to fight for Russia in Ukraine.[26] Russia has also provided targeting intelligence to support Iranian strikes on Saudi Arabia and other regional targets during the current conflict in the Middle East, according to unspecified sources speaking to the Associated Press.[27] Russian intelligence sharing with Iran and its partners in the ongoing war demonstrates how Russia is directly supporting Iranian and Iranian-backed efforts to disrupt global energy markets and raise the cost of oil.[28]
Key Takeaways
- Russia and Ukraine continued observing a limited ceasefire in occupied Kherson Oblast on October 28, but it remains unclear whether Ukrainian civilians will have a legitimate and duress-free choice to return to Ukrainian government-controlled Ukraine.
- The Kremlin continues efforts to persuade the Trump administration to make economic concessions and pursue business cooperation with Russia even as Russia continues to refuse to make any concessions of its own to end its war in Ukraine.
- Kremlin officials continue attempts to exclude Europe from peace negotiations to end the war in Ukraine while reiterating Russia’s 2021 demand for NATO to roll back its presence in Europe.
- Three unidentified — possibly Russian — unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) struck a cargo ship off the coast of Bulgaria on October 28.
- Russia continues to actively support Iranian-backed operations against US allies in the Middle East.
- Ukrainian forces recently advanced southeast of Oleksandrivka and northeas

articles.summary: Real estate CEO and family shot, attacked with hammer by masked intruders in home invasion robbery  Fox BusinessVictim of violent Bridle Path home invasion speaks out, says family is 'traumatized'  CBCManhunt under way after Toronto CEO and family violently attacked in home invasion  BBCReal Estate CEO, His 2 Daughters and Wife Shot After Masked Men Invade Their Home  People.comToronto CEO speaks out after he and daughters shot in ‘horrific and violent’ Br...
articles.full_text:
A Canadian real estate CEO and his family were attacked by three masked intruders at their multi-million-dollar home in Toronto this week, leaving two of them with "life-altering injuries," according to police and reports.
David Morton, the CEO of the MAC Group, and his two daughters were shot in the attack, police said, and his wife, Doriana Zohil-Morton, was attacked with a hammer.
"A struggle ensued during this altercation in which the suspects fired their guns multiple times and one victim was struck with a hammer," Toronto Police Insp. Kristy Smith said at a Thursday press conference.
She added, "We recognize how frightening and disturbing an incident like this is. People should be able to feel safe in their homes."
Smith said the intruders entered through a locked back door in the exclusive Bride Path neighborhood of Toronto early Thursday morning.
Police don’t yet have a detailed description of the suspects. They fled in an SUV, Smith said.
Morton was shot in the leg along with one of his daughters, the Toronto Sun reported. His other daughter was shot under the arm.
"There was a violent interaction. There was a demand made for valuables from within the home," Smith said. "Whether or not they escaped with anything is uncertain at this point."
She added, "An affluent area where people would have things that are sought after would be the motivation for this."
Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow said she was "deeply troubled" by the attack.
"My thoughts are with the family and their loved ones, who are going through something no family should ever have to face," she said. "I am praying for their full recovery. This attack has understandably shaken the neighbourhood and many residents across Toronto."
She continued, "This violence is not acceptable in our city. People must be safe in their own homes. Toronto Police are investigating and they have my full support as they work to find those responsible and hold them accountable to the fullest extent of the law."

A historian has detailed what country she believes would start World War III as tensions continue through multiple wars across the world.
With the situation involving Russia and Ukraine in Europe, as well as the tensions continuing in the Middle East, the world is certainly an ever-changing place.
Discussion surrounding a potential World War III is the loudest it's ever been and speaking on a recent podcast, an historian detailed which country would likely start it.
Appearing on The Diary of a CEO, Dr. Sarah Paine, a historian and professor, claimed World War Three would happen 'if we continue in the current direction of travel'.
Advert
Steven Bartlett, the host of the podcast, suggested it would be a Russian invasion of Poland which would start a third World War, which Dr. Paine agreed with.
Advert
The historian then provided an 'obscene' prognosis about what that could potentially look like.
Dr. Paine told Bartlett: "I have no idea (what World War Three would look like). But you can get on a nice computer program, pick your mega tonnage of a nuclear weapon and you can put it over a city of your choice and see how many people die. It's obscene.
Advert
"And that's the problem with having these dark personalities running countries like Putin. He doesn't care how many people he kills."
She added elsewhere in the podcast: "We're potentially barreling our way into a world war. We have reckless people running some very large and important countries around the world.
"I believe that Russia has unlimited objectives, that Putin wants to restore the old Soviet empire."
As Poland is a NATO member, the alliance's Article 5 mutual defense clause would be triggered if Putin the European nation.
All NATO allies would be bound to their alliance to one another and would have to respond to the attack with their own forces.
Advert
The NATO article states: "The Parties agree that an armed attack against one or more of them in Europe or North America shall be considered an attack against them all and consequently they agree that, if such an armed attack occurs, each of them, in exercise of the right of individual or collective self-defense recognized by Article 51 of the Charter of the United Nations, will assist the Party or Parties so attacked by taking forthwith, individually and in concert with the other Parties, such action as it deems necessary, including the use of armed force, to restore and maintain the security of the North Atlantic area."

articles.full_text:
Fragments of personal objects, from makeup tools and a perfume bottle to coins and a child’s necklace, have been found tucked away in a wooden wardrobe sealed off for almost 2,000 years in the ruins of Pompeii.
The artifacts provide an intimate glimpse of daily life in the ancient Roman city before it was devastated by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD79. The wardrobe was discovered in a room of a home on Via dell’Abbondanza, which was one of the most bustling streets in Pompeii.
The items inside included tweezers, a small glass perfume bottle, an incense burner and a bronze lantern.
But the most intriguing relic was a necklace featuring more than 20 small charms crafted from various materials and representing several deities, including depictions of the gods Bes and Mercury.
The type of necklace, known as a crepundia, was traditionally worn by children. Its decorative charms rattled to help parents keep track of their children and could also help them be identified.
“A crepundia had a very special function,” said Gabriel Zuchtriegel, the director of Pompeii archaeological park.
“It was a reminder of their parents who perhaps lived far away … it was very typical of this society of people, who were often displaced. Many people moved around in the Mediterranean area and tended to carry personal objects with them.”
The wardrobe contained other items including 38 bronze coins, cooking pots and a wooden box with lead weights, suggesting that someone who lived in the home was a tradesperson.
The fact that money and personal objects were left behind could point to the owners having to flee the eruption at short notice, Zuchtriegel said.
Archaeologists also found the fragmented skeletons of two mice inside an amphora that had been kept in a storage area of the home.
The home had previously been associated with a person called Cornelius Maximus owing to the discovery of inscriptions, which are no longer visible. Its facade was first excavated in 1912, but experts are only now delving into some of its rooms as part of a wider restoration project.
There are also excavations under way at the Villa of the Mysteries in a suburb of Pompeii, which also first came to light in the early 20th century.
“It’s never been completely excavated, so we kind of want to finish the job,” said Zuchtriegel. “What’s interesting is that we’re not excavating in the part where the owners lived and where great frescoes are to be expected, but in the servants’ quarters.
“So what we hope to find there is more insight into the daily life and economy of those who were somehow in the shadow of history. The majority of the inhabitants in the Villa of the Mysteries were actually servants.”
Excavations at Pompeii regularly yield discoveries from the ruins of the ancient city. In 2025, a large and sophisticated thermal bath complex, which was thought to have been used by its owner to woo well-heeled guests, was found during excavations of a home on Via di Nola in Regio IX, a wealthy district of the city.
A home containing a cramped bakery, where enslaved people were believed to have been imprisoned and made to produce bread, was found in the same district in 2023.

Russia and Ukraine traded strikes on each other’s energy infrastructure overnight as the Ukrainian city of Dnipro saw a near-total blackout and an oil refinery in western Russia was engulfed in flames after a drone attack.
Emergency power cuts came into force in Dnipro and Dnipropetrovsk Oblast early Friday after damage from Russian attacks, according to Ukrainian private energy company DTEK.
More than 350,000 people were left without power and work is ongoing to restore supply, Oleksandr Hanzha, the head of the military administration in the region, said in a Telegram post.
An oil refinery in the Russian city of Novokuibyshevsk in Samara Oblast that produced jet fuel for the Russian armed forces was set on fire after being hit by a Ukrainian drone.
Late Thursday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces had destroyed two Russian Su-34 fighter jets and struck an Iskander missile launcher.
He also warned that Russia was preparing further high-speed missile attacks and urged Ukraine’s allies to urgently supply more air defense interceptors, particularly for Patriot systems.
“We now have intel about the Russians preparing new ballistic missile attacks,” Zelenskyy said in an evening address from Kyiv. “We need the capabilities to shoot down this Russian evil and are awaiting the decisions,” he added, referring to anti-ballistic defense capabilities provided by allies.
Ukraine is facing an acute shortage of interceptors to shoot down incoming Russian ballistic missiles.
Early Thursday, at least 14 people were killed in an attack on a Ukrainian rail platform in Dnipro, while at least six more people died in additional strikes throughout the day, according to officials.
The attacks came as a six-day local ceasefire in Kherson in southern Ukraine appeared to hold for a third day, raising cautious optimism that a broader truce may be possible.
While attempts at a peace deal have so far been unsuccessful, a new round of U.S.-brokered peace negotiations is expected next month in Abu Dhabi. Both sides have emphasized the need for security guarantees.
Tensions have run high between Zelenskyy and President Donald Trump in recent weeks, amid a series of moves by the Trump administration that appeared to favor Russia, including easing of economic sanctions.
Reuters reported Friday that the Pentagon has told NATO allies to tone down public criticism of Russia, citing four people familiar with the matter.
Trump has also accused Ukraine of raising fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3 with attacks on Russian energy facilities.
An “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine announced by Trump on Oct. 11 failed to yield any meaningful outcome.

articles.full_text:
Unprecedented Barrage Triggers Regional Security Alerts
North Korea fired a barrage of approximately 10 to 12 short-range ballistic missiles toward its eastern sea between October 28 and October 29, 2026, triggering emergency alerts in Japan and drawing immediate condemnation from regional allies. The coordinated launches represent a significant escalation in Pyongyang’s recent weapons testing cycle, raising security concerns across the Korean Peninsula.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff detected the multiple projectiles fired from the Pyongyang area toward the East Sea, also known as the Sea of Japan. Japan’s Coast Guard and Prime Minister’s Office issued emergency alerts within minutes of the first launch, with Japanese authorities instructing residents in northern regions to take precautionary measures. The sheer volume of the simultaneous launches is highly unusual and signals a deliberate attempt to demonstrate operational readiness and saturation capabilities.
Technical Assessment and Strategic Capabilities
Military analysts suggest the barrage likely involved advanced solid-fuel short-range ballistic missiles, such as the KN-23 or KN-24 variants. These systems are specifically designed to evade regional missile defense networks through depressed trajectories, unpredictable mid-air maneuvers, and low-altitude flight profiles that complicate radar tracking and interception efforts.
By launching a dozen missiles simultaneously, Pyongyang is effectively testing its ability to overwhelm theater missile defense systems, including the Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) batteries deployed by the United States and South Korea. Defense experts note that this saturation tactic is a core component of North Korea’s asymmetric warfare doctrine, aimed at ensuring that a sufficient number of warheads can penetrate allied defenses in a potential conflict scenario.
- Launch Origin: Detected from multiple sites within the Pyongyang metropolitan area.
- Flight Trajectory: Estimated range of 350 to 400 kilometers, covering key military targets in South Korea.
- Apogee: Flew at a depressed trajectory, complicating standard ballistic missile early warning systems.
- System Type: Likely solid-fuel SRBMs, offering rapid deployment and launch capabilities.
Geopolitical Context and Diplomatic Fallout
The show of force coincides with heightened military drills involving the United States and South Korea, which Pyongyang routinely condemns as invasion rehearsals and acts of aggression. The timing also follows recent diplomatic maneuvers by Kim Jong Un, including strategic engagements with Beijing and Moscow, suggesting a coordinated effort to project strength amid shifting global alliances.
South Korea’s presidential office convened an emergency national security council meeting, vowing to maintain a robust defense posture and promising severe consequences for any provocation. Japan lodged a formal protest through diplomatic channels in Beijing, calling the launches a direct threat to regional peace and a clear violation of multiple United Nations Security Council resolutions. The Japanese Prime Minister emphasized that such repeated provocations are absolutely unacceptable and undermine the stability of the entire Indo-Pacific region.
Implications for Regional Alliances and Defense Posture
The latest tests are expected to accelerate trilateral security cooperation between Seoul, Tokyo, and Washington. The three nations have recently enhanced real-time data sharing regarding North Korean missile launches, a critical step in improving early warning times and coordinated response capabilities. Analysts predict that this incident will further justify the deployment of additional advanced interceptors and the expansion of joint military exercises in the region.
However, the international community remains divided on how to effectively respond to Pyongyang's advancements. The United Nations Security Council remains paralyzed by the geopolitical interests of China and Russia, both of which have historically shielded North Korea from stringent economic sanctions and formal censure. This diplomatic gridlock ensures that Kim Jong Un faces minimal international consequences for his accelerated weapons development program.
Future Trajectory and Nuclear Ambitions
While the immediate trajectory of the missiles posed no direct threat to mainland Japan or US territories, the rapid frequency of these tests indicates an acceleration in North Korea’s tactical nuclear delivery systems. Intelligence assessments suggest that Pyongyang is actively working to miniaturize nuclear warheads to fit these short-range platforms, creating a direct and immediate threat to US forces stationed in South Korea and Japan.
Experts warn that the normalization of such large-scale missile barrages lowers the threshold for future provocations and increases the risk of miscalculation. As North Korea continues to refine its solid-fuel missile technology, the window for diplomatic intervention narrows, leaving regional allies to rely increasingly on deterrence and military preparedness to manage the escalating threat landscape. The coming months will likely see further tests as Pyongyang seeks to validate new delivery systems and demonstrate its strategic relevance on the global stage.

France will deploy some 70,000 police officers in Paris and other cities ahead of a new round of nationwide protests on Saturday, with Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warning of "very high risk of public disorder". The minister pledged an "extremely firm" response after mass protests on October 17 degenerated into rioting and looting.
France's interior minister on Thursday warned of a "very high risk of public disorder" and announced the deployment of around 70,000 police officers for a new wave of protests this weekend.
France has been rocked by widespread anger over the rising cost of living and inequality, with nationwide demonstrations on October 17 degenerating into some of the country's worst rioting in years.
The Yellow Vest movement and student unions have called for a new day of protests on Saturday.
The demonstrations come in an increasingly tense political climate, with presidential elections six months away and far-right leader Marine Le Pen leading opinion polls.
"The day of October 31 presents a very high risk of public disorder", Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez told reporters.
Around 70,000 police officers and gendarmes will be deployed across France, matching the number mobilised a week ago, he said.
The security measures introduced last week to protect shops will be strengthened, Nuñez added.
Demonstrations will be allowed, but "not in city centres, where there is a risk of public disorder", he said.
"We will tolerate no excesses," he added, pledging an "extremely firm" response.
Nuñez also said that authorities had detected social media calls for Halloween gatherings on Saturday evening calling for a "revolution".
He said those appeals were being circulated by radical left groups and some radicalised Yellow Vest activists.
"These gatherings will be banned," he said.
An interior ministry source said street violence on a scale "comparable" to the unrest of October 17 is expected.
"Incidents of urban violence comparable to those seen on October 17 are expected throughout Saturday and after nightfall," an aide to Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said.
'Dialogue of deaf'
Authorities have admitted to security and intelligence failures that paved the way for the clashes, large-scale looting and vandalism of public property that erupted on October 17.
Read moreFrance faces reckoning with public order policing after violent protest weekend
Although last weekend's rallies were largely peaceful, incidents of street violence still occurred.
The unrest followed weeks of demonstrations by students campaigning for better learning conditions.
On Monday, the government announced a series of measures aimed at addressing student protesters' demands, including replacing the university admissions platform and providing loans for school renovations.
Students said the proposals did not go far enough.
The police response has been criticised as heavy-handed and sparked a broader movement against the cost of living and police violence. Several teenage protesters have been seriously injured.
On Thursday, representatives of youth organisations met Nuñez but emerged disappointed.
"We went to this meeting to discuss our demands, but above all the last four weeks of mobilisation, which have been marked by unprecedented police violence," said Manon Moret, secretary-general of the student union Unef. "This meeting was a dialogue of the deaf."
Some of the attendees accused Nuñez of refusing to acknowledge violence committed against protesters.
Louis Letoublon, deputy head of the association Les Lycéens!, denounced "an irresponsible minister, incapable of answering for police repression".

articles.title: Are Nuclear Weapons Becoming Unusable Against Non-Nuclear States? - Small Wars Journal
articles.summary: Are Nuclear Weapons Becoming Unusable Against Non-Nuclear States?  Small Wars Journal
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Russia’s war on Ukraine and the US and Israeli campaign against Iran are the first major interstate wars since the end of the Cold War in which nuclear-armed states have failed to achieve their central objectives against non-nuclear opponents. Both are being fought amid explicit nuclear signaling and the collapse of the arms control architecture that framed earlier conflicts of this kind. This analysis asks whether nuclear weapons are becoming unusable against non-nuclear states. It compares the two current wars with earlier wars between nuclear-armed and non-nuclear states since 1950, then assesses the four constraints usually credited with preventing nuclear use. It finds that the answer depends on what use means. As instruments of warfighting, nuclear weapons have been largely unusable against non-nuclear states since 1945. As instruments of coercion aimed at those states’ nuclear-armed backers, they remain in constant use. What is new is not this usability gap but the condition of the constraints that sustain it. The legal and normative constraints are weakening, which leaves restraint resting increasingly on strategic calculation—the constraint least reliable when a war is going badly.
Introduction
Two of the most consequential wars of the decade thus far share a feature that ought to unsettle strategic theory more than it does. In each, a nuclear-armed state is fighting a state that possesses no nuclear weapons, and in each, the nuclear power has been unable to convert its ultimate advantage into a decisive result. Russia, holder of the world’s largest arsenal, has waged war on a non-nuclear Ukraine since February 2022 without breaking Ukrainian resistance. The United States and Israel have struck a non-nuclear Iran repeatedly since June 2025, most heavily in the campaign that began on February 28, 2026, without ending the program those strikes were meant to eliminate.
Nuclear-armed states have fought non-nuclear states before, so it is fair to ask why these two wars warrant fresh attention. The answer lies in a combination of features that no earlier case shared. First, both are interstate wars in which the nuclear-armed side has so far failed to achieve its central objective, unlike the Gulf War of 1991, the Iraq War of 2003, or Russia’s war with Georgia in 2008. Second, nuclear signaling has been explicit rather than implicit. In October 2022, President Joe Biden warned that, for the first time since the Cuban Missile Crisis, the world faced a direct threat of nuclear use, as the Foundation for Strategic Research (FRS) recorded at the time. Third, the non-nuclear belligerents are backed by nuclear-armed patrons, the precise circumstance that the exclusion clauses in several nuclear-weapon states’ security assurances were written to cover. Fourth, these wars are unfolding as the arms control architecture that framed earlier conflicts collapses. The last US-Russian strategic arms treaty expired in February 2026, and three successive review conferences of the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty have now failed to agree on an outcome. Earlier wars of this type occurred while that architecture was being built. These are occurring while it is being dismantled.
This analysis therefore asks whether nuclear weapons are becoming unusable against non-nuclear states, and its answer turns on a distinction between two meanings of use. As instruments of warfighting, meaning detonation to achieve a military result, nuclear weapons appear close to unusable against non-nuclear states and have been for most of the nuclear age. As instruments of coercion, meaning the manipulation of risk to shape the behavior of others, they remain very much in use, but their main audience is the non-nuclear state’s nuclear-armed backers rather than the non-nuclear state itself. Nuclear weapons are therefore not becoming irrelevant. They continue to deter direct great-power intervention, to shape every rung of the escalation ladder, and to define the outer limits of what belligerents dare attempt. What these wars expose is a gap between the possession of overwhelming nuclear superiority and the ability to convert it into victory against an adversary that has forsworn the bomb.
The analysis proceeds in three steps. It first sets out the two current cases and compares them with earlier wars between nuclear-armed and non-nuclear states since 1950 to establish whether the usability gap is new. It then examines how the arsenals are still being used in the current wars, despite never being detonated. Finally, it assesses the four constraints usually credited with keeping nuclear weapons unused. The doctrinal constraint consists of nuclear-armed states’ declared commitments not to use nuclear weapons against non-nuclear states. The normative constraint is the taboo against nuclear use that has developed since 1945. The military constraint is the judgment that conventional forces can achieve whatever is militarily necessary, so nuclear weapons add little. The strategic constraint is the calculation that the costs of nuclear use, including escalation, isolation, and precedent, would exceed any gain.
This approach yields three principal findings. First, the usability gap is longstanding rather than new, since outcomes in these wars have tracked the conventional balance and the opponent’s resolve rather than the nuclear balance. Second, the arsenals remain in active coercive use, with nuclear-armed patrons as their primary audience. Third, the four constraints are of unequal strength: the doctrinal and normative constraints are the weakest in these cases, and the evidence suggests that they are also the ones eroding over time. Restraint thus rests increasingly on military and strategic calculation, which is most vulnerable in what this analysis calls the frustration scenario, in which a nuclear power faces defeat. The final sections examine that scenario and its implications for proliferation.
The Two Cases: Superiority Without Victory
The asymmetry between the two sides is stark. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) estimates that, at the start of 2026, the nine nuclear-armed states together held some 12,187 warheads, of which around 9,745 sat in military stockpiles for potential use. According to the Federation of American Scientists (FAS), Russia and the United States between them account for roughly 86% of that inventory, with Russia holding about 5,420 warheads and the United States about 5,040. Against this stand the arsenals of Ukraine and Iran, both of which are empty.
Chart 1: Approximate Total Nuclear Warhead Inventories, Early 2026
Sources: FAS, Status of World Nuclear Forces 2026; SIPRI Yearbook 2026.
If military outcomes were a simple function of destructive capacity, both wars would already be over, and the fact that they are not shows that nuclear superiority does not convert easily into results against non-nuclear states. The imbalance is also misleading in another respect. Of the warheads in global military stockpiles, around 4,000 are deployed, and between 2,100 and 2,200 are on high alert; almost all of them are Russian, American, British, or French. This readiness is configured overwhelmingly for one purpose, which is deterring other nuclear powers. It was never designed for the coercion of a determined non-nuclear adversary on the ground.
Ukraine’s position is often described as doubly instructive, because it emerged from the Soviet collapse with the world’s third-largest nuclear arsenal. Under the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, Kyiv transferred those warheads to Russia and acceded to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) in exchange for assurances from Russia, the United States, and the United Kingdom to respect its sovereignty and borders. The popular claim that Ukraine thereby gave up its deterrent needs careful handling, however. Under the 1991 Minsk agreement, charge of the former Soviet arsenal passed to the Russian government, with Kyiv holding (at most) veto power over use, so what Ukraine surrendered was latent leverage and the option of an independent force rather than a ready deterrent. Those assurances were broken in 2014 and again in 2022. Even so, Ukraine has fought Russia to an attritional standstill along much of the front, has struck deep into Russia, including in a mass drone attack on Moscow in May 2026, and remains undefeated.
Iran presents the mirror image: a state that never acquired the bomb and has been bombed to stop what Israel and the United States allege was an advance toward the nuclear threshold.
Tehran denies seeking nuclear weapons, and in June 2025, the Director General of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said that the agency had no proof of a systematic Iranian effort to build one, even as it found Iran in breach of its safeguards obligations.
The June 2025 strikes, which included the first combat use of the largest conventional bomb in the US arsenal against the buried Fordow enrichment plant, inflicted severe damage.
Yet both the IAEA Director General and a leaked US intelligence assessment judged that the program had been set back by months, and the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) concluded that the strikes disrupted Iran’s program without destroying its key facilities.
Iran then legislated an end to cooperation with the IAEA.
A far heavier US and Israeli campaign from February 2026 killed the Supreme Leader and widened into a regional war, during which Iran’s effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz produced a global energy shock.
According to the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR) conflict tracker, a Pakistan-mediated interim deal in June halted large-scale fighting, but both sides have since traded strikes over alleged violations, and the tracker now rates the conflict as worsening.
In October, Washington accused Tehran of once again enriching uranium to 60%.

articles.title: How Civilian Are Pakistan’s and India’s “Civilian” Nuclear Programs? - Small Wars Journal
articles.summary: How Civilian Are Pakistan’s and India’s “Civilian” Nuclear Programs?  Small Wars Journal
articles.full_text:
The phrase “civilian nuclear program” implies a clean line: reactors that generate electricity, isotopes for medicine, and research neutrons on one side, and the enrichment plants and plutonium reactors that feed a weapons stockpile on the other. Across most of the world, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) polices that line through comprehensive safeguards. In South Asia, the line barely exists. India and Pakistan both operate power reactors under IAEA inspection while running weapons complexes a short distance away, drawing on shared expertise, shared institutions, and, in important respects, a shared fuel cycle. The “civilian” label survives less as a technical description than as a diplomatic and commercial instrument. Asking how civil these programs are exposes how porous the boundary is and why that porousness matters for the wider non-proliferation order.
The ambiguity is not a recent complication; it is foundational. India’s first nuclear detonation in 1974 was carried out with plutonium produced in the Canadian-supplied CIRUS reactor, material provided on the understanding that it would be used only for peaceful purposes. New Delhi described the test as a “peaceful nuclear explosion,” a phrase that captured, perhaps unintentionally, just how indistinct the civil and military categories already were. Pakistan’s program was similarly ambiguous at birth. The Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission (PAEC), nominally a civilian body for peaceful development that functioned directly under the President and Prime Minister, became the institutional vehicle for the weapons effort pursued under Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto in the early 1970s. In both countries, the civilian institution and the weapons ambition grew from a single root, and the fuel cycle was never engineered to keep them apart.
The Non-NPT Starting Point
Both states belong to the small group that never joined the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT). That single fact shapes everything that follows. Under the NPT bargain, a non-nuclear-weapon state accepts comprehensive, or full-scope, safeguards covering all nuclear material on its territory. India and Pakistan accepted neither the treaty nor comprehensive safeguards. Instead, each place only names installations under inspection through item-specific safeguards agreements, the category the IAEA reserves for states outside the NPT, and leaves the remainder, including everything of direct weapons significance, entirely outside the Agency’s reach. Safeguards in South Asia are therefore an opt-in list rather than a wall. As the Arms Control Association has observed of India, facility-specific inspection at a handful of reactors leaves the unsafeguarded military sector free to produce fissile material and to design and build warheads. The same logic applies, with local variations, to Pakistan. The label “civilian” thus attaches to whichever facilities a state chooses to declare, not to a category the inspectorate can independently define.
India: A Civilian Umbrella Over a Weapons Core
India’s nuclear enterprise is administered by the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE), created in 1954 and placed, unusually, directly under the Prime Minister rather than any line ministry. A single umbrella covers the Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL), which runs the grid-connected reactors; the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC), which conducts weapons research and reprocessing; and the fast-reactor establishment at Kalpakkam. Power generation, weapons-grade material, and basic research sit inside one department, answering to one office. The civil and military programs are not neighboring enterprises with a fence between them; they are branches of the same institution.
The 2005 joint statement by Prime Minister Manmohan Singh and President George W. Bush, alongside the arrangements that followed it, required India to draw a line it had never drawn before. In 2006, India adopted a Civil-Military Separation Plan, and the United States amended its domestic law to permit cooperation. In 2008, the IAEA Board of Governors approved an India-specific safeguards agreement, and in September of that year the Nuclear Suppliers Group granted India a waiver. Yet India drew the line itself and drew it generously. Of the 22 power reactors then operating or under construction, only 14 were designated for safeguards; the remaining eight stayed outside. The Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam, together with the CIRUS and Dhruva plutonium reactors and the reprocessing lines at BARC, was kept firmly on the military side of the ledger.
India’s own atomic managers made the entanglement explicit. Anil Kakodkar, then chairman of the Atomic Energy Commission, resisted placing the breeder program under safeguards on the ground that the fuel cycle serves “the same infrastructure which also feeds the strategic program,” describing the civil and military fuel cycles as intimately intertwined. The deal’s practical effect reinforced that point. By allowing India to import uranium for its safeguarded reactors, the arrangement freed scarce domestic uranium for plutonium production on the military side. According to the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, custody of the warheads themselves rests with two nominally civilian scientific agencies, BARC and the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), which hold the fissile cores and the non-nuclear firing assemblies, respectively. Since 2003, command has rested with the Nuclear Command Authority, whose Political Council is chaired by the Prime Minister and remains the sole body able to authorize use.
The most consequential recent development sits squarely on the unsafeguarded side. On April 6, 2026, the 500-megawatt PFBR at Kalpakkam reached first criticality after more than two decades of construction. According to the government’s own account, the reactor is fueled with plutonium recovered by reprocessing spent fuel from India’s pressurized heavy-water reactors, and its uranium blanket breeds more plutonium than the reactor consumes. India presents the plant, accurately, as the entry point to the second stage of its three-stage energy program. Yet because the reactor was excluded from the 2006 civilian list, the plutonium it breeds falls entirely outside international accounting. A flagship of civil energy policy is, by design, also an unmonitored source of fissile material.
In December 2025, Parliament also enacted the SHANTI Act, which repealed the Atomic Energy Act of 1962 and the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act of 2010. The new law opens power generation to licensed private operators and gives the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) statutory standing for the first time. It is equally notable for what it withholds, since enrichment beyond a notified threshold, reprocessing and other spent-fuel management, and heavy-water production remain reserved for the central government and its wholly owned entities. The reform therefore liberalizes the reactor layer while keeping state control over precisely the fuel-cycle nodes that connect civil and military activity. The Indian model can be summarized in a sentence: the civilian energy establishment is the weapons establishment, gathered under one civilian umbrella and topped by civilian political control.
Pakistan: A Military Hand on the Civilian Lever
Pakistan’s civil power program is, if anything, more thoroughly safeguarded than India’s in proportional terms, because almost all of it was foreign-supplied and came with inspection attached. The Chashma reactors, the Karachi units, and the two research reactors at the PINSTECH laboratory near Islamabad all operate under item-specific IAEA safeguards. That pattern continues to the present. In September 2026, on the sidelines of the IAEA General Conference, Pakistan signed a safeguards agreement for Chashma Unit-5, its largest planned reactor. The program also carries real civilian weight. According to the PAEC, its six operating plants, with a combined capacity of 3,530 megawatts, supplied about 18.5 percent of national grid generation in 2025, compared with India’s nuclear share of 3.1 percent in 2024–25.
The weapons complex, however, sits entirely outside that fleet. The four heavy-water reactors at Khushab, dedicated to weapons-grade plutonium; the reprocessing plant known as New Labs at PINSTECH; and the uranium-enrichment facilities at Kahuta are not subject to IAEA inspection. The institutional entanglement is sharper than India’s in one respect. The same PAEC that operates the safeguarded power reactors is also reported to operate the Khushab production complex, so a single body straddles both sides of the declared boundary.
More striking still is who administers that body. The PAEC, together with Khan Research Laboratories (KRL), the National Engineering and Scientific Commission (NESCOM), and the National Development Complex (NDC), is administered by the Strategic Plans Division (SPD), the secretariat of the National Command Authority (NCA), which is headed by a serving three-star Army general. The ostensibly civilian atomic establishment thus operates under military administration, an arrangement without real parallel in India, where the corresponding institutions answer to the Prime Minister’s Office.
Recent constitutional changes have deepened this pattern. The 27th Amendment, passed in November 2025, abolished the post of Chairman Joint Chiefs of Staff Committee (CJCSC), made the Army chief concurrently Chief of Defence Forces, and created a four-star Commander of the National Strategic Command. In August 2026, Parliament passed the National Command Authority (Amendment) Act, which substitutes the Army chief, as Chief of Defence Forces, for the CJCSC throughout the 2010 NCA Act and adds the Commander of the National Strategic Command as a member of the Authority. articles.full_text:
Four years after the start of the large-scale invasion of Ukraine, the industrial power balance in the European continent is experiencing an unprecedented and contradictory transformation. The twenty-seven member states of the European Union allocated nearly 418 billion euros to defense, an unprecedented historical figure that represents an increase of over 20% annually. However, the coldness of macroeconomic data hides an uncomfortable reality: the gap in operational and production capacities compared to the Russian Federation has not only not been completely closed, but it also shows signs of structural bureaucratic stagnation in the West.
A recent executive report from the European Defence Agency (EDA) warns that the massive increase in capital has not yet translated into sufficiently deployable, sustainable, and interoperable forces. While the European Union debates guidelines and percentages for joint procurement, the Kremlin has completed the transition to a centrally planned economy—dubbed by analysts as Gosplan 2.0—that already allocates nearly 10% of its GDP and half of its state budget exclusively to sustaining the front.
The International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) quantified the drama: Russia's defense spending exceeded 462 billion dollars, surpassing the combined expenditure of all EU countries and the United Kingdom together. Although the EU's GDP dwarfs Russia's by a ratio of twenty to one, Moscow has achieved what no Western democracy can afford without declaring a state of emergency: completely "cannibalizing" its civil economic fabric to transform it into a vast military foundry that spends 250 billion euros annually to sustain its combat brigades.
The Russian industrial base: towards Soviet volume against technological suffocation
The current Russian army's defense technology does not stand out for its disruptive vanguard but for its massive resilience and its ability to adapt to war of attrition.
Russian state companies have optimized production lines capable of pumping out between 4.5 and 7 million artillery shells annually, tripling the joint production of the entire NATO bloc. This surge is not due to an engineering revolution but to the artisanal and massive reactivation of thousands of Soviet tank chassis stored during the Cold War and the simplification of their assembly lines.
Moscow's real Achilles' heel lies in its chronic inability to achieve the desired "import substitution." Despite strict state control, the best Russian technologies—such as their electronic warfare systems and integrated air defense radars—continue to suffer critical bottlenecks due to reliance on optical components, precision machinery, and advanced Western dual-use semiconductors acquired through smuggling.
From a technological perspective, it is tempting to join the thesis that Russia is a power in irreversible decline. It is true that its flagship projects, such as the fourth-generation T-14 Armata tank or the Su-75 Checkmate stealth fighter, are propaganda fantasies that the Russian industrial base cannot mass-produce due to a lack of advanced microelectronics.
Sanctioned to the core, Russia struggles to obtain everything from high-quality ball bearings to computer numerical control machinery. Russia has become what strategic studies institutes define as an "aging power," a giant with a massive industrial muscle to melt iron and low-cost explosives but unable to manufacture next-generation chips or stealth air fleets from scratch.
The debate in Brussels: better or worse than in 2022?
The answer to whether the European Union is in a superior or inferior position compared to Russia after the invasion of Ukraine is complex. In terms of strategic awareness and investment, the improvement is undeniable. Europe has broken the taboo of community financing of armaments, and the European Commission has set the ambitious goal of having 50% of defense production be of local origin by 2030. Shared European programs are beginning to bear their first fruits in projects of common interest focused on drones, satellites, and advanced armored vehicles.
However, on a strictly logistical and immediate level, the EU continues to suffer from commercial fragmentation that hinders its competitiveness. The European defense industry operates under free market rules and is composed of private corporations competing with each other. This results in an alarming lack of standardization. While Russia unifies all its artillery into just two dominant calibers, EU armies operate dozens of different variants of 155 mm howitzers, preventing economies of scale.
Additionally, dependence on imports outside the EU has skyrocketed. Faced with the urgency of replenishing inventories transferred to Kiev, European countries have doubled their purchases of foreign armaments, with more than 55% of supplies coming from the United States. With Spain as one of its honorable exceptions. This dynamic weakens European strategic autonomy, especially in light of the global fear of a withdrawal in Washington's military commitments to NATO.
The EU has awakened industrially, but it has done so at a markedly institutional and fragmented pace. Russia, long-term stifled by its technological and demographic weaknesses, retains the dictator's advantage: the immediate ability to direct every factory, worker, and resource in the country toward the continuous war effort, posing a sustained challenge for which Brussels' parliamentary timelines still lack an agile response.
Russia operates under a total war economy that has reached its productive ceiling and consumes its historical reserves at a forced march, suffering from a critical shortage of skilled labor due to mobilization. It is an aging power, yes, but armed with a colossal club that is already ready in the arsenals. We shoot much less, though we aim better.
The European Union, on the other hand, is a young economic giant brimming with high technology, but whose military muscles remain atrophied by decades of budgetary pacifism and political disunity. The EU's rearmament has begun, but in the chronology of real geopolitics, community factories advance at a civil pace while the drums of war on the eastern flank demand a military speed that Europe, as of today, is still unable to replicate.

articles.title: The Economist: Europe is preparing for a future war, and Russia is already waging it ᐉ News from Fakti.bg - World - Fakti.bg
articles.summary: The Economist: Europe is preparing for a future war, and Russia is already waging it ᐉ News from Fakti.bg - World  Fakti.bg
articles.full_text:
Europe is accelerating its preparations for a possible future war with Russia, while Moscow is already waging a conflict against European countries that is already on the brink of open hostilities. Sabotage, cyberattacks, disinformation, airspace violations and drone operations are becoming a constant test of the readiness of the European Union and NATO.
The European Council condemned in October Russia's "escalating and increasingly reckless behavior" and called for greater resilience, protection of critical infrastructure and an acceleration of action against drones. NATO discussed the same risks at a meeting in Bucharest, where allies focused on energy, digital networks and coordination with the private sector.
“Europe is facing a rapid spread of sabotage attacks and airspace violations,“ said EU foreign policy chief Kaia Kallas. She said Moscow was trying to intimidate European countries into reducing their support for Ukraine. But European ministers drew a distinction between the campaign and the immediate risk of a direct attack on NATO.
Between hybrid pressure and future clash
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said Russia was “testing” allies through airspace violations, arson, sabotage and other hostile acts. He stressed that there was no immediate military attack on the Alliance, but warned that the campaign would continue and that countries must remain vigilant. According to Rutte, the Kremlin's goal is to divide allies and weaken Western support for Ukraine.
This poses a difficult problem for European governments. Hybrid actions are often serious enough to cause economic damage and public tension, but remain below the threshold that would automatically lead to a collective military response. The European Parliament points out that it is precisely the difficulties in identifying the perpetrator, coordinating between countries and choosing a proportionate response that limit the possibilities of deterrence.
Several European intelligence services estimate that Russia could try to test NATO with a limited attack by the end of the decade. This does not mean that Moscow has decided on direct war with the Alliance. Rather, the analyses warn that the Kremlin is using the current period to test the reactions, weaknesses and political cohesion of European countries.
Europe increases defense spending
The preparations are already visible in the budgets. According to the International Institute for Strategic Studies, European NATO members are expected to spend about $639 billion on defense in 2026. The amount is nominally over 90% higher than in 2022, and an average of 36.2% of the budgets are directed to investments, including new weapons, scientific research and production.
The five largest European NATO countries - France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom - said that Europe must take greater responsibility for its own security. This includes increased ammunition production, air defense, protection of critical infrastructure, and the ability to conduct sustained operations without complete reliance on the United States.
The fundamental contradiction remains between preparing for a future conventional conflict and the fact that the pressure has already begun in a less visible form. Russia denies organizing sabotage operations in NATO countries, and European governments have not reported any immediate preparations by Moscow for a full-scale attack. At the same time, NATO and the EU accept that the series of attacks, incidents, and interventions can no longer be viewed as isolated incidents.

articles.full_text:
A serious issue confronting NATO in the early and mid-1950s was the negotiation of West Germany’s participation in the alliance. The prospect of a rearmed Germany was understandably greeted with widespread unease and hesitancy in western Europe, but the country’s strength had long been recognized as necessary to protect western Europe from a possible Soviet invasion. Accordingly, arrangements for West Germany’s “safe” participation in the alliance were worked out as part of the Paris Agreements of October 1954, which ended the occupation of West German territory by the western Allies and provided for both the limitation of West German armaments and the country’s accession to the Brussels Treaty. In May 1955 West Germany joined NATO, which prompted the Soviet Union to form the Warsaw Pact alliance in central and eastern Europe the same year. The West Germans subsequently contributed many divisions and substantial air forces to the NATO alliance. By the time the Cold War ended, some 900,000 troops—nearly half of them from six countries (United States, United Kingdom, France, Belgium, Canada, and the Netherlands)—were stationed in West Germany.
News •
The role of France
France’s relationship with NATO became strained after 1958, as Pres. Charles de Gaulle increasingly criticized the organization’s domination by the United States and the intrusion upon French sovereignty by NATO’s many international staffs and activities. He argued that such “integration” subjected France to “automatic” war at the decision of foreigners. In July 1966 France formally withdrew from the military command structure of NATO and required NATO forces and headquarters to leave French soil; nevertheless, de Gaulle proclaimed continued French adherence to the North Atlantic Treaty in case of “unprovoked aggression.” After NATO moved its headquarters from Paris to Brussels, France maintained a liaison relationship with NATO’s integrated military staffs, continued to sit in the council, and continued to maintain and deploy ground forces in West Germany, though it did so under new bilateral agreements with the West Germans rather than under NATO jurisdiction. In 2009 France rejoined the military command structure of NATO.
NATO during the Cold War
From its founding, NATO’s primary purpose was to unify and strengthen the Western Allies’ military response to a possible invasion of western Europe by the Soviet Union and its Warsaw Pact allies. In the early 1950s NATO relied partly on the threat of massive nuclear retaliation from the United States to counter the Warsaw Pact’s much larger ground forces. Beginning in 1957, this policy was supplemented by the deployment of American nuclear weapons in western European bases. NATO later adopted a “flexible response” strategy, which the United States interpreted to mean that a war in Europe did not have to escalate to an all-out nuclear exchange. Under this strategy, many Allied forces were equipped with American battlefield and theatre nuclear weapons under a dual-control (or “dual-key”) system, which allowed both the country hosting the weapons and the United States to veto their use. Britain retained control of its strategic nuclear arsenal but brought it within NATO’s planning structures; France’s nuclear forces remained completely autonomous.
A conventional and nuclear stalemate between the two sides continued through the construction of the Berlin Wall in the early 1960s, détente in the 1970s, and the resurgence of Cold War tensions in the 1980s after the Soviet Union’s invasion of Afghanistan in 1979 and the election of U.S. Pres. Ronald Reagan in 1980. After 1985, however, far-reaching economic and political reforms introduced by Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev fundamentally altered the status quo. In July 1989 Gorbachev announced that Moscow would no longer prop up communist governments in central and eastern Europe and thereby signaled his tacit acceptance of their replacement by freely elected (and noncommunist) administrations. Moscow’s abandonment of control over central and eastern Europe meant the dissipation of much of the military threat that the Warsaw Pact had formerly posed to western Europe, a fact that led some to question the need to retain NATO as a military organization—especially after the Warsaw Pact’s dissolution in 1991. The reunification of Germany in October 1990 and its retention of NATO membership created both a need and an opportunity for NATO to be transformed into a more “political” alliance devoted to maintaining international stability in Europe.
