articles.summary: Binance says user funds are safe after thieves make off with billions in largest-ever crypto hack  NBC NewsExpert warns of 'AI hacking bloodbath' following massive Binance cryptocurrency theft  Fox BusinessWorld in Brief: Tech stock slump continues; Hackers attempt a crypto heist  The EconomistBlockchain intelligence firms link North Korea to $6.3B hack on Binance  NPRWhat Protections Exist for Binance’s Customers?  The New York Times
articles.full_text:
A record-setting cyberattack targeting the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange rocked the digital assets industry Friday, delivering another blow to a sector already struggling to achieve mainstream adoption.
The exchange, Binance, announced late Thursday that more than $6 billion appeared to have moved through wallets connected to a security breach, the highest dollar amount ever associated with a crypto cyber attack. Around $3 billion of that had potentially been located and frozen across several exchanges, though it was not immediately clear if those funds were recoverable.
It was not immediately clear whether hackers were able to access individual customer accounts or holdings. Binance co-CEO Richard Teng released a video statement Friday morning that sought to reassure platform users that only Binance’s corporate holdings were targeted.
“Your assets are safe,” he said, adding the platform had preexisting reserves totaling more than $1 billion designed to cover customer losses, and that it was setting aside an additional $6 billion from its $167 billion balance sheet to shore up further losses.
“Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users,” Teng said in an X post late Friday.
U.S. officials said they are working with Binance to investigate the hack.
President Donald Trump said his administration was “looking at” the incident, telling reporters Friday he was reassured by Binance’s pledge to reimburse any losses.
The Secret Service said it was working with private-sector partners to identify, freeze, trace and recover funds stolen from Binance, but that the investigation remained in early stages.
The hack is the latest setback for crypto, which continues to reckon with a reputation for being too volatile — and too vulnerable to criminal activity — for widespread use. The scale of the hack echoes collapse of crypto exchange FTX, which, though not the result of a cyberattack, led to billions in losses.
The renewed doubts were reflected in the value of Bitcoin, which dropped as much as 5% to below $76,000, accelerating a month-long downturn. Other affected cryptocurrencies fell as much as 9%.
The crypto industry was already recovering from the failure in Congress of the Clarity Act, a bill that would have granted comprehensive legal protections for crypto assets in the U.S.
Despite bipartisan support for the core elements of the legislation, its passage was torpedoed by a battle over conflict-of-interest rules for elected officials, notably President Donald Trump.
The president has disclosed in filings that he earned more than $1 billion from crypto last year.
The Binance hack stands to prolong this reckoning, experts said.
“There will be an imperative for Binance to cover losses not only for its own reputation and value, but I expect there will be a level of co-operation within the space as they look at the collective reputational harm this may, rightly or wrongly, cause to the sector,” Laura Clatworthy, head of digital assets at the law firm Edwin Coe, said in a statement.
That cooperation was evident in the immediate responses of other mainstream crypto players. Tether and Circle, which operate the world’s two largest stablecoins, both worked quickly to freeze assets implicated in the hack.
The Trump-backed crypto platform World Liberty Financial also worked to freeze USD1 and WLFI holdings tracked to the attackers, a spokesperson told NBC News.
Most USD1 and WLFI transactions occur on Binance, according to blockchain data.
More than $27 million-worth of USD1 was implicated in the attack, the analysis group TRM Labs reported. The group also assessed that $2.4 billion in Bitcoin and Ethereum will never be recovered.
The hack’s origins remain murky. The entire heist unfolded in just 20 minutes starting at approximately 4 p.m. ET Thursday.
Binance initially said the attack involved a compromised laptop, but that a subsequent investigation uncovered “additional points of breach.”
Multiple blockchain analysis firms said the hack had attributes associated with previous operations believed to have been carried out by North Korean actors.
Teng, the Binance co-CEO, said Binance’s investigation had not yet identified the attackers.
At least one prominent tech CEO could not resist making light of the situation. Elon Musk left a “yikes” emoji in response to an X user who noted that the collapsed crypto exchange FTX had initially also told users their funds were safe amid a wave of losses.
Binance co-founder CZ Zhao responded:“Elon, have a lot of respect for you, but bad time to troll. Please stop.”
Zhao noted that his SpaceX shares — the product of a Binance-related $500 million investment in Twitter, were now worth more than $1 billion.
“Would appreciate if you show a little support. Thanks!”

articles.title: Can the Nordic Model Save NATO?
articles.summary: A new way to deter Russia.
articles.full_text:
In August, at Finland’s request, the Swedish government deployed fighter aircraft and a warship to help patrol Finland’s eastern airspace and the Gulf of Finland against Russian air incursions and drones straying from Ukrainian operations. Critically, the Swedish assets involved were placed under Finnish command and followed Finnish rules of engagement. It was the latest example of how Finland and Sweden, the two newest additions to NATO, have made qualitative leaps in defense coordination.
The Nordic countries have expanded regional collaboration significantly in the past four years. Between them, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, and Sweden now boast a new long-term defense strategy, a cross-border transit area, frequent joint exercises, and unprecedented levels of command integration. In effect, these governments are forming their own regional deterrence cluster: a like-minded group of states deepening military cooperation to strengthen deterrence and, if required, ensure NATO’s broader collective defense.
The Nordic model offers a glimpse of the adaptive solutions that may sustain NATO through uncertain times. Moscow’s appetite for risk is growing; its military buildup and escalating attacks on European infrastructure suggest that Russia constitutes a long-term threat to the alliance. At the same time, the Trump administration is pushing its European allies to take primary responsibility for the continent’s defense. Europeans must therefore deter a more dangerous Russia with less help.
To strengthen their deterrence and defense capabilities, member states along NATO’s extended frontline—and in the Baltic and Black Sea regions, in particular—should build their own regional clusters and foster a strong latticework of bilateral and “minilateral” partnerships with their neighbors. Regionalization remains a taboo subject among most of the alliance’s political leadership; NATO is, after all, a collective defense alliance founded on indivisible security. But regional efforts at the military level will both make NATO more effective and advance the United States’ vision of a more European NATO.
Nordic-style deterrence clusters are thus a win-win. Yet in its erratic, occasionally aggressive approach to Greenland and the North Atlantic, Washington has risked undercutting the very allies that are delivering what it wants. The United States should use the recently signed Greenland deal as a reset to embrace Nordic defense efforts and create incentives for other allies to follow suit.
Marriage of Convenience
Nordic defense collaboration took its current institutional form in 2009, when recession-era budgetary constraints pushed the region’s five countries to rethink their defense commitments. Finland and Sweden joined NATO members Denmark, Iceland, and Norway in establishing the Nordic Defense Cooperation, primarily in hopes of cutting procurement costs. NORDEFCO boasted some early wins, including cross-border air force training in the uncongested airspace of northern Finland, Norway, and Sweden. But because NORDEFCO spanned NATO members and nonallied states, bureaucratic hurdles and a lenient threat environment quickly sapped momentum from joint procurement.
Only after Russia’s 2014 invasion of Ukraine did some Nordic countries begin to see cooperation as a security imperative, not just a way to save money. Finland and Sweden launched a no-limits military partnership that included joint wartime planning. And Norway, despite maintaining its NATO-first approach, gradually embraced operational cooperation with its two non-NATO neighbors in times of crisis. By 2020, when the countries signed a trilateral statement of intent, they were conducting extensive joint exercises, sharing intelligence on common threats, and discussing their national defense plans with an eye toward coordinated crisis response.
Any remaining limits on Nordic military cooperation evaporated once Finland and Sweden joined NATO following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, in 2022. The region’s five countries agreed that Moscow posed an urgent security threat to themselves and to Europe as a whole. Even Denmark, which was previously reticent about regional collaboration, warmed to collective defense efforts. In 2023, it joined Finland, Norway, and Sweden in developing the Nordic Airpower Concept, which will give them the ability to fight as one force with their combined 250 advanced fighter aircraft. Denmark has also pledged to contribute personnel to the Swedish-led Forward Land Forces Finland, the NATO battle group that rotates between northern Finland and Sweden. When Denmark served as chair of NORDEFCO in 2024, the five governments also signed NORDEFCO Vision 2030, which outlines their ambition for joint operations that are aligned with both national and NATO defense interests. To support the logistical underpinnings of land force cooperation, the initiative established a seamless, borderless Nordic military mobility corridor.
A division of labor is now emerging: Finland commands regional land operations, Norway hosts the regional headquarters for air operations, and Sweden is becoming the logistics hub and transit area for joint military operations in northern Europe. Denmark, for its part, hosts a regional headquarters for special operations. The Nordic deterrence cluster also functions smoothly within NATO’s collective defense framework. Larger NATO allies—including France, Germany, the United Kingdom, and the United States—routinely operate and exercise in the Nordic space alongside their regional partners and fill capability gaps in areas such as intelligence, reconnaissance, and surveillance. The result is an increase in defense capabilities in NATO’s Joint Operations Area Northwest, which covers the North Atlantic and includes vital sea-lanes, critical undersea infrastructure, and the Arctic and Nordic regions bordering Russian strategic hot spots.
Imitation Game
Deterrence clusters could well be the future of NATO’s frontline posture. In addition to NATO’s Joint Operations Area Northwest, NATO has two more regional plans—Center, covering the Baltic states and central Europe, and Southeast, covering Turkey and the Balkans—each with its own operations area and command center network. Governments in these two regions should follow the Nordic example and take the initiative to strengthen their own minilateral ties within the NATO framework.
An obvious starting point is the southeastern Baltic Sea, which sits at the heart of NATO’s Joint Operations Area Center. Although the Baltic states have a shared vulnerability to Russian encroachment, defense cooperation has been modest since they joined NATO, with Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania preferring to rely on extraregional patrons such as the United States. Recent moves, however, suggest that regional collaboration is gathering pace: Estonia and Latvia have jointly procured the IRIS-T air defense system, and all three countries are coordinating their HIMARS rocket systems and building the Baltic Defense Line, a fortification project designed to channel, delay, and block a Russian ground invasion.
But Baltic cooperation would benefit from a more comprehensive minilateral layer resembling NORDEFCO. In practice, this could mean coordinating national defense plans, conducting joint exercises, and sharing missile stocks for air defense systems. It could also entail merging HIMARS launchers for joint fires capability, better integrating national contributions to the Baltic Defense Line, and jointly operating uncrewed vessels to monitor the sea and underwater infrastructure. The aim would be to enable three militaries to fight together as seamlessly as possible, generating a combined power greater than the sum of its parts.
Such a format, if realized, should also involve Poland—an emerging European military powerhouse that currently plays a limited role in Baltic defense. Although Warsaw maintains a relatively robust defense partnership with Lithuania, involving joint exercises and working groups, the two neighbors have previously failed to establish a joint exercise area in the Suwalki Gap, a key strategic corridor and vulnerable supply line connecting the Baltic states to continental Europe. A stronger minilateral framework would create a standing process for joint planning and consultation that could resolve the local objections and divergent strategic priorities that have dogged previous negotiations over the gap.
 In extreme circumstances, subregional clusters would offer a hedge.
Within such a framework, Warsaw could reinforce regional defense by connecting its East Shield—Poland’s own program of fortifications, barriers, and surveillance systems along its borders with Russia and Belarus—with the Baltic Defense Line and by contributing ground-based air defenses to NATO’s Baltic Air Policing mission. The fundamental aim should be to strengthen Poland’s role as a leading security provider in the Baltic region alongside Germany, which is permanently stationing a brigade in Lithuania.
The other frontline arena that would most benefit from a deterrence cluster is the Black Sea region, which sits within NATO’s Joint Operations Area Southeast. Bulgaria, Romania, and Turkey have struggled to cooperate because of divergent assessments of the threat posed by Russia. Building minilateral latticework here is clearly harder than in the Nordic or Baltic Sea areas. But in a more European NATO, the rest of the alliance would expect Black Sea allies to contribute more to collective defense, and the conditions for doing so are improving.
The most promising domain for expanded minilateral cooperation is maritime. In July 2024, Bulgaria, Romania, and Turkey launched a joint mine-clearing operation, which led to the establishment of a joint mission to protect energy infrastructure, telecommunications networks, and undersea pipelines owned and operated by the three allies. Vice President JD Vance is facing backlash after responding to a young voter's question about housing affordability with an off-topic joke about Ohio Senator Jon Husted's rear.
The exchange unfolded Thursday during a Fox News town hall at Texas Christian University, where student Kate White, vice president of the school's Turning Point USA chapter, pressed Vance on how young Americans could afford to start a life amid soaring housing costs.
“How does the right and yourself expect us to start families young when you know the average price of a home in America now costs more than $415,000, which just feels out of reach for us,” White asked.
Vance thanked White for the question before diverting to Husted, the Republican senator from Ohio who previously held Vance's Senate seat.
“I want to point out that I think that I've been asked four or maybe five questions by my count, I've only been asked one question about Jon Husted's a** and it was by Jesse Watters,” Vance said about the Fox News host, who moderated the town hall.
Watters laughed at Vance’s response and said it was what people were talking about.
"Maybe you should run for Senate on the Democratic side here in Texas, Jesse,” Vance said.
After the joke, Vance acknowledged that Republicans had not done enough to address the financial pressures facing younger Americans.
“Most Republicans don't… I think that I'm an exception,” he said, adding that he believed President Donald Trump was focused on restoring the American dream and making homeownership more attainable.
Vance attributed rising housing costs partly to undocumented immigration under previous administrations and home purchases by Wall Street firms and foreign investors. He also claimed Texas home listing prices had fallen 2.5 percent, following a 100 percent increase under former President Joe Biden.
He then finally answered White’s question.
“My personal advice is one guy talking to a person who's been in similar shoes is it's never the right time, so go ahead and do it, because you're never going to regret getting married and having kids,” Vance told the student.
Watters agreed with Vance's advice, adding his own perspective: "And sometimes, you know, when you're in love, you just get pregnant, and you figure it out. That's not a great political answer, but it usually works well."
Vance’s off-topic quip about Husted's derriere comes amid a series of comments Trump has made about Husted's physique while campaigning for the Ohio senator, who is seeking election to a full Senate term on November 3.
Trump first made headlines with the remarks during an October 12 rally in Youngstown, Ohio, when he recalled examining Husted's body after learning the senator had been an All-American football player at the University of Dayton.
“I looked at his a**,” Trump told the crowd, before describing his legs, shoulders and hands.
Trump later repeated the comments at several campaign appearances, even suggesting his remarks had helped improve Husted's standing in the polls.
Like Trump, Vance is now facing backlash over the odd talking point.
Krystal Ball, a political commentator and podcast host, called it a “tone-deaf moment,” while former NASA astronaut Scott Kelly said the remark was “disgusting, but not surprising.”
The official X account for California Governor Gavin Newsom Press Office simply reacted to the clip with three question marks, while former Trump White House Press Secretary Sarah Matthews wrote: “I genuinely cannot believe this is a real exchange between a voter and the Vice President of the United States.”

articles.summary: New Jersey governor threatens to block delivery of Russian diesel cargoes  Financial TimesSix oil tankers carrying 268,000 tonnes of Russian diesel sail towards US  The GuardianRussia plans to export 2.15 million tons of diesel in November, media say  ReutersDemocrat governor threatens to block Putin’s diesel shipments  The TelegraphThree Russian diesel tankers steam for US — including two under sanctions  Financial Times

Your guide to what Trump’s second term means for Washington, business and the world
The governor of New Jersey is weighing measures to block tankers laden with Russian diesel from offloading their cargoes in the state, which hosts the largest petroleum distribution and import hub on the US east coast.
Mikie Sherrill told the FT that Donald Trump’s deal with Vladimir Putin would line the pockets of the Russian president at the “expense of American consumers and our democratic ally Ukraine”.
“Donald Trump isn’t doing anything to bring down [petrol] prices, diesel prices or costs,” she said. “Trump’s diesel deal with Putin is corrupt and illegal, and I am evaluating options to stop it from arriving at a port in New Jersey.”
Her comments come as three tankers — including one blacklisted by the US and another blacklisted by the EU — are scheduled to arrive at American ports just days after the midterm elections. The combined shipments of about 140,000 tonnes are the first licensed by US authorities under the president’s recent deal to exempt Russian diesel from sanctions in an attempt to quell soaring US fuel prices and help Republicans retain control of Congress.
The vessels departed from St Petersburg earlier this month following Trump’s announcement of the agreement on October 9. One, the Agioi Fanendes, was originally signalling New York as its destination but its owner, Eastern Mediterranean Maritime, told the FT it was now “proceeding for orders as discharging port is not confirmed yet”. It is on a route through the north Atlantic Ocean towards the US.
If a ship signals “for orders” it means it is awaiting further instructions from its owner or charterer.
The other two ships are a Russian-owned tanker Talisman, which has just passed through the English Channel, and the Hong Kong-owned tanker Leruo, which has followed Agioi Fanendes through the North Sea. Talisman is sanctioned by European and US authorities, while Leruo is blacklisted by the EU, UK and Canada. Both have signals for “Atlantic Coast”.
Neither of the owners could be reached for comment.
Trump’s diesel deal with Putin has provoked a ferocious backlash from Democrat politicians and some Republicans, who have called on the US president to rescind it, warning it could be illegal. The US Treasury has issued a general licence that it says temporarily authorises transactions for Russian diesel but Democrats allege it is not legally valid because Congress passed the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act in 2022. 
Claire McCleskey, partner at Clarity Consulting Compliance and an ex-Treasury official, said there was “a lot of scrutiny on these shipments, so some companies won’t touch this from a purely reputational risk perspective”, but others may do it to be in position if Trump does more energy deals with Russia after the election. 
“Besides the Russians, companies outside the US, EU and UK are the biggest winners — they can now move Russian diesel to third countries without fear of US sanctions,” she added.
On Monday senior Democrats and a single Republican senator, Thom Tillis, warned US businesses they would face investigation if they facilitated the import of Russian diesel into the US. On Tuesday Richard Blumenthal, a Democratic senator and member of the Senate armed services committee, wrote to two shipping companies that own tankers carrying Russian diesel to the US, demanding they recall the vessels that intended to ship fuel for “illegal delivery”.
It remains unclear what powers Sherrill has to block tankers arriving at New Jersey’s ports but her threat adds to pressure on businesses, which are being encouraged by the Trump administration to handle and purchase the diesel.
Legal experts have said the arrival of a tanker sanctioned by Washington and other western authorities at a US port would be highly problematic.
The port of New York and New Jersey is the dominant petroleum import, storage and distribution centre on the US east coast, with most of its petroleum infrastructure concentrated on the New Jersey side of New York Harbour.
Its main facilities include Bayonne and Linden, which are major petroleum storage terminals, pipelines and distribution infrastructure. Diesel tankers typically discharge cargoes at privately operated petroleum terminals at Bayonne, Linden, Carteret, Perth Amboy, Port Reading and Sewaren.
Oil industry sources said the White House had reached out to trading companies and others in the sector willing to purchase and handle the diesel but without much interest.
Rapidan Energy Group said in a note: “Several Russian diesel cargoes are signalling the US as their destination, but we see little buyer interest so far, even among grey-market traders, given the legal, political and reputational risks associated with the transaction.”
“Our sense is that no one has bitten yet, despite offers of steep discounts. Moscow and Washington are still scrambling to find takers, but we wouldn’t be surprised if the cargoes ultimately head to Brazil.”

articles.summary: Russian drone attack on Ukrainian train station kills at least 14, officials say  BBCRussian drone strike kills 14 on Ukrainian rail platform, 6 die in other attacks  ReutersRussia strikes Dnipro train station in central Ukraine, killing 15  CNNUkraine war briefing: Outrage in Europe after Russian drone kills 14 on rail platform in Dnipro  The Guardian20 Dead in Russian Strikes—Ukraine Convenes Emergency UN Meeting and Demands Russia Out  UNITED2...
articles.full_text:
At least 14 people have been killed after a Russian jet-powered drone hit a crowded platform at the main railway station in the central Ukrainian city of Dnipro, local officials have said.
Dnipropetrovsk regional head Oleksandr Hanzha said at least 14 others were wounded in the attack, including an 11-year-old boy.
Ukraine's state railway operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, said a passenger train headed for the southern city of Zaporizhzhia was at one of the platforms in Dnipro when the drone hit.
Russia's military has not publicly commented. It has repeatedly hit Ukraine's large railway network, but Moscow denies deliberately targeting civilians.
In Dnipro, an elevated threat level was announced ahead of Thursday's strike, according to the railway operator chief, Oleksandr Pertsovsky.
"But unfortunately there were still a large number of people on the platform" when the drone struck, he said.
Dnipro Mayor Borys Filatov said the incident was a tragedy, adding that a drone hit an electric civilian train.
Pictures from the Ukrainian rescue services show a large hole in a platform that is strewn with blurred-out bodies, near a blast-damaged train with smashed windows.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said "the Russians used a drone to attack a platform where a regular commuter train and a regular passenger train were standing."
He called for further US, European and G7 sanctions on Russia and repeated his criticism of a controversial deal that was struck earlier this month between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, which eased some sanctions on Moscow, allowing the US to import Russian diesel.
Elsewhere in Ukraine, two girls aged 15 were killed in a Russian missile attack on the centre of Chernihiv city, in the north of the country, regional head Vyacheslav Chaus said. At least 25 others, including four children, were injured, he added.
A day of mourning has been declared for Chernihiv and Dnipro on Friday.
In the city of Kremenchuk, in the central Poltava region, three people were killed and 28 injured in a Russian drone attack that hit residential buildings and a school, regional head Vitaliy Diakivnych said.
The latest Russian strikes came during efforts to uphold a fragile ceasefire in the besieged city of Oleshky, which has been under Russian occupation since 2022 and where residents have been trapped without food, water, medicine and electricity for years.
Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, wrote on Telegram that the truce was holding into a third day.
Meanwhile, the Kremlin has condemned Ukrainian drone attacks on Moscow whilst the city hosts the Russia-Africa Summit, the Tass news agency has reported. The two-day event is attended by African leaders and government delegations from 48 countries.
The mayor of Moscow said 613 Ukrainian drones were launched overnight towards the region, most of which were shot down during their flight.
Russia's defence ministry has always denied targeting Ukrainian civilians and says its attacks on railways target the infrastructure used to transport military personnel and equipment.
However, the dangers to passengers are very real, and attacks on Ukraine's train infrastructure have risen sharply.
Of the 521 locomotives hit since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, almost 60% have been hit this year, according to statistics released by Ukrzaliznytsia supplied to AFP news agency.
Overall attacks on railway facilities have risen from 1,206 in 2025 to 1,700 so far this year.
There appears to have been a wider assault on Ukraine's infrastructure in recent weeks, with two bridges attacked in the capital Kyiv, and a metro train hit during one of the strikes.

“During terrorist attacks on the civilian infrastructure of our region and country, the despicable enemy in Kyiv launched a record number of drones,” Samara region Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev wrote in a post on VKontakte.
He said emergency personnel were responding to damage caused by the airstrikes, as videos circulating on social media showed large plumes of black smoke rising from multiple buildings. Fedorishchev did not say which sites were struck.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reportedly told journalists that “our guys tried to be a little more careful during these days,” but added that they were not explicitly told to avoid hitting Russian refineries.

articles.summary: Iran hits Hormuz tanker with limpet mines in apparent tactical shift  Financial TimesIran war live: 4 tankers hit in Hormuz; Trump says conflict will end soon  Al JazeeraOman navy evacuates 25 crew from vessel off Musandam  ReutersIran’s Revolutionary Guard reports three tankers on fire in Strait of Hormuz as talks continue  Euronews.comIran claims four tankers struck mines in Hormuz as strike fears grow after U.S. midterms  CNBC

Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
Iranians in a small speedboat have attacked a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz by attaching limpet mines to the hull for the first time since 2019, suggesting a change in tactics by Tehran as it confronts the threat of fresh US and Israeli military strikes.
The Louise 1, a Dubai-owned tanker, was transiting the contested waterway when it was approached by a small craft at about 10.15pm local time on Thursday night, according to reports from two maritime security companies and UK Maritime Trade Operations.
People on the boat attached “two explosive devices” to the hull above the waterline, which detonated and caused a fire in the engine room, UKMTO said.
The tanker continued to the anchorage off Khor Fakkan on the United Arab Emirates’ south coast, ship-tracking data showed.
Such explosive devices are known as limpet mines, after the limpet shellfish that cling to rocks on the seashore. Three marine security directors told the FT that this was the first time limpet mines had been used against shipping in the Middle East since June 2019, when a Japanese ship and a Norwegian one were attacked with limpet mines in the Gulf of Oman.
In May 2019, four vessels were attacked using limpet mines while at anchor off Fujairah.
At the time, tensions between Iran and the west were high following US President Donald Trump’s decision in 2018 to reinstate sanctions against Iran’s nuclear programme and withdraw from the Iran nuclear deal.
The renewed use of the explosive devices is part of an intensified campaign by Iran to disrupt shipping. Tankers continue to pass through the strait carrying oil for export from Gulf producers, albeit at levels far below what they were before the start of the latest war launched by the US and Israel.
Exports via the strait were 8.7mn barrels a day over the seven days to October 29, according to data from commodities platform Kpler, about 51 per cent below the pre-conflict baseline. The number of vessels that used to pass through Hormuz has fallen sharply from the 135 before the war because of the threat to shipping, which has increased as the US approaches its midterm elections next week.
Trump has warned Middle Eastern allies to prepare for a possible military campaign and fresh strikes against Iran following the vote.
“If Iran is bringing limpet mines back out of the wardrobe I would be worried for ships across the Gulf,” said Martin Kelly, chief executive of the maritime security consultancy Orbital Risk Intelligence, who is advising three ships due to pass through the strait this weekend.
Kelly said that Iran was “doing everything they can to stop ships getting through”, including issuing false information campaigns about ships being hit by mines, increasing the geographical area in which its forces attack ships and increasing the tempo of strikes.
The first two weeks of October were the heaviest period of strikes against shipping since the war began.
“Shipowners will begin to say, ‘shit, there are now limpet mines, we’re not going through’,” he said, adding that ships in local anchorages could be particularly at risk.
Iran has also used cruise missiles against shipping in recent weeks, as well as using drones to target the vessels’ funnels, because that increases the damage by focusing the blast on a part of the ship connected to the engine room, maritime security experts said.
Because most ships are sailing through Omani territorial waters, they are not permitted to have armed guards on board but typically sail with response officers from security consultancies on the bridge who advise crews as they transit the strait.
Dubai’s PRY Shipping, the owner of Louise 1, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Another tanker and a dhow in the strait suffered fires on Thursday after being hit by missiles.

The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen has reported that it intercepted a drone launched by the Houthis towards Saudi Arabia’s Mecca region.
The drone was “intercepted and destroyed” on Friday morning, coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said in a social media post. It was also reported that a missile aimed at western Saudi Arabia was earlier brought down, as hostilities between the Riyadh-backed Yemen government and Iran-backed Houthis continue to escalate.
A Houthi spokesperson denied targeting the Muslim holy city or surrounding region, reiterating that the group’s cross-border attacks remain strictly focused on Saudi energy and military infrastructure.
The Saudi-led coalition has previously accused the Houthis of launching drones towards Islam’s two holiest cities: Mecca and Medina.
“Our operations target [Saudi] oil facilities and military bases, and there is no longer anyone in this world who believes these fabrications and lies propagated by the criminal Al Saud regime,” the Houthi spokesman wrote.
Escalating hostilities
The opposing claims come as hostilities continue with no sign of slowing, and humanitarian agencies warn of worsening conditions for civilians.
On Thursday, the Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis towards the kingdom’s eastern region. It later said two ballistic missiles launched towards the Saudi capital, Riyadh, were also intercepted and destroyed.
Al-Malki reported early on Friday that the coalition’s air defences intercepted and destroyed a Houthi cruise missile that targeted western Saudi Arabia.
Media outlets affiliated with the Houthis reported later that coalition air attacks were targeting the Mahliyah district in Marib, Haifan in Taiz, and Huwaishan in al-Jawf in the country.
Al Jazeera Arabic’s Hadeel al-Yamani reported from Taiz that fighting along the front lines was persisting.
The governor of Taiz said the city was suffering heavy shelling, with residential neighbourhoods taking hits.
“Aircraft can be heard frequently over the city, which remains under a suffocating siege, with no medical supplies, water or fuel getting in,” al-Yamani reported.
“On the western front, there were intermittent clashes around dawn. The northern fronts were relatively calm, but still saw sporadic fighting. There has been a notable escalation in hostilities around Jabal Saber and Jabal Habashi,” he said.

articles.title: Kim Jong Un attends a North Korean drone exhibition and calls for boosting the technology - AP News
articles.summary: Kim Jong Un attends a North Korean drone exhibition and calls for boosting the technology  AP NewsNorth Korea's Kim urges drone dominance, greater military AI use amid border tensions  ReutersNorth Korea fires missile barrage toward the sea as tensions with South rise  AP NewsNorth Korea tests attack drones as Kim calls for 'absolute superiority'  France 24North Korea’s Kim calls for rapid expansion of drone technology and observes weapons tests &nbsp...
articles.full_text:
SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — North Korean leader Kim Jong Un attended an exhibition devoted to drones and called for rapidly expanding the country’s drone technology, state media reported Friday, as his military escalates threats against South Korea and the U.S.
Acquiring advanced drones is a top priority for Kim, who now wants to strengthen conventional and nuclear capabilities to counter what he calls U.S.-led security threats.
It’s unclear how far North Korea’s drone program has progressed. Experts say Kim’s troops sent to Russia to support its war against Ukraine likely gained experience in drone warfare from Russian forces and their own battlefield experiences.
Exhibition highlights Kim’s focus on drone program
The North’s official Korean Central News Agency said Kim visited the exhibition Thursday, viewing attack drones and other models that it said show recent achievements in drone technology. In a speech there, Kim announced unspecified steps needed to “rapidly expand and strengthen the unmanned aeronautical technology,” KCNA said.
South Korea’s Unification Ministry said it appeared to be North Korea’s first exhibition exclusively dedicated to drones. South Korean media reported the exhibition displayed more than 30 kinds of drones, including stealth drones and first-person-view attack drones.
In an analysis for the North Korea-focused 38 North website in September 2025, analyst Martyn Williams said the country’s drone program dates back to at least 2011 and that “further drone development and deployment should be expected as the country works to enhance preparedness for modern warfare.”
“The use of drones has been critical in the wars currently being fought in Europe and the Middle East. This trend is likely to ring true for future conflicts — a lesson that all countries are learning, including North Korea,” Williams wrote.
South Korea’s state-run Institute for National Security Strategy said in a report last year that Russian assistance could help North Korea overcome technological and industrial limitations on its drone program.
Kim observes weapons tests alongside his daughter
To mark the event, KCNA said North Korea tested various drones, missiles and 600 mm-caliber ultraprecision multiple rocket launchers.
KCNA photos showed Kim watching soaring weapons and clenching his fist while his teenage daughter stood beside him and clapped. South Korea’s spy agency believes the girl, reportedly about 13, is Kim’s designated heir.
South Korea’s military said it detected the launches of about 10 short-range ballistic missiles off the North’s east coast Thursday.
Tensions between the two Koreas have been high since mine blasts at their border last month wounded three South Korean soldiers. Seoul accused North Korea of burying the mines south of the military demarcation line and demanded an apology. Pyongyang has denied responsibility for the explosions and warned of retaliation if provoked.
Last week, North Korea threatened to resume propaganda loudspeaker broadcasts and place new weapons systems along the border.
North Korea’s Defense Ministry on Friday condemned a joint U.S.-South Korea air exercise as “provocative” and warned it was increasing the danger of an armed conflict. South Korea’s military has said the two-week biannual Freedom Flag drill was to run until Nov. 6 and was meant to improve combined operational capabilities. It said fighter jets, helicopters and drones would take part.
North Korea pulled out of talks with the U.S. and South Korea after Kim’s high-stakes diplomacy with U.S. President Donald Trump collapsed in 2019. In recent weeks, North Korea has dialed up weapons testing activities in a likely attempt to boost its leverage in potential diplomacy with the U.S. after Trump expressed his eagerness to restore talks with Kim.
Meanwhile, Switzerland’s Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis arrived in North Korea on Thursday for the reopening of Switzerland’s diplomatic office in Pyongyang. He also met with North Korean Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui and discussed promoting dialogue between the countries, KCNA said Saturday.

articles.title: The Backdoor to American Innovation
articles.summary: How military partnerships make Washington vulnerable to its adversaries.
articles.full_text:
In late May, a shipment of F-35 stealth fighter jet parts heading for the United States from Australia was misrouted to Hong Kong and into Chinese hands. Since 2007, Chinese intelligence operatives and their proxies had been stealing data to do with the F-35. Now, some of the jet’s closely guarded components, including a cockpit canopy and weapons-bay door, had landed on Chinese soil—handing Beijing stealth technology that only the United States and its allies have access to. China will surely attempt to reverse-engineer the technologies it was lucky to acquire. U.S. officials do not believe there was foul play here and they think the delivery was likely an accident: the result of a shipping delay and a missed email. But even without active foreign interference, the mere logistics of coordinating F-35 production and delivery among Washington, Canberra, Lockheed Martin, and a third-party shipping company exposed defense secrets to the greatest U.S. rival.
The U.S. defense industrial base—the network of domestic and international companies and organizations responsible for the research, production, delivery, and maintenance that undergird American military operations—is growing at a pace not seen in decades, as Washington seeks to place arms manufacturing back on a “wartime footing,” in the words of U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The United States is working with allies, notably in the Indo-Pacific, to expand military production and make supply chains resilient to shocks. South Korea has begun performing maintenance and repairs on U.S. naval vessels, Japan is set to quadruple its production of vital antiballistic missiles, and American Precision Strike Missiles will soon be rolling off assembly lines in Australia.
Although this expansion is sensible and necessary, it also carries significant risks. As the U.S. defense base spreads, it becomes more exposed to espionage, theft, and sabotage.
Since the Cold War, U.S. adversaries have targeted the research and infrastructure that give the United States its military advantage. Now, the likes of Russia, China, and North Korea can also learn about American capabilities by mounting espionage campaigns against U.S. allies. Because the U.S. military is more dependent on supply chains that snake around the world, it has become more vulnerable to the disruptive actions of hostile powers.
If the United States fails to safeguard its deepening military partnerships, adversaries will have more opportunities than ever before to at once undermine American defenses and improve their own militaries. Washington must help its partners raise their security standards, share intelligence and best practices more widely, and fortify monitoring programs. If pursued judiciously, this emphasis on security will not hinder cooperation between the United States and its allies but rather strengthen it. But if the United States does not address this threat, one of the country’s great advantages will become a perilous weakness.
BACK ON BASE
In the 1990s, the United States began working more closely with allies to bolster defense production and supply chains amid post–Cold War cuts to military spending. Washington established the National Technology and Industrial Base in 1993, a policy framework that institutionalized cooperation between U.S. and Canadian defense companies. In the following decades, the United Kingdom, Australia, and New Zealand were added to the agreement. But until recently, a number of legal, bureaucratic, and cultural barriers among the five countries hampered this partnership, keeping it from fulfilling its potential.
Over the last five years, however, Washington’s efforts to expand its defense base have begun to speed up. In 2021, the trilateral AUKUS security pact between the United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia—in which the three countries pledged to work together to produce advanced military technologies, including nuclear-powered submarines—was a milestone for defense industrial cooperation. In the 2023 National Defense Industrial Strategy, Washington outlined its commitment to further collaboration with allies, arguing that “the global activity of pacing threats increasingly requires a global approach to defense industrial relationships, concerns, and competition.”
The next year, the United States helped launch the Partnership for Indo-Pacific Industrial Resilience, a forum that brings together some Western and Asian countries to coordinate defense manufacturing and protect important supply chains. Washington has supplemented these multilateral initiatives with bilateral defense production agreements, including pacts with Australia, Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan to partner on critical defense systems, missile production, and shipbuilding. The United States is also planning to accelerate collaboration with India, Indonesia, and the Philippines. Washington has a growing appetite for defense industrial cooperation in the Indo-Pacific, and its partnerships there can thrive—as long as they can be adequately secured.
SPY HEAVEN
States have long used espionage to gauge enemy weaknesses and steal cutting-edge technologies. They have also executed sabotage operations to disrupt opponents’ supply chains and hinder their battlefield performance. The Soviet Union, for instance, gained nuclear weapons in part by penetrating the Manhattan Project; more recently, China stole secrets related to the F-22 and F-35 stealth fighter jets and the C-17 cargo plane. Galloping advances in technology invite subterfuge and theft. New breakthroughs in artificial intelligence and quantum computing could have strategic implications on par with the atomic bomb, and U.S. rivals are tenacious in seeking to acquire such technologies themselves.
Today, the American defense base is “under a state of constant, multivector siege” in cyberspace, according to a February report by the Google Threat Intelligence Group. U.S. adversaries are working to steal sensitive information, trade secrets, and intellectual property at every possible level, from recruiting individual employees to hacking manufacturers’ IT networks.
In addition to staging digital attacks, foreign governments such as China and North Korea are cultivating sources inside firms and research institutions focused on defense and dual-use innovation. Governments hostile to the United States, notably China, have sought to establish seemingly legitimate business and academic relationships to gain access to proprietary information. A September 2025 report from the U.S. House Select Committee on China found more than 100 academic partnerships between American universities and Chinese entities that pose a national security risk. State-sponsored actors have also embedded themselves inside American firms and research departments; for instance, North Korean remote IT workers in 2024 infiltrated a U.S. defense contractor and stole data about export-controlled technology. Perhaps most strikingly, U.S. adversaries have used foreign investment, mergers, and even the acquisition of entire companies—sometimes using subsidiaries to mask their involvement—to gain control of critical dual-use technologies. The Times reported that the 2008 buyout of the British-based Dynex Semiconductor by a subsidiary of a Chinese state-owned railway company, for example, gave the Chinese navy access to technology crucial to developing rail guns and electromagnetic launch systems for aircraft carriers.

As the United States has deepened its defense cooperation efforts in the Indo-Pacific, China and North Korea have increasingly targeted U.S. allies in the region. In 2024, South Korea’s National Police Agency revealed that North Korean hackers had mounted all-out cyberattacks against South Korean defense companies for over a year, breaching their networks and stealing technical data. Last January, the agency reported a 40 percent increase in illegal technology transfer cases—that is, of insiders leaking proprietary information on critical technologies to do with semiconductors, batteries, and shipbuilding. Many of those leaks were connected to China.
Japan, which the KGB nicknamed “spy heaven” during the Cold War, remains a hub for espionage. A July New York Times investigation found that members of a Tokyo-based Russian military intelligence unit called the 20th Directorate have spent years posing as diplomats and businesspeople to help Moscow acquire defense technologies that it is banned from importing. This equipment—which includes Japanese components used to guide Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles—has been essential to Russia’s war effort in Ukraine. From 2019 to 2024, the Chinese hacking group MirrorFace conducted over 200 cyberattacks against Japanese defense, national security, and advanced technology targets. And in February 2025, the Japanese military discovered that some of its members had unknowingly circulated for over a year USB sticks that carried malware used by Chinese hacker groups.
In Australia, U.S. adversaries have worked to infiltrate AUKUS in a number of ways. Last year, the Iranian-backed Cyber Toufan hacker group mounted a series of cyberattacks on Israeli defense contractors that gave it access to sensitive material on Australian weapons programs, including the multibillion-dollar Redback infantry fighting vehicle. Mike Burgess, the director general of Australia’s domestic intelligence service, has repeatedly warned that Australia has become a priority espionage mark where “defense personnel are being targeted in person and online.” In 2024, Burgess revealed that a spy ring run by an unspecified foreign government, referred to as “the A-team,” had cultivated and recruited a former Australian politician to assist them. articles.title: How to Secure the Straits
articles.summary: Why Iran and the Houthis keep winning the waterways.
articles.full_text:
Over the past month, Iran has made its most intense attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz since the United States and Israel declared war, in February. More than 100 drone and missile launches into the strait have been recorded since the war began; in October alone, a container ship and a bulk vessel sank in the waterway. Meanwhile, in the Red Sea, Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis have sustained their campaign to throttle seaborne trade as they target Saudi Arabia more directly, seizing new territory along the Bab el Mandeb Strait.
These dual maritime crises form part of the same strategic problem—one that, despite its new intensity, has existed for years. In 2019, Iran attacked shipping across the Gulf in response to the first Trump administration’s maximum-pressure sanctions campaign; in 2023, the Houthis launched assaults in the Red Sea following Hamas’s October 7 massacre in Israel. After each of these campaigns, the United States and its partners established maritime coalitions to protect these vital seaborne trade routes. The efforts helped secure the waterways, but they never fundamentally persuaded Iran and its proxies that asymmetric attacks on shipping were an ineffective way to project power. On the contrary, such tactics have only become more appealing to Tehran.
Even now, some shipping persists through both waterways. On October 15, Lloyd’s List Intelligence reported that transit through the Bab el Mandeb Strait was up modestly from August. U.S. naval patrols—as well as creative logistical adaptation by Gulf states, including ship-to-ship transfers, have allowed some oil to move through Hormuz. But shipping still remains throttled, and international actors have not yet found a way to update their deterrence playbook. In 2019 and 2023–24, U.S., European, and Middle Eastern navies formed separate, overlapping defensive maritime coalitions to escort vessels, collect intelligence on evolving threats, and intercept missile and drone attacks. In the United States’ case in 2024, a separate multinational coalition also conducted offensive strikes in Yemen to undermine Houthi maritime capabilities. Today, governments are falling back on the same instinct—to join forces, but not all their forces. The British and the French have proposed a multinational maritime defense coalition to secure the Strait of Hormuz once the war ends, while Saudi Arabia is planning, but has not yet deployed, its own alliance to protect the Red Sea. Neither project includes the United States, which has deployed nearly one-third of its naval warships to the Middle East in an attempt to reestablish freedom of navigation, enforce a naval blockade against Iran, and support U.S. attacks on Iran.
Multiple short-term, insufficiently coordinated defensive missions organized around voluntary contributions can buy down marginal risk for shippers in the near-term but they cannot deliver long-term deterrence. Separate missions embolden Iranian and Houthi leaders, who will interpret them as half-measures that are easily strained by resource scarcity, an inability to adapt quickly to evolving threats, and the absence of real-time intelligence sharing across the two chokepoints. As crises in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea become more linked amid an expanding regional war, replicating the patchwork maritime strategy that never fully worked would be a serious mistake. What is needed instead is a single, sustained multinational effort to secure both waterways that combines American military capabilities with the imprimatur of a unified coalition of Asian, European, and Middle Eastern countries. Otherwise, Iran and the Houthis will again learn that threatening global commerce in maritime chokepoints is a strategy worth repeating.
OVERLAPPING, UNDERPERFORMING
The maritime coalitions now taking shape share a troubling precedent. Twice before, international actors have mounted similar efforts, and their mixed results show why even effective defensive operations fail to prevent renewed attacks in Middle Eastern waterways. In mid-2019, after the first Trump administration launched its “maximum pressure” sanctions campaign against Iran, Tehran attacked tankers off the coast of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and in the Gulf of Oman and seized a British-flagged oil tanker from international waters in the Strait of Hormuz. Insurance premiums spiked tenfold, and freight rates for crude-oil-carrying tankers jumped nearly 40 percent. In response, Washington established the International Maritime Security Construct (IMSC), headquartered in Bahrain; the mission sought to maintain naval vessels across key waterways in the Middle East to deter Iran and collect intelligence on Iranian maritime activities to share with commercial shippers.
By the end of 2019, Albania, Australia, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and the United Kingdom had joined the IMSC. But despite Washington’s efforts to expand the coalition further, most European countries abstained from joining. They were frustrated with the Trump administration’s withdrawal from the 2015 nuclear deal with Tehran and wary that joining the IMSC—with its focus on confronting Iran—would be seen by Tehran as aggressive or an endorsement of Washington’s maximum pressure campaign. Instead, eight European countries joined a French-led mission called European Maritime Awareness in the Strait of Hormuz (EMASoH), which emphasized de-escalation, surveillance, and encouraging regional dialogue with Iran.
Four years later, when the Houthis began to threaten shipping in the Red Sea—spiking maritime insurance rates and forcing vessels to detour around the Cape of Good Hope—the United States and Europe once again organized separate responses. In December 2023, the United States launched Operational Prosperity Guardian (OPG), a naval coalition soon joined by more than 20 countries. The mission maintained four to eight warships in the Red Sea area at any given time and successfully shot down Houthi drones and missiles; within its first month, its leaders said it had facilitated safe transit for more than a thousand commercial vessels. The European Union formed its own, substantially smaller defensive maritime operation that escorted European commercial vessels through the southern Red Sea and also intercepted Houthi drone and missile attacks.
In both crises, the United States, Europe, and the Gulf states broadly agreed that Iranian and Houthi threats to freedom of navigation required a response. Because freedom of navigation was viewed as a fundamental principle of the global order, assembling large groups committed to upholding this pillar was intended to demonstrate international resolve and isolate the bad actor. But disagreement over how to confront the challenge diluted the missions. Many governments declined to join offensive strikes or coalitions explicitly directed at a state. Political divides further splintered the response, as Europe sought to put distance between itself and the United States’ Iran strategy.
The 2019–24 missions achieved important tactical successes by improving maritime awareness, intercepting some attacks, and stopping a complete shutdown of shipping. But the lack of a long-term, coordinated strategy for ending Iran’s aggression weakened the response. The missions never fully persuaded shippers that these waterways were safe—especially the Red Sea—or prevented Iran and the Houthis from eventually returning to their efforts to exploit the chokepoints. According to a 2021 assessment by the Dutch government, the Netherlands assumed that Iran could differentiate between the European maritime mission and the American-led one and would be less aggressive toward European vessels, underscoring Tehran’s ability to exploit the gaps between overlapping operations and the need for a unified front.
GREATER THAN THE SUM OF ITS PARTS
The lessons from these missions matter enormously today. After years of shadow warfare, the United States and Israel have now fought Iran directly. In 2025, the United States and Israel also launched separate months-long campaigns against the Houthis in Yemen, following a decadelong Saudi-led effort to dislodge the rebel group. These campaigns badly battered Iran and the Houthis. But they also gave them a chance to hone their asymmetric tactics. Having survived wars intended to collapse their regimes, Iran and the Houthis have emerged more willing to hold global commerce at risk and impose costs on actors not directly involved in the wars against them. Both have learned that they do not need to fully close maritime chokepoints. Simply threatening them can change decision-making in the halls of power.
Nobody wants tolls or unilaterally imposed service payments on these waterways, proposals that Iran has tabled. Instead, to try to deal with the crises, there has been a flowering of disjointed maritime coalition planning efforts. The British-French plan resembles previous European maritime efforts, proposing a defensive multinational mission to escort vessels. It excludes the United States and will not activate until the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran ends for good—a condition that essentially guarantees its uselessness in the near term. Houthi aggression, meanwhile, has sent Saudi Arabia scrambling to secure Red Sea transit, which is increasingly vital given disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. In late July, Riyadh announced the formation of its own defensive maritime coalition with 14 countries from across Africa and the Middle East, as well as Bangladesh and Pakistan, which will be distinct from both European efforts on Hormuz and the U.S. mission. The United States has put up its own military effort to secure Gulf waterways focused on escorting vessels through Omani waters and actively defending commercial shippers from daily Iranian attacks. Concurrently, the U.S. Navy is enforcing a naval blockade against Iranian ports and disabling tankers that ignore its warnings.

articles.title: North Korea’s Enemies Within
articles.summary: How long will elites stay loyal to Kim Jong Un?
articles.full_text:
In 2015, the North Korean diplomat Thae Yong Ho received an unusual assignment. Kim Jong Chol, the older brother of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, was coming to London to attend an Eric Clapton concert, and Thae, who was then stationed in London, was assigned to look after him. Providing direct service to the ruling family confers honor on North Korean officials and their households, so Thae expected his two sons to be impressed.
To Thae’s surprise, his sons were outraged. Ordinary North Koreans could be expelled from university (or worse) for listening to Western music, they told him. And now the Kim family was spending thousands of dollars in a single evening to enjoy entertainment forbidden to all other North Koreans. In the eyes of his children, Thae later wrote in his memoir, Password to the Third Floor, he was a prisoner forced to take care of a prison warden. Their reaction left him ashamed.
The next year, Thae, his wife, and their sons escaped to South Korea. His defection surprised the international community. Only weeks earlier, Thae had been defending the North Korean regime with great fervor. Yet this incongruous behavior is familiar to those who understand life among North Korea’s elite: officials can profess full devotion to the Kim family right until the day they run.
The gap between public conduct and private belief is difficult to observe from the outside. For over a decade, I interviewed dozens of former diplomats, Korean Workers’ Party cadres, military officers, businesspeople, and technicians, all of whom had lived, studied, or worked in Pyongyang. These people ran the party, military, embassies, foreign-currency businesses, and technical programs on which the state depends for its survival. They received the best education, housing, food, and access to influential social networks their country could provide. Some once believed sincerely in the system; others learned early that loyalty was a role they had to pantomime in a nationwide, lifelong performance—now with Kim Jong Un as the maestro. Nearly all described an elite class under growing strain.
Since Kim Jong Un came to power in December 2011, he has tightened his grip on the country’s elites by carrying out sweeping purges of the old guard of senior party officials and military officers and executing others for minor political missteps. Many members of North Korea’s elite fear that they or their families can be killed at the drop of a hat. And their escape routes are narrowing; since Kim sealed off the borders during the COVID-19 pandemic, the number of North Korean defectors reaching South Korea has plummeted.
Those North Koreans who still manage to escape increasingly come from the elite. As of August 2024, South Korea’s National Intelligence Service reported that the number of defections from North Korea’s upper class recorded under Kim Jong Un was two and a half times the combined total observed during the reigns of Kim Il Sung (1948 to 1994) and Kim Jong Il (1994 to 2011). The absolute number remains small—in the hundreds—and it would be a mistake to interpret this trend as a harbinger of imminent regime collapse. North Korea is remarkably effective at preventing private grievances from becoming organized opposition. The regime does not need every official to believe in it. But it needs its doubters to feel isolated and alone in their skepticism and disillusionment.
North Korea has long been referred to as the “Hermit Kingdom,” but that term offers the wrong impression of the country. It is not totally isolated from the world. It is a nuclear-armed state with diplomatic relations with over 160 countries, and it has the world’s fourth-largest standing army and highly skilled cyber-operators. The vast majority of the population may be fed a robust diet of state propaganda, but most elites are exposed to life outside North Korea. They have a reasonable sense of how the world works and their country’s place in it. And yet they have to live with intense cognitive dissonance, at once understanding the real world and having to create, enforce, and trumpet the state’s official narratives to their countrymen and foreigners.
Many high-ranking North Koreans are finding it harder to sustain this balancing act. Access to privilege can purchase compliance—and terror can enforce it—but the state will not give elites what they increasingly want: guaranteed security for them and their families and a viable future for their children. Kim can allay some frustrations by doling out luxury apartments, promotions, and access to extravagant lifestyles. He cannot address the deeper sources of discontent without relaxing the very controls that protect his family’s rule from challenges to its power. The regime remains capable of suppressing any organized resistance in the country, but the growing disaffection of the elite threatens to weaken the state from within. Kim presides over a system increasingly marked by doubt, suspicion, and pervasive anxiety. When the chips are down and North Korea faces a true crisis, its most powerful leaders may not know who they can trust and where they can turn.
TOO CLOSE TO THE SUN
Most of the more than 34,000 North Koreans now living in South Korea came from the poor northern provinces along the Chinese border. Many of them fled to the south to escape famine and economic hardship. They had little access to the regime’s inner workings, even if they had tremendous experience of its cruelty and depredations. In contrast, elite escapees come from a wholly different world. They are products of Pyongyang, a capital of roughly three million that is closed to most of the country’s 25 million citizens. They grew up with relatively reliable electricity and running water, and attended schools designed to educate the next generation of regime operators. They benefited from the new construction of luxury residential districts, extravagant resort towns such as Samjiyon and Wonsan-Kalma, and the country’s sustained economic growth in the face of heavy international sanctions. North Korea’s elite serve in a range of occupations beyond just the party cadre ranks, the military, and the security services; they can be artists, software engineers, restaurant managers, and much else. The regime groomed them from birth to serve the party and the Kim family.
Consider the family of Ri Jong Ho and his son Hyunseung Lee. Ri spent three decades in Office 39, which earns and manages foreign currency for the leadership. Kim Jong Il appointed him to senior trade and economic posts, and in 2002 the state awarded him a Hero of Labor medal and a Kim Il Sung watch, prestigious honors and a recognition of his loyalty and patriotism. Ri’s son attended some of the country’s finest educational institutions, including Kumsong Academy and Pyongyang Foreign Language Institute, which prepare the children of senior cadres to enter high positions in the party. Hyunseung and his sister were also among the rare few North Koreans who were permitted to study abroad in China. By his mid-20s, Hyunseung was already a party member, working in China, and was trusted to chair a branch of the Kim Il Sung Youth League while helping facilitate millions of dollars in trade between Chinese companies and North Korea. This family faithfully served their country while living at the highest echelons of their society and enjoying the best creature comforts. But their privileged positions did not make them safe.
The shocking 2013 execution of Jang Song Thaek, Kim Jong Un’s uncle, unnerved Ri. The slain Jang had been married to Kim Il Sung’s daughter and had served all three Kims. If the regime could eliminate such a decorated official—and a member of the ruling family—and seek to erase him from the country’s history and memory, then no one was untouchable. Ri’s family escaped to South Korea from their posts in China in 2014, and Hyunseung and his sister later earned master’s degrees from Columbia University. Despite the many privileges their family received from the regime, they fled because their proximity to power made them feel deeply vulnerable.
North Koreans live under institutions designed to make independent organization impossible. Party committees operate inside every school, embassy, farm, military unit, office, and factory. Security bureaus obsessively police information flows and political conduct, while neighborhood units monitor every household. Every citizen, starting at a young age, belongs to a state-directed organization. For elites, closeness to power invites suffocating scrutiny; it places them more deeply within the grasp of the state rather than freeing them from the overbearing system.
The Organization and Guidance Department, the party’s most powerful agency, oversees appointments, inspections, and discipline everywhere—in Pyongyang as well as rural villages. No escapee is known to have come from the OGD’s central ranks, an indication of the control imposed on the country’s most influential officials. Diplomats and workers sent abroad must surrender their passports and leave relatives in North Korea as collateral to deter defection. When they come home, they must account for what they saw, heard, and did abroad, enumerate every single political sin they committed, and then undergo extensive ideological deprogramming and reprogramming.
Kim Se Yun (a pseudonym), a former senior party cadre who traveled overseas, described the monthlong central review she underwent every time she returned to Pyongyang. Officials have to “cleanse” themselves of what they have encountered and report even small details, including whether they had gone out drinking with colleagues after dinner. A late night out could require a written piece of self-flagellation to account for a lapse unbecoming of “a devoted worker for the state.” The review was meant to minimize the effects of foreign exposure: a person could see how others lived but, upon returning, had to renounce what she had seen
